# File Summary

## Purpose
This file contains a packed representation of the entire repository's contents.
It is designed to be easily consumable by AI systems for analysis, code review,
or other automated processes.

## File Format
The content is organized as follows:
1. This summary section
2. Repository information
3. Directory structure
4. Multiple file entries, each consisting of:
  a. A header with the file path (## File: path/to/file)
  b. The full contents of the file in a code block

## Usage Guidelines
- This file should be treated as read-only. Any changes should be made to the
  original repository files, not this packed version.
- When processing this file, use the file path to distinguish
  between different files in the repository.
- Be aware that this file may contain sensitive information. Handle it with
  the same level of security as you would the original repository.

## Notes
- Some files may have been excluded based on .gitignore rules and Repomix's configuration
- Binary files are not included in this packed representation. Please refer to the Repository Structure section for a complete list of file paths, including binary files
- Files matching patterns in .gitignore are excluded
- Files matching default ignore patterns are excluded
- Line numbers have been added to the beginning of each line
- Security check has been disabled - content may contain sensitive information
- Files are sorted by Git change count (files with more changes are at the bottom)

 2: 
 3: COPY /demos/setup_tpch.sh setup_tpch.sh
 4: 
 5: # Install uv for command line editing.
 6: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl ca-certificates

 9: 
10: ENV HOME=/root
11: 
12: RUN sh /uv-installer.sh && rm /uv-installer.sh
13: 
14: ENV PATH="/root/.local/bin/:$PATH"
15: 
16: # Download the TPC-H database.
17: RUN ./setup_tpch.sh /usr/local/share/tpch.db

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/.github/workflows/build_pip.yml
````yaml
 1: name: Build PyDough Pip Wheel
 2: 
 3: on:
 4:   workflow_dispatch:
 5:   release:
 6:     types: [published]
 7: 
 8: jobs:
 9:   build_pydough_wheels:
10:     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
11:     permissions:
12:       id-token: write
13:       contents: read
14:     name: Build PyDough Wheels
15: 
16:     steps:
17:       - name: Configure AWS Credentials
18:         uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
19:         with:
20:           aws-region: us-east-2
21:           role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::427443013497:role/PyDoughBuildWheelRole
22:           role-session-name: PyDoughBuildWheelSession
23:           role-skip-session-tagging: true
24: 
25:       - uses: actions/checkout@v4
26: 
27:       - name: Install uv
28:         uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v3
29:         with:
30:           version: "0.4.23"
31: 
32:       - name: Build Wheels
33:         run: |
34:           uv build
35: 
36:       - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
37:         with:
38:           name: pydough-wheel
39:           path: ./dist/*.whl
40: 
41:   test_pydough_wheels:
42:     needs: [build_pydough_wheels]
43:     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
44:     name: Test PyDough Wheels
45: 
46:     strategy:
47:       matrix:
48:         python_version: ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"]
49: 
50:     steps:
51:       - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
52:         id: download-artifact
53:         with:
54:           pattern: pydough-wheel*
55:           path: .
56: 
57:       - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
58:         with:
59:           python-version: ${{ matrix.python_version }}
60: 
61:       - name: Install
62:         run: |
63:           # Install pydough from the local wheel
64:           pip install pydough --find-links "$(find . -name "pydough-wheel*" -print)" --no-index --no-deps
65:           # Install dependencies from pypi
66:           pip install pydough
67:       - name: Test Import
68:         run: |
69:           python -c "import pydough; assert pydough.active_session is not None"
70:       # TODO: Consider a more detailed test of functionality.
71: 
72: 
73:   upload_pydough_wheels:
74:     needs: [build_pydough_wheels, test_pydough_wheels]
75:     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
76:     permissions:
77:       id-token: write
78:     name: Upload PyDough Wheels
79: 
80:     if: github.event_name == 'release' && github.event.action == 'published'
81:     steps:
82:       - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
83:         with:
84:           pattern: pydough-wheel*
85:           path: dist
86:           merge-multiple: true
87: 
88:       - uses: pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/.github/workflows/pr_testing.yml
````yaml
 1: name: PR Testing
 2: 
 3: on:
 4:   pull_request:
 5: 
 6: # Limit CI to cancel previous runs in the same PR
 7: concurrency:
 8:   group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.head_ref || github.ref_name }}
 9:   cancel-in-progress: true
10: 
11: jobs:
12:   get-msg:
13:     name: Get Commit Message
14:     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
15:     outputs:
16:       commitMsg: ${{ steps.get_msg.outputs.commitMsg }}
17:     steps:
18:       # Fetch the branch for the history only
19:       - uses: actions/checkout@v4
20:         with:
21:           ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
22:           sparse-checkout: .
23:       - name: Get Commit Message
24:         id: get_msg
25:         run: |
26:           set -xe pipefail
27:           echo "commitMsg=$(git log -1 --pretty=format:'%s')" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
28: 
29:   run-tests:
30:     strategy:
31:       matrix:
32:         python-version:
33:           - "3.10"
34:           - "3.11"
35:           - "3.12"
36:     needs: [get-msg]
37:     name: python
38:     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
39:     # https://docs.github.com/en/actions/learn-github-actions/expressions#contains
40:     # contains is case-insensitive
41:     if: contains(needs.get-msg.outputs.commitMsg, '[run ci]')
42:     steps:
43:       - name: Checkout code
44:         uses: actions/checkout@v4
45: 
46:       - name: Install uv
47:         uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v3
48:         with:
49:           # Install a specific version of uv.
50:           version: "0.4.23"
51: 
52:       - name: Download TPCH DB
53:         run: ./demos/setup_tpch.sh ./tpch.db
54: 
55:       - name: Run Ruff
56:         run: uv run --python ${{ matrix.python-version }} ruff check .
57: 
58:       - name: Run Tests
59:         run: uv run --python ${{ matrix.python-version }} pytest tests/
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/demos/notebooks/1_introduction.ipynb
````
  1: {
  2:  "cells": [
  3:   {
  4:    "cell_type": "markdown",
  5:    "id": "f1fd4015-5281-4f56-bf88-5db4a8de93e0",
  6:    "metadata": {},
  7:    "source": [
  8:     "# Introduction\n",
  9:     "\n",
 10:     "Welcome to the PyDough demos. PyDough is a new Python compatible DSL that leverages a rich document model to simplify analytics queries. PyDough's goal is to enable \"WHAT-IF\" style question by making it easier to reuse previous question components and improve iteration speed by making it both faster to construct a query and easier to debug.  \n",
 11:     "\n",
 12:     "This notebook is intended to explain the structure of the PyDough notebook and the fundamental operations. At the end we will link to followup notebooks to will explain how to use PyDough in more detail."
 13:    ]
 14:   },
 15:   {
 16:    "cell_type": "code",
 17:    "execution_count": null,
 18:    "id": "0850592d-e6eb-4905-8291-21056617fc74",
 19:    "metadata": {},
 20:    "outputs": [],
 21:    "source": [
 22:     "import pydough"
 23:    ]
 24:   },
 25:   {
 26:    "cell_type": "markdown",
 27:    "id": "e7dfb2db-191d-4dac-8b88-76aea581f167",
 28:    "metadata": {},
 29:    "source": [
 30:     "## Metadata Setup\n",
 31:     "\n",
 32:     "PyDough simplifies the query writing experience by leveraging a metadata describing the relevant tables and their relationships. For these demos we will provide all metadata for you, but future demos may walk through the metadata creation process. A followup notebook will provide you a deeper look into the inner workings of the metadata.\n",
 33:     "\n",
 34:     "To setup the metadata, the PyDough `active_session` is used. This is a simple class to encapsulate configuration information. To attach our metadata graph, we can use:"
 35:    ]
 36:   },
 37:   {
 38:    "cell_type": "code",
 39:    "execution_count": null,
 40:    "id": "1550f057-7a73-471c-a312-510e6d946ee7",
 41:    "metadata": {},
 42:    "outputs": [],
 43:    "source": [
 44:     "pydough.active_session.load_metadata_graph(\"../metadata/tpch_demo_graph.json\", \"TPCH\");"
 45:    ]
 46:   },
 47:   {
 48:    "cell_type": "markdown",
 49:    "id": "23c73480-8651-49e6-be9f-578febfccfd8",
 50:    "metadata": {},
 51:    "source": [
 52:     "The graph we loaded is a metadata representation of the standard TPC-H schema, with some names modified to be more human readable. In all future cells we will be able to reference the entities from this metadata.\n",
 53:     "\n",
 54:     "We won't dive into the details of the relationships for this notebook, but note that it is able to reference the tables involved and move between them based on pre-defined relationships."
 55:    ]
 56:   },
 57:   {
 58:    "cell_type": "markdown",
 59:    "id": "a016516c-7d30-4c97-9dba-604a33fa220c",
 60:    "metadata": {},
 61:    "source": [
 62:     "## Jupyter Extension\n",
 63:     "\n",
 64:     "To actually execute PyDough we have written a Jupyter extension to allow defining cells that contain PyDough expressions which are not valid Python. For example, now that the metadata is loaded, you are able to directly refer to `nations`, but this is not valid Python syntax.\n",
 65:     "\n",
 66:     "This is done with the Jupyter cell magic: `%%pydough`. This first attempts to resolve any variables with the regular Python environment and then leverages the metadata. In the future we intend for this to be a cell drop down option that will automatically append this magic to the relevant cells, but for now we feel this accurate represents the \"feel\" of working in PyDough.\n",
 67:     "\n",
 68:     "When you first setup the notebook you need to load the extension: \n",
 69:     "\n",
 70:     "```\n",
 71:     "%load_ext pydough.jupyter_extensions\n",
 72:     "```\n",
 73:     "\n",
 74:     "*Note*: If running outside our demo setup you may need manually install the extension, which is also found in this repository."
 75:    ]
 76:   },
 77:   {
 78:    "cell_type": "code",
 79:    "execution_count": null,
 80:    "id": "db20909e-33c1-4c27-9dce-54afbd44b38f",
 81:    "metadata": {},
 82:    "outputs": [],
 83:    "source": [
 84:     "%load_ext pydough.jupyter_extensions"
 85:    ]
 86:   },
 87:   {
 88:    "cell_type": "markdown",
 89:    "id": "0e3605f6-7e43-4bb8-bdbf-a2774cee07be",
 90:    "metadata": {},
 91:    "source": [
 92:     "Now we can define our access to nations, where we may only want to load the key."
 93:    ]
 94:   },
 95:   {
 96:    "cell_type": "code",
 97:    "execution_count": null,
 98:    "id": "81891b2c-8bc8-44d0-9e33-c80f5202c4c6",
 99:    "metadata": {},
100:    "outputs": [],
101:    "source": [
102:     "%%pydough\n",
103:     "\n",
104:     "nations.CALCULATE(nkey=key, nname=name)"
105:    ]
106:   },
107:   {
108:    "cell_type": "markdown",
109:    "id": "10534caa-9d2f-47d1-8093-d2988a502484",
110:    "metadata": {},
111:    "source": [
112:     "As you can see, this step resolved without any Python errors. However, this isn't actually useful because we can't use this result anywhere. Instead, we can assign this result to a Python variable to make it accessible in future cells, whether they are Python cells or more PyDough cells."
113:    ]
114:   },
115:   {
116:    "cell_type": "code",
117:    "execution_count": null,
118:    "id": "475883eb-97ee-46c2-bc87-450e8930412b",
119:    "metadata": {},
120:    "outputs": [],
121:    "source": [
122:     "%%pydough\n",
123:     "\n",
124:     "nation_keys = nations.CALCULATE(nkey=key, nname=name)"
125:    ]
126:   },
127:   {
128:    "cell_type": "markdown",
129:    "id": "105e087d-5dc4-4bf9-95e4-8a1fd27cc4d9",
130:    "metadata": {},
131:    "source": [
132:     "It's important to note that so far we haven't actually **executed** anything. Although we have determined that nations and key may be a valid name in the graph, this is example of what we call a **contextless expression**, meaning that its actual resolution may differ depending on how this variable is inserted into an actual expression that we execute.\n",
133:     "\n",
134:     "We won't showcase this behavior in this demo, but its important to note that the namebinding for `nations` does not require it to only refer to a top level collection/table.\n",
135:     "\n",
136:     "We can then further use this name if we decide we want to select only on 2 nations with the fewest customers. This step consists of a few parts, but in essence what we are doing is saying:\n",
137:     "1. Select our nations as defined above.\n",
138:     "2. Use the TOP_K operation which gives the first 2 elements as defined by the `by` section.\n",
139:     "3. We define our sorting result to be by customer count. What this is saying is that for each nation, count the number of customers connected to it, which works because `nations.customers` is a defined path in our metadata. By calling the `COUNT` operation we reduce this result to 1 value per entry, which can be then be used for sorting.\n",
140:     "4. We indicate that we want to sort in ascending order."
141:    ]
142:   },
143:   {
144:    "cell_type": "code",
145:    "execution_count": null,
146:    "id": "8763fa2a-4119-49bd-8423-313e291972ab",
147:    "metadata": {},
148:    "outputs": [],
149:    "source": [
150:     "%%pydough\n",
151:     "\n",
152:     "lowest_customer_nations = nation_keys.CALCULATE(nkey, nname, cust_count=COUNT(customers)).TOP_K(2, by=cust_count.ASC())\n",
153:     "lowest_customer_nations"
154:    ]
155:   },
156:   {
157:    "cell_type": "markdown",
158:    "id": "97abb00c-9bba-43a9-b2f1-c99ad041832e",
159:    "metadata": {},
160:    "source": [
161:     "## Evaluating PyDough\n",
162:     "\n",
163:     "Right now there are two primary ways to evaluate PyDough expressions.\n",
164:     "1. Convert PyDough expressions into a SQL query using `pydough.to_sql()`\n",
165:     "2. Execute PyDough expressions on a SQL database using `pydough.to_df()`\n",
166:     "\n",
167:     "Setting up either situation requires making a change the underlying active session. By default PyDough will allow generating ANSI SQL (but not executing on a Database).\n",
168:     "\n",
169:     "These APIs can be used from Python if only used directly on a Python variable that has already been resolved from PyDough. If there are more complex expressions please use PyDough cells."
170:    ]
171:   },
172:   {
173:    "cell_type": "code",
174:    "execution_count": null,
175:    "id": "0797d353-fcde-492b-8bff-0bfd11b83d1e",
176:    "metadata": {},
177:    "outputs": [],
178:    "source": [
179:     "%%pydough\n",
180:     "\n",
181:     "pydough.to_sql(nation_keys)"
182:    ]
183:   },
184:   {
185:    "cell_type": "markdown",
186:    "id": "23549c86-e192-4ccc-a36d-84eb465c648f",
187:    "metadata": {},
188:    "source": [
189:     "To enable execution on a Database, we need to setup the `pydough.active_session.connect_database()` to indicate where we want to target our SQL. This API is intended to work with any DB 2.0 compatible database connection, although right now it is only setup to work with SQLite. This step is done by providing the database name and the required `connect(...)` arguments. This API will then automatically load the appropriate dialect, which is maintained through integration with `SQLGlot`."
190:    ]
191:   },
192:   {
193:    "cell_type": "code",
194:    "execution_count": null,
195:    "id": "1747e080-eb2f-49a7-bf40-6bdfdb387e4f",
196:    "metadata": {},
197:    "outputs": [],
198:    "source": [
199:     "pydough.active_session.connect_database(\"sqlite\", database=\"../../tpch.db\");"
200:    ]
201:   },
202:   {
203:    "cell_type": "code",
204:    "execution_count": null,
205:    "id": "12624591-8916-436a-a0f2-f3b666d98a7f",
206:    "metadata": {},
207:    "outputs": [],
208:    "source": [
209:     "%%pydough\n",
210:     "\n",
211:     "pydough.to_df(nation_keys)"
212:    ]
213:   },
214:   {
215:    "cell_type": "markdown",
216:    "id": "fd41a3e5-9292-4145-9e20-06f3b5b395d3",
217:    "metadata": {},
218:    "source": [
219:     "Similarly, we can compute our more complex expression with the two nations containing the fewest customers."
220:    ]
221:   },
222:   {
223:    "cell_type": "code",
224:    "execution_count": null,
225:    "id": "d704f7c7-d189-4baa-8475-e0e2c46bd436",
226:    "metadata": {},
227:    "outputs": [],
228:    "source": [
229:     "%%pydough\n",
230:     "\n",
231:     "pydough.to_df(lowest_customer_nations)"
232:    ]
233:   },
234:   {
235:    "cell_type": "markdown",
236:    "id": "f52dfcfe-6e90-44b8-b9c4-7dc08a5b28ca",
237:    "metadata": {},
238:    "source": [
239:     "Finally, while building a statement from smaller components is best practice in Pydough, you can always evaluate the entire expression all at once within a PyDough cell, such as this example that loads the all Asian nations in the dataset.\n",
240:     "\n",
241:     "We can use the optional `columns` argument to `to_sql` or `to_df` to specify which columns to include, or even what they should be renamed as."
242:    ]
243:   },
244:   {
245:    "cell_type": "code",
246:    "execution_count": null,
247:    "id": "e46afe0f-d0fe-476c-a4c1-81320d358b6f",
248:    "metadata": {},
249:    "outputs": [],
250:    "source": [
251:     "%%pydough\n",
252:     "\n",
253:     "asian_countries = nations.WHERE(region.name == \"ASIA\")\n",
254:     "print(pydough.to_df(asian_countries, columns=[\"name\", \"key\"]))\n",
255:     "pydough.to_df(asian_countries, columns={\"nation_name\": \"name\", \"id\": \"key\"})"
256:    ]
257:   },
258:   {
259:    "cell_type": "markdown",
260:    "id": "2ddb4d8d-9e70-4d38-babb-4897edce61c7",
261:    "metadata": {},
262:    "source": [
263:     "# Additional Notebooks\n",
264:     "\n",
265:     "This notebook is intended as a simple introduction into pydough and it runs in a Jupyter notebook. To get a better understanding of PyDough's most impactful features, we have the following additional notebooks:\n",
266:     "* [2_pydough_operations](./2_pydough_operations.ipynb): Provides a detailed overview of many of the core operations you can currently perform in PyDough, include some best practices and possible limitations.\n",
267:     "* [3_exploration](./3_exploration.ipynb): Explores our provided TPC-H metadata to help highlight some of the key metadata features and to teach users how to interact with the metadata.\n",
268:     "* [4_tpch](./4_tpch.ipynb): Compares the SQL queries used in the TPC-H benchmarks to equivalent statements written in PyDough.\n",
269:     "* [5_what_if](./5_what_if.ipynb): Shows how to do WHAT-IF analysis with PyDough.\n"
270:    ]
271:   },
272:   {
273:    "cell_type": "code",
274:    "execution_count": null,
275:    "id": "2c4e2a66-70f8-47f7-bee9-a5b76668c063",
276:    "metadata": {},
277:    "outputs": [],
278:    "source": []
279:   }
280:  ],
281:  "metadata": {
282:   "kernelspec": {
283:    "display_name": "Python 3 (ipykernel)",
284:    "language": "python",
285:    "name": "python3"
286:   },
287:   "language_info": {
288:    "codemirror_mode": {
289:     "name": "ipython",

````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/demos/notebooks/2_pydough_operations.ipynb
````
  1: {
  2:  "cells": [
  3:   {
  4:    "cell_type": "markdown",
  5:    "id": "0c8f7ee9-40ec-48d7-a763-1d51ff503c5b",
  6:    "metadata": {},
  7:    "source": [
  8:     "# PyDough Operations\n",
  9:     "\n",
 10:     "This notebook aims to provide an overview of the various builtin PyDough operations. We do not intend for this to be exhaustive and especially the functions listed are not complete, but we believe these operations can act as a foundation for getting started."
 11:    ]
 12:   },
 13:   {
 14:    "cell_type": "code",
 15:    "execution_count": null,
 16:    "id": "0a2eb068-60ab-48ef-8332-4876d8d53c87",
 17:    "metadata": {},
 18:    "outputs": [],
 19:    "source": [
 20:     "%load_ext pydough.jupyter_extensions\n",
 21:     "\n",
 22:     "import pydough\n",
 23:     "# Setup demo metadata\n",
 24:     "pydough.active_session.load_metadata_graph(\"../metadata/tpch_demo_graph.json\", \"TPCH\");\n",
 25:     "pydough.active_session.connect_database(\"sqlite\", database=\"../../tpch.db\");"
 26:    ]
 27:   },
 28:   {
 29:    "cell_type": "markdown",
 30:    "id": "f28e0b68-333d-4e40-bc97-286806656564",
 31:    "metadata": {},
 32:    "source": [
 33:     "## Collections\n",
 34:     "\n",
 35:     "A collection in PyDough is an abstraction for any \"document\", but in most cases represents a table. Starting with the TPC-H schema, if we want to access the regions table, we will use our corresponding PyDough collection."
 36:    ]
 37:   },
 38:   {
 39:    "cell_type": "code",
 40:    "execution_count": null,
 41:    "id": "04886bb9-e46f-424a-8437-fd62ff368d31",
 42:    "metadata": {},
 43:    "outputs": [],
 44:    "source": [
 45:     "%%pydough\n",
 46:     "\n",
 47:     "print(pydough.to_sql(regions))\n",
 48:     "pydough.to_df(regions)"
 49:    ]
 50:   },
 51:   {
 52:    "cell_type": "markdown",
 53:    "id": "d1ffa88a-1c44-49e3-8691-205ef30781ed",
 54:    "metadata": {},
 55:    "source": [
 56:     "Collections contain properties, which either correspond to the entries within a document or a sub collection (another document that can be reached from the current document). This is explored in more detail in our notebook on metadata, but what is important to understand is that the path between collections is how we integrate data across multiple tables.\n",
 57:     "\n",
 58:     "For example, each region is associated with 1 or more nations, so rather than just looking at the region we can look at \"each nation for each region\". This will result in outputting 1 entry per nation."
 59:    ]
 60:   },
 61:   {
 62:    "cell_type": "code",
 63:    "execution_count": null,
 64:    "id": "b1a70fd7-bc94-44a6-8616-187ce471031d",
 65:    "metadata": {},
 66:    "outputs": [],
 67:    "source": [
 68:     "%%pydough\n",
 69:     "\n",
 70:     "print(pydough.to_sql(regions.nations))\n",
 71:     "pydough.to_df(regions.nations)"
 72:    ]
 73:   },
 74:   {
 75:    "cell_type": "markdown",
 76:    "id": "a911b535-b580-41d1-8679-9eca40303431",
 77:    "metadata": {},
 78:    "source": [
 79:     "Notice how in the generated SQL we create a join between `region` and `nation`. The metadata holds this relationship, effectively abstracting joins away from the developer whenever possible."
 80:    ]
 81:   },
 82:   {
 83:    "cell_type": "markdown",
 84:    "id": "a25a2965-4f88-4626-b326-caf931fdba9c",
 85:    "metadata": {},
 86:    "source": [
 87:     "## Calculate\n",
 88:     "\n",
 89:     "The next important operation is the `CALCULATE` operation, which takes in a variable number of positioning and/or keyword arguments."
 90:    ]
 91:   },
 92:   {
 93:    "cell_type": "code",
 94:    "execution_count": null,
 95:    "id": "5ea63942-d894-4bd8-9003-68f0be812f2c",
 96:    "metadata": {},
 97:    "outputs": [],
 98:    "source": [
 99:     "%%pydough\n",
100:     "\n",
101:     "print(pydough.to_sql(nations.CALCULATE(key, nation_name=name)))"
102:    ]
103:   },
104:   {
105:    "cell_type": "markdown",
106:    "id": "f89da4ca-5493-493f-bfe3-41d8a5f5d2a1",
107:    "metadata": {},
108:    "source": [
109:     "Calculate has a few purposes:\n",
110:     "* Select which entries you want in the output.\n",
111:     "* Define new fields by calling functions.\n",
112:     "* Allow operations to be evaluated for each entry in the outermost collection's \"context\".\n",
113:     "* Define aliases for terms that get down-streamed to descendants ([see here](#down-streaming)).\n",
114:     "\n",
115:     "The terms of the last `CALCULATE` in the PyDough logic are the terms that are included in the result (unless the `columns` argument of `to_sql` or `to_df` is used)."
116:    ]
117:   },
118:   {
119:    "cell_type": "code",
120:    "execution_count": null,
121:    "id": "c658d7ec-af49-4a06-b487-424d6d7a6603",
122:    "metadata": {},
123:    "outputs": [],
124:    "source": [
125:     "%%pydough\n",
126:     "\n",
127:     "print(pydough.to_sql(nations.CALCULATE(adjusted_key = key + 1)))"
128:    ]
129:   },
130:   {
131:    "cell_type": "markdown",
132:    "id": "24031aa2-1df7-441d-b487-aa093b852504",
133:    "metadata": {},
134:    "source": [
135:     "Here the context is the \"nations\" at the root of the graph. This means that for each entry within nations, we compute the result. This has important implications for when we get to more complex expressions. For example, if we want to know how many nations we have stored in each region, we can do via `CALCULATE`."
136:    ]
137:   },
138:   {
139:    "cell_type": "code",
140:    "execution_count": null,
141:    "id": "6b361449-4072-4e76-831f-bc2428337111",
142:    "metadata": {},
143:    "outputs": [],
144:    "source": [
145:     "%%pydough\n",
146:     "\n",
147:     "pydough.to_df(regions.CALCULATE(name, nation_count=COUNT(nations)))"
148:    ]
149:   },
150:   {
151:    "cell_type": "markdown",
152:    "id": "d86928a1-7ff2-4a38-8e47-54d89b43cd27",
153:    "metadata": {},
154:    "source": [
155:     "Internally, this process evaluates `COUNT(nations)` grouped on each region and then joining the result with the original `regions` table. Importantly, this outputs a \"scalar\" value for each region.\n",
156:     "\n",
157:     "This shows a very important restriction of `CALCULATE`: each final entry in the operation must be scalar with respect to a current context. For example, the expression `regions(region_name=name, nation_name=nations.name)` is not legal because region and nation is a one to many relationship, so there is not a single nation name for each region. \n",
158:     "\n",
159:     "**The cell below will result in an error because it violates this restriction.**"
160:    ]
161:   },
162:   {
163:    "cell_type": "code",
164:    "execution_count": null,
165:    "id": "e5c462db-afaf-401c-9d54-c2c3c49d594e",
166:    "metadata": {},
167:    "outputs": [],
168:    "source": [
169:     "%%pydough\n",
170:     "\n",
171:     "pydough.to_df(regions.CALCULATE(region_name=name, nation_name=nations.name))"
172:    ]
173:   },
174:   {
175:    "cell_type": "markdown",
176:    "id": "854455ec-5f75-4389-967b-17d9c54d219f",
177:    "metadata": {},
178:    "source": [
179:     "In contrast, we know that every nation has 1 region (and this is defined in the metadata). As a result the alternative expression, `nations(nation_name=name, region_name=region.name)` is legal."
180:    ]
181:   },
182:   {
183:    "cell_type": "code",
184:    "execution_count": null,
185:    "id": "1c14e6a7-1d0d-4cad-bc2c-4ab2b152beda",
186:    "metadata": {},
187:    "outputs": [],
188:    "source": [
189:     "%%pydough\n",
190:     "\n",
191:     "pydough.to_df(nations.CALCULATE(nation_name=name, region_name=region.name))"
192:    ]
193:   },
194:   {
195:    "cell_type": "markdown",
196:    "id": "b02b9a4f-1038-4b8d-9078-4bc0261b760c",
197:    "metadata": {},
198:    "source": [
199:     "This illustrates one of the important properties of the metadata, defining one:one, many:one, one:many, and many:many relationships can allow developers the flexiblity to write simpler queries."
200:    ]
201:   },
202:   {
203:    "cell_type": "markdown",
204:    "id": "70d2c6b9-0a7a-48e2-9323-a6690855c939",
205:    "metadata": {},
206:    "source": [
207:     "### Functions\n",
208:     "\n",
209:     "PyDough has support for many builtin functions. Whenever possible we try and support standard Python operators. However, this is not completely possible. In addition, to avoid namespace conflicts, for functions that require regular function call semantics we use all capitalization by convention. Here are some examples."
210:    ]
211:   },
212:   {
213:    "cell_type": "code",
214:    "execution_count": null,
215:    "id": "1d64f52b-3726-48ee-bd3e-20954cae931b",
216:    "metadata": {},
217:    "outputs": [],
218:    "source": [
219:     "%%pydough\n",
220:     "\n",
221:     "# Numeric operations\n",
222:     "print(\"Q1\")\n",
223:     "print(pydough.to_sql(nations.CALCULATE(key + 1, key - 1, key * 1, key / 1)))\n",
224:     "\n",
225:     "# Comparison operators\n",
226:     "print(\"\\nQ2\")\n",
227:     "print(pydough.to_sql(nations.CALCULATE(key == 0, key < 0, key != 0, key >= 5)))\n",
228:     "\n",
229:     "# String Operations\n",
230:     "print(\"\\nQ3\")\n",
231:     "print(pydough.to_sql(nations.CALCULATE(LENGTH(name), UPPER(name), LOWER(name), STARTSWITH(name, \"A\"))))\n",
232:     "\n",
233:     "# Boolean operations\n",
234:     "print(\"\\nQ4\")\n",
235:     "print(pydough.to_sql(nations.CALCULATE((key != 1) & (LENGTH(name) > 5)))) # Boolean AND\n",
236:     "print(\"\\nQ5\")\n",
237:     "print(pydough.to_sql(nations.CALCULATE((key != 1) | (LENGTH(name) > 5)))) # Boolean OR\n",
238:     "print(\"\\nQ6\")\n",
239:     "print(pydough.to_sql(nations.CALCULATE(~(LENGTH(name) > 5)))) # Boolean NOT        \n",
240:     "print(\"\\nQ7\")  \n",
241:     "print(pydough.to_sql(nations.CALCULATE(ISIN(name, (\"KENYA\", \"JAPAN\"))))) # In\n",
242:     "\n",
243:     "# Datetime Operations\n",
244:     "# Note: Since this is based on SQL lite the underlying date is a bit strange.\n",
245:     "print(\"\\nQ8\")\n",
246:     "print(pydough.to_sql(lines.CALCULATE(YEAR(ship_date), MONTH(ship_date), DAY(ship_date),HOUR(ship_date),MINUTE(ship_date),SECOND(ship_date))))\n",
247:     "\n",
248:     "# Aggregation operations\n",
249:     "print(\"\\nQ9\")\n",
250:     "print(pydough.to_sql(TPCH.CALCULATE(NDISTINCT(nations.comment), SUM(nations.key))))\n",
251:     "# Count can be used on a column for non-null entries or a collection\n",
252:     "# for total entries.\n",
253:     "print(\"\\nQ10\")\n",
254:     "print(pydough.to_sql(TPCH.CALCULATE(COUNT(nations), COUNT(nations.comment))))"
255:    ]
256:   },
257:   {
258:    "cell_type": "markdown",
259:    "id": "4d626691-df45-4cc6-9d6d-e4cb3c1ce3f6",
260:    "metadata": {},
261:    "source": [
262:     "#### Limitations\n",
263:     "\n",
264:     "There are a few limitations with regular Python. Most notably:\n",
265:     "* You cannot use Python's builtin `and`, `or`, `not`, or `in` with PyDough expressions.\n",
266:     "* We do not support chained comparisons (e.g. `2 < x < 5`).\n",
267:     "* We only support Python literals that are `integers`, `floats`, `strings`, `datetime.date`, or a `tuple`/`list` of those supported types.\n",
268:     "* Lists and tuples can only be used with `ISIN`."
269:    ]
270:   },
271:   {
272:    "cell_type": "markdown",
273:    "id": "b70993e8-3cd2-4c45-87e3-8e68f67b92a0",
274:    "metadata": {},
275:    "source": [
276:     "### Down-Streaming\n",
277:     "\n",
278:     "Sometimes you need to load a value from a previous context to use at a later step in a PyDough statement. Any expression from an ancestor context that is placed in a `CALCULATE` is automatically made available to all descendants of that context. However, an error will occur if the name of the term defined in the ancestor collides with a name of a term or property of a descendant context, since PyDough will not know which one to use.\n",
279:     "\n",
280:     "Notice how in the example below, `region_name` is defined in a `CALCULATE` within the context of `regions`, so the calculate within the context of `nations` also has access to `region_name` (interpreted as \"the name of the region that this nation belongs to\")."
281:    ]
282:   },
283:   {
284:    "cell_type": "code",
285:    "execution_count": null,
286:    "id": "faa320b6-cedf-4af0-8896-5e8ad63f33e5",
287:    "metadata": {},
288:    "outputs": [],
289:    "source": [
290:     "%%pydough\n",
291:     "\n",
292:     "pydough.to_df(regions.CALCULATE(region_name=name).nations.CALCULATE(region_name, nation_name=name))"
293:    ]
294:   },
295:   {
296:    "cell_type": "markdown",
297:    "id": "6040a7c5-fc82-4e33-8b2b-a1b3ef394f71",
298:    "metadata": {},
299:    "source": [
300:     "Here is a more complex example showing intermediate values. Here we will first compute `total_value` and then reuse it downstream."
301:    ]
302:   },
303:   {
304:    "cell_type": "code",
305:    "execution_count": null,
306:    "id": "45953043-bc30-42cc-bd8e-c4da371f1755",
307:    "metadata": {},
308:    "outputs": [],
309:    "source": [
310:     "%%pydough\n",
311:     "\n",
312:     "nations_value = nations.CALCULATE(nation_name=name, total_value=SUM(suppliers.account_balance))\n",
313:     "pydough.to_df(nations_value)"
314:    ]
315:   },
316:   {
317:    "cell_type": "code",
318:    "execution_count": null,
319:    "id": "bd935638-0c81-4060-9271-a717280b0f97",
320:    "metadata": {},
321:    "outputs": [],
322:    "source": [
323:     "%%pydough\n",
324:     "suppliers_value = nations_value.suppliers.CALCULATE(\n",
325:     " key,\n",
326:     " name,\n",
327:     " nation_name,\n",
328:     " account_balance=account_balance,\n",
329:     " percentage_of_national_value=100 * account_balance / total_value\n",
330:     ")\n",
331:     "top_suppliers = suppliers_value.TOP_K(20, by=percentage_of_national_value.DESC())\n",
332:     "pydough.to_df(top_suppliers)"
333:    ]
334:   },
335:   {
336:    "cell_type": "markdown",
337:    "id": "5be9616e-4eb4-430a-b949-1295c330136c",
338:    "metadata": {},
339:    "source": [
340:     "## WHERE\n",
341:     "\n",
342:     "The `WHERE` operation by be used to filter unwanted entries in a context. For example, we can filter `nations` to only consider the `AMERICA` and `EUROPE` regions. A WHERE's context functions similarly to a `CALCULATE` except that it cannot be used to assign new properties; it only contains a single positional argument: the predicate to filter on. "
343:    ]
344:   },
345:   {
346:    "cell_type": "code",
347:    "execution_count": null,
348:    "id": "b05cd1db-b050-4ee2-8327-882ad89e2a07",
349:    "metadata": {},
350:    "outputs": [],
351:    "source": [
352:     "%%pydough\n",
353:     "\n",
354:     "pydough.to_df(nations.WHERE((region.name == \"AMERICA\") | (region.name == \"EUROPE\")))"
355:    ]
356:   },
357:   {
358:    "cell_type": "markdown",
359:    "id": "d91e6ab7-bc7a-4c5b-8264-f7e46ded2c4a",
360:    "metadata": {},
361:    "source": [
362:     "## TOP_K\n",
363:     "\n",
364:     "The TOP K operation is used to reduce a collection to maximum number of values. The `by` arugument is used to order the output based on a sorting condition. As an example, consider this query to only calculate the first 5 nations by alphabetical name order."
365:    ]
366:   },
367:   {
368:    "cell_type": "code",
369:    "execution_count": null,
370:    "id": "a02a00e9-7df8-431d-8fe8-ec3ae42fbf4a",
371:    "metadata": {},
372:    "outputs": [],
373:    "source": [
374:     "%%pydough\n",
375:     "\n",
376:     "pydough.to_df(nations.TOP_K(5, by=name.ASC()))"
377:    ]
378:   },
379:   {
380:    "cell_type": "markdown",
381:    "id": "da15de47-1a56-4130-b801-56ad6eba9de7",
382:    "metadata": {},
383:    "source": [
384:     "The `by` argument requirements are:\n",
385:     "* Anything that can be an expression used in a `CALCULATE` or a `WHERE` can be used a component of a `by`.\n",
386:     "* The value in the `by` must end with either `.ASC()` or `.DESC()`\n",
387:     "\n",
388:     "You can also provide a tuple to by if you need to break ties. Consider this alternatives that instead selects the 20 parts with the largest size, starting with the smallest part id."
389:    ]
390:   },
391:   {
392:    "cell_type": "code",
393:    "execution_count": null,
394:    "id": "27d13368-8265-4a33-99a3-b6724f8c54de",
395:    "metadata": {},
396:    "outputs": [],
397:    "source": [
398:     "%%pydough\n",
399:     "\n",
400:     "pydough.to_df(parts.TOP_K(20, by=(size.DESC(), key.ASC())))"
401:    ]
402:   },
403:   {
404:    "cell_type": "markdown",
405:    "id": "9e4a1458-d52e-4970-955b-35ed1ec29cc7",
406:    "metadata": {},
407:    "source": [
408:     "## ORDER_BY\n",
409:     "\n",
410:     "If you just want to return your output in a sorted order, you can use `ORDER_BY`. The functionality is the same as in `TOP_K` except that there is no `K` argument so the rows are not reduced. Each argument must be an expression that can be used for sorting.\n",
411:     "\n",
412:     "Below can transform our nations collection to sort the output by the alphabetical ordering of the nation names."
413:    ]
414:   },
415:   {
416:    "cell_type": "code",
417:    "execution_count": null,
418:    "id": "840ccde6-3e32-46db-9b97-a15507427f33",
419:    "metadata": {},
420:    "outputs": [],
421:    "source": [
422:     "%%pydough\n",
423:     "\n",
424:     "pydough.to_df(nations.ORDER_BY(name.ASC()))"
425:    ]
426:   },
427:   {
428:    "cell_type": "markdown",
429:    "id": "ed9922ec-8021-4664-a0ed-f32520e0e4a5",
430:    "metadata": {},
431:    "source": [
432:     "## PARTITION\n",
433:     "\n",
434:     "The partition operation allows grouping collections under interesting keys similar to a SQL `GROUP BY`. Keys can be specified using the `by` argument and data columns to be aggregated can be referenced using the name argument. For example, we can use this to bucket nations by name length."
435:    ]
436:   },
437:   {
438:    "cell_type": "code",
439:    "execution_count": null,
440:    "id": "274824ca-5d54-43df-b18a-dbdd50aaa472",
441:    "metadata": {},
442:    "outputs": [],
443:    "source": [
444:     "%%pydough\n",
445:     "\n",
446:     "updated_nations = nations.CALCULATE(key, name_length=LENGTH(name))\n",
447:     "grouped_nations = updated_nations.PARTITION(\n",
448:     "    name=\"lengths\", by=(name_length)\n",
449:     ").CALCULATE(\n",
450:     "    name_length,\n",
451:     "    nation_count=COUNT(nations)\n",
452:     ")\n",
453:     "pydough.to_df(grouped_nations)"
454:    ]
455:   },
456:   {
457:    "cell_type": "markdown",
458:    "id": "f1043412-75c0-4535-a935-894cb83d30e2",
459:    "metadata": {},
460:    "source": [
461:     "A couple important usage details:\n",
462:     "* The data inside each partitioned group can be accessed as a sub-collection using its original name (see `nations` in the example above).\n",
463:     "* The `name` argument specifies the name of the collection of partitioned data (needed in case the partitioned data gets partitioned again and needs to be accessed by name).\n",
464:     "* `keys` can be either be a single expression or a tuple of them, but it can only be references to expressions that already exist in the context of the data (e.g. `name`, not `LOWER(name)` or `region.name`)\n",
465:     "* Terms defined from the context of the `PARTITION` can be down-streamed to its descendants. An example is shown below where we select brass parts of size 15, but only the ones whose supply is below the average of all such parts."
466:    ]
467:   },
468:   {
469:    "cell_type": "code",
470:    "execution_count": null,
471:    "id": "c8514760-7c58-440b-82ee-773b0564b43f",
472:    "metadata": {},
473:    "outputs": [],
474:    "source": [
475:     "%%pydough\n",
476:     "\n",
477:     "selected_parts = parts.WHERE(ENDSWITH(part_type, \"BRASS\") & (size == 15))\n",
478:     "part_types = selected_parts.PARTITION(name=\"types\", by=part_type).CALCULATE(avg_price=AVG(parts.retail_price))\n",
479:     "output = part_types.parts.WHERE(retail_price < avg_price)\n",
480:     "pydough.to_df(output)"
481:    ]
482:   },
483:   {
484:    "cell_type": "markdown",
485:    "id": "981d2c0b-03ff-408a-b2d8-d68e2336da48",
486:    "metadata": {},
487:    "source": [
488:     "## HAS and HASNOT\n",
489:     "\n",
490:     "The `HAS` and `HASNOT` operations are used for filtering based on if any match occurs between an entry and another collection. For example, consider consider only regions that have at least 1 nation whose name is length > 10."
491:    ]
492:   },
493:   {
494:    "cell_type": "code",
495:    "execution_count": null,
496:    "id": "e0358f83-2bb7-448a-bf50-2075e3e14de5",
497:    "metadata": {},
498:    "outputs": [],
499:    "source": [
500:     "%%pydough\n",
501:     "\n",
502:     "length_10_nations = nations.WHERE(LENGTH(name) > 10)\n",
503:     "pydough.to_df(regions.WHERE(HAS(length_10_nations)))"
504:    ]
505:   },
506:   {
507:    "cell_type": "markdown",
508:    "id": "1e888a5e-9ad9-45ba-a080-585154673057",
509:    "metadata": {},
510:    "source": [
511:     "Alternatively we can only consider regions where all of its nations names of length 10 or less."
512:    ]
513:   },
514:   {
515:    "cell_type": "code",
516:    "execution_count": null,
517:    "id": "948fb323-4e03-411c-9792-ead8597cbc6c",
518:    "metadata": {},
519:    "outputs": [],
520:    "source": [
521:     "%%pydough\n",
522:     "\n",
523:     "pydough.to_df(regions.WHERE(HASNOT(length_10_nations)))"
524:    ]
525:   },
526:   {
527:    "cell_type": "markdown",
528:    "id": "49b670d6",
529:    "metadata": {},
530:    "source": [
531:     "# SINGULAR\n",
532:     "\n",
533:     "In PyDough, it is required that if we are accessing a sub-collection in a collection context, the collection must be singular with regards to the sub-collection. For example, consider the following PyDough code, that results in an error:"
534:    ]
535:   },
536:   {
537:    "cell_type": "code",
538:    "execution_count": null,
539:    "id": "f16f0057",
540:    "metadata": {},
541:    "outputs": [],
542:    "source": [
543:     "%%pydough\n",
544:     "pydough.to_df(regions.CALCULATE(name, nation_name=nations.name))"
545:    ]
546:   },
547:   {
548:    "cell_type": "markdown",
549:    "id": "dcbb5293",
550:    "metadata": {},
551:    "source": [
552:     "This results in an error as nations is plural with regards to regions and PyDough does not know which nation name to use for each region. Let's say we want a field nation_4_name that contains the name of the nation with key 4. The PyDough code to do this is as follows:"
553:    ]
554:   },
555:   {
556:    "cell_type": "code",
557:    "execution_count": null,
558:    "id": "7ec056c8",
559:    "metadata": {},
560:    "outputs": [],
561:    "source": [
562:     "%%pydough\n",
563:     "nation_4 = nations.WHERE(key == 4)\n",
564:     "pydough.to_df(regions.CALCULATE(name, nation_4_name=nation_4.name))"
565:    ]
566:   },
567:   {
568:    "cell_type": "markdown",
569:    "id": "7992d4e4",
570:    "metadata": {},
571:    "source": [
572:     "We see that the above code results in an error as even though we know that there is at most a single value of `nation_4` for each instance of `regions`, PyDough does not know this and therefore prohibits the operation.\n",
573:     "To fix this, we can use the `.SINGULAR()` modifier to tell PyDough that the data should be treated as singular."
574:    ]
575:   },
576:   {
577:    "cell_type": "code",
578:    "execution_count": null,
579:    "id": "e0c45bca-7c28-48cc-a42f-dea82f67eb63",
580:    "metadata": {},
581:    "outputs": [],
582:    "source": [
583:     "%%pydough\n",
584:     "nation_4 = nations.WHERE(key == 4).SINGULAR()\n",
585:     "pydough.to_df(regions.CALCULATE(name, nation_4_name=nation_4.name))"
586:    ]
587:   },
588:   {
589:    "cell_type": "markdown",
590:    "id": "04a95cb2",
591:    "metadata": {},
592:    "source": [
593:     "In summary, certain PyDough operations, such as specific filters, can cause plural data to become singular. In this case, PyDough will still ban the plural data from being treated as singular unless the `.SINGULAR()` modifier is used to tell PyDough that the data should be treated as singular. It is very important that this only be used if the user is certain that the data will be singular, since otherwise it can result in undefined behavior when the PyDough code is executed."
594:    ]
595:   }
596:  ],
597:  "metadata": {
598:   "kernelspec": {
599:    "display_name": "Python 3 (ipykernel)",
600:    "language": "python",

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/demos/notebooks/3_exploration.ipynb
````
  1: {
  2:  "cells": [
  3:   {
  4:    "cell_type": "markdown",
  5:    "id": "f1fd4015-5281-4f56-bf88-5db4a8de93e0",
  6:    "metadata": {},
  7:    "source": [
  8:     "# Exploration\n",
  9:     "\n",
 10:     "This notebook is intended to explain various APIs available in PyDough to explain and explore the PyDough metadata and PyDough logical operations."
 11:    ]
 12:   },
 13:   {
 14:    "cell_type": "markdown",
 15:    "id": "3042b7ae-8eb7-4147-b00f-7e2d54f8c3fa",
 16:    "metadata": {},
 17:    "source": [
 18:     "## Setup\n",
 19:     "\n",
 20:     "This notebook uses our TPC-H schema metadata and SQLite database connection for all examples."
 21:    ]
 22:   },
 23:   {
 24:    "cell_type": "code",
 25:    "execution_count": null,
 26:    "id": "0850592d-e6eb-4905-8291-21056617fc74",
 27:    "metadata": {},
 28:    "outputs": [],
 29:    "source": [
 30:     "import pydough\n",
 31:     "\n",
 32:     "pydough.active_session.load_metadata_graph(\"../metadata/tpch_demo_graph.json\", \"TPCH\")\n",
 33:     "pydough.active_session.connect_database(\"sqlite\", database=\"../../tpch.db\")\n",
 34:     "%load_ext pydough.jupyter_extensions"
 35:    ]
 36:   },
 37:   {
 38:    "cell_type": "markdown",
 39:    "id": "e7dfb2db-191d-4dac-8b88-76aea581f167",
 40:    "metadata": {},
 41:    "source": [
 42:     "## Using `pydough.explain` on metadata\n",
 43:     "\n",
 44:     "The API `pydough.explain` can be used to dump information about various PyDough metadata objects or logical operations. The simplest version is to call it on the entire graph, which displays basic information about the graph such as its name and the collections inside it. The `pydough.explain` API takes in an optional `verbose` argument. If this is True, then it displays more information about its arguments, and if it is False it displays a more compact summary.\n",
 45:     "\n",
 46:     "`pydough.explain` can be called from either inside a normal Python cell or inside a pydough cell.\n",
 47:     "\n",
 48:     "Below is an example of using this API on the TPCH graph that has been loaded into the active sesssion."
 49:    ]
 50:   },
 51:   {
 52:    "cell_type": "code",
 53:    "execution_count": null,
 54:    "id": "1550f057-7a73-471c-a312-510e6d946ee7",
 55:    "metadata": {
 56:     "scrolled": true
 57:    },
 58:    "outputs": [],
 59:    "source": [
 60:     "graph = pydough.active_session.metadata\n",
 61:     "\n",
 62:     "print(pydough.explain(graph, verbose=True))"
 63:    ]
 64:   },
 65:   {
 66:    "cell_type": "markdown",
 67:    "id": "23c73480-8651-49e6-be9f-578febfccfd8",
 68:    "metadata": {},
 69:    "source": [
 70:     "Just like the hint suggests, below is an example of calling `pydough.explain` to learn more about the `regions` collection of TPCH:"
 71:    ]
 72:   },
 73:   {
 74:    "cell_type": "code",
 75:    "execution_count": null,
 76:    "id": "8e8eb60b-ade1-4e16-871b-7ffe6c7a9381",
 77:    "metadata": {},
 78:    "outputs": [],
 79:    "source": [
 80:     "print(pydough.explain(graph[\"regions\"], verbose=True))"
 81:    ]
 82:   },
 83:   {
 84:    "cell_type": "markdown",
 85:    "id": "6b68f493-5b53-4c84-8fc7-96da2de7109c",
 86:    "metadata": {},
 87:    "source": [
 88:     "The information displayed tells us information about this collection, including:\n",
 89:     "\n",
 90:     "* The real data table that `regions` maps to in the database is called `main.REGION`.\n",
 91:     "* Every record in the `regions` collection has a `comment`, a `key`, and a `name`, which are scalar properties of the region.\n",
 92:     "* Each unique `key` value corresponds to a single unique record in `regions`.\n",
 93:     "* There is a subcollection of `regions` called `nations`.\n",
 94:     "\n",
 95:     "Below is another example, this time on the collection `supply_records`:"
 96:    ]
 97:   },
 98:   {
 99:    "cell_type": "code",
100:    "execution_count": null,
101:    "id": "b9afda52-f766-4888-98cd-664de96ebd5e",
102:    "metadata": {},
103:    "outputs": [],
104:    "source": [
105:     "print(pydough.explain(graph[\"supply_records\"], verbose=True))"
106:    ]
107:   },
108:   {
109:    "cell_type": "markdown",
110:    "id": "f67979ef-55b2-4530-80ff-4ffb0aad86ba",
111:    "metadata": {},
112:    "source": [
113:     "This time, the information displayed tells us the following:\n",
114:     "\n",
115:     "* The real data table that `supply_records` maps to in the database is called `main.PARTSUPP`.\n",
116:     "* Every record in the `supply_records` collection has an `availqty`, a `comment`, a `part_key`, a `supplier_key` and a `supplier_cost`.\n",
117:     "* Each unique combination of the values of `part_key` and `supplier_key` corresponds to a single unique record in `supply_records`.\n",
118:     "* There are subcollections of `supply_records` called `lines`, `part`, and `supplier`.\n",
119:     "\n",
120:     "Just like the hint suggests, below is an example of calling `pydough.explain` to learn more about one of the scalar properties, in this case: the `name` property of `regions`."
121:    ]
122:   },
123:   {
124:    "cell_type": "code",
125:    "execution_count": null,
126:    "id": "a7f062ab-2f3f-4893-87c0-1ff06fbb56bc",
127:    "metadata": {},
128:    "outputs": [],
129:    "source": [
130:     "print(pydough.explain(graph[\"regions\"][\"name\"], verbose=True))"
131:    ]
132:   },
133:   {
134:    "cell_type": "markdown",
135:    "id": "63ffc26d-a558-49a2-93b5-4b1bddb409c2",
136:    "metadata": {},
137:    "source": [
138:     "The information displayed tells us that the property `regions.name` corresponds to the `r_name` column of the table `main.REGION`, which has a type of `string`. \n",
139:     "\n",
140:     "Below is an example of using `pydough.explain` to learn about a subcollection property, in this case: the `nations` property of `regions`."
141:    ]
142:   },
143:   {
144:    "cell_type": "code",
145:    "execution_count": null,
146:    "id": "b3d8281c-f6cc-4165-8d33-4ba572c1a4c9",
147:    "metadata": {},
148:    "outputs": [],
149:    "source": [
150:     "print(pydough.explain(graph[\"regions\"][\"nations\"], verbose=True))"
151:    ]
152:   },
153:   {
154:    "cell_type": "markdown",
155:    "id": "02cd4286-e2a4-442b-b1f6-08b35401ed3b",
156:    "metadata": {},
157:    "source": [
158:     "The information displayed explains how `regions.nations` connects the `regions` collection to the `nations` connection, including:\n",
159:     "\n",
160:     "* Each record of `regions` can connect to multiple records in `nations`\n",
161:     "* Each record of `nations` can connect to at most one record of `regions`\n",
162:     "* A record of `regions` is connected to a record of `nations` if the `key` property of `regions` equals the `naiton_key` property of `nations`.\n",
163:     "* The `nations` collection has a corresponding twin property to `regions.nations` called `nations.region`, displayed below:"
164:    ]
165:   },
166:   {
167:    "cell_type": "code",
168:    "execution_count": null,
169:    "id": "ddba3a75-0ec5-4ce4-818c-13256c650785",
170:    "metadata": {},
171:    "outputs": [],
172:    "source": [
173:     "print(pydough.explain(graph[\"nations\"][\"region\"], verbose=True))"
174:    ]
175:   },
176:   {
177:    "cell_type": "markdown",
178:    "id": "c1e1acd7-ab11-4c08-9613-d81782e26eae",
179:    "metadata": {},
180:    "source": [
181:     "The information displayed is essentially the same as `regions.nations`, but from the perspective of each record of `nations` instead of each record of `regions`."
182:    ]
183:   },
184:   {
185:    "cell_type": "markdown",
186:    "id": "152362da-f260-42f2-9770-dd078e6246c6",
187:    "metadata": {},
188:    "source": [
189:     "## Using `pydough.explain_structure`\n",
190:     "\n",
191:     "The API `pydough.explain_structure` can be called on an entire metadata graph, just like `pydough.explain`. Instead of providing a summary of a single graph, collection, or property, `pydough.explain_structure` gives a wholistic summary of how everything in the graph connects. It displays all of the collections in the graph, the names of their properties, and for the ones that are subcollections it provides a brief summary of what other collection they map to and what the cardinality of the collection looks like.\n",
192:     "\n",
193:     "Below is an example of using this API on the TPCH graph to gain a summary of the entire graph."
194:    ]
195:   },
196:   {
197:    "cell_type": "code",
198:    "execution_count": null,
199:    "id": "b1959ea8-c826-4503-b136-3f85c60ceb8f",
200:    "metadata": {},
201:    "outputs": [],
202:    "source": [
203:     "print(pydough.explain_structure(graph))"
204:    ]
205:   },
206:   {
207:    "cell_type": "markdown",
208:    "id": "ac150d1a-3ea8-46c9-9613-b117b8023d0b",
209:    "metadata": {},
210:    "source": [
211:     "Focusing on the `regions` section of this information shows us some of the information observed earlier with `pydough.explain`:\n",
212:     "\n",
213:     "* The scalar properties of `regions` are displayed (`comment`, `key` and `name`)\n",
214:     "* The `nations` property is shown, and indicates that it connects each record of `regions` to potentially multiple records of `nations`, and that the reverse is `nations.region`."
215:    ]
216:   },
217:   {
218:    "cell_type": "markdown",
219:    "id": "4279af88-4461-4cb9-8d60-6f009a3c88eb",
220:    "metadata": {},
221:    "source": [
222:     "## Using `pydough.explain` and `pydough.explain_term` on PyDough code\n",
223:     "\n",
224:     "The API `pydough.explain` can also be called on PyDough code to display information about what it logically does. There is one important constraint: **`pydough.explain` can only be called on PyDough code if it that resolves into a collection** (e.g. `regions` or `nations.suppliers.WHERE(account_balance > 0)`, but not `customers.name`).\n",
225:     "\n",
226:     "To explain other PyDough code, such as an expression, `pydough.explain_term` must be used (more on that later).\n",
227:     "\n",
228:     "Below is an example of using `pydough.explain` on simple PyDough code to learn about the `nations` collection:"
229:    ]
230:   },
231:   {
232:    "cell_type": "code",
233:    "execution_count": null,
234:    "id": "1690b70c-3c68-4283-bc98-cf03fd1e0c55",
235:    "metadata": {},
236:    "outputs": [],
237:    "source": [
238:     "%%pydough\n",
239:     "\n",
240:     "print(pydough.explain(nations, verbose=True))"
241:    ]
242:   },
243:   {
244:    "cell_type": "markdown",
245:    "id": "06f69db6-d4b9-481d-8977-f592a47ffd73",
246:    "metadata": {},
247:    "source": [
248:     "There are several pieces of information displayed here, including:\n",
249:     "\n",
250:     "* The PyDough code `nations` just accesses the data from the `nations` collection, which we can learn more about as shown earlier by calling `pydough.explain` on the metadata for `nations`.\n",
251:     "* If `pydough.to_sql` or `pydough.to_df` is called on `nations`, all four of its scalar properties will be incldued in the result.\n",
252:     "* The properties `comment`, `key`, `name`, and `region_key` can be accessed by the collection as scalar expressions.\n",
253:     "* The properties `customers`, `region` and `suppliers` can be accessed by the collection as subcollections (unknown if they are singular or plural, without gaining more information).\n",
254:     "\n",
255:     "Below is an example of how to use `pydough.explain_term` to learn more about the `name` expression of `nations`:"
256:    ]
257:   },
258:   {
259:    "cell_type": "code",
260:    "execution_count": null,
261:    "id": "ddc4e741-0650-4bd1-9679-e140a996c773",
262:    "metadata": {},
263:    "outputs": [],
264:    "source": [
265:     "%%pydough\n",
266:     "\n",
267:     "print(pydough.explain_term(nations, name, verbose=True))"
268:    ]
269:   },
270:   {
271:    "cell_type": "markdown",
272:    "id": "b8577c17-59c9-4126-b485-feb57d78aee1",
273:    "metadata": {},
274:    "source": [
275:     "And below is an example of how to use `pydough.explain_term` to learn more about the `suppliers` collection of `nations`:"
276:    ]
277:   },
278:   {
279:    "cell_type": "code",
280:    "execution_count": null,
281:    "id": "a087b30c-6c8c-4402-8b7c-2c9c3eb6bc9e",
282:    "metadata": {},
283:    "outputs": [],
284:    "source": [
285:     "%%pydough\n",
286:     "\n",
287:     "print(pydough.explain_term(nations, suppliers, verbose=True))"
288:    ]
289:   },
290:   {
291:    "cell_type": "markdown",
292:    "id": "a1d45b4b-ee59-45d8-8a53-a9c3d0e782cc",
293:    "metadata": {},
294:    "source": [
295:     "But `pydough.explain` and `pydough.explain_term` do not need to just be used on simple collections and columns. Below is a slightly more complex example that will be dissected in several steps by calling `pydough.explain` and `pydough.explain_term` on various snippets of it. The code in question calculates the top 3 asian countries by the number of orders made by customers in those nations in the year 1995."
296:    ]
297:   },
298:   {
299:    "cell_type": "code",
300:    "execution_count": null,
301:    "id": "2d2405a1-39c1-452e-bab4-ec36ac17c7d4",
302:    "metadata": {},
303:    "outputs": [],
304:    "source": [
305:     "%%pydough\n",
306:     "\n",
307:     "asian_countries = nations.WHERE(region.name == \"ASIA\")\n",
308:     "\n",
309:     "orders_1995 = customers.orders.WHERE(YEAR(order_date) == 1995)\n",
310:     "\n",
311:     "asian_countries_info = asian_countries.CALCULATE(country_name=LOWER(name), total_orders=COUNT(orders_1995))\n",
312:     "\n",
313:     "top_asian_countries = asian_countries_info.TOP_K(3, by=total_orders.DESC())\n",
314:     "\n",
315:     "pydough.to_df(top_asian_countries)"
316:    ]
317:   },
318:   {
319:    "cell_type": "markdown",
320:    "id": "de071cd1-9d35-4472-85e8-f21c79f8cc56",
321:    "metadata": {},
322:    "source": [
323:     "First, here is the results of calling `pydough.explain` on the final result:"
324:    ]
325:   },
326:   {
327:    "cell_type": "code",
328:    "execution_count": null,
329:    "id": "1b0ac75a-8ac1-41ee-96f9-8e49f6930d13",
330:    "metadata": {},
331:    "outputs": [],
332:    "source": [
333:     "%%pydough\n",
334:     "\n",
335:     "print(pydough.explain(top_asian_countries, verbose=True))"
336:    ]
337:   },
338:   {
339:    "cell_type": "markdown",
340:    "id": "cbb4ba87-d1b0-4974-a91d-ecd003c502cc",
341:    "metadata": {},
342:    "source": [
343:     "There are several pieces of information displayed, including the following:\n",
344:     "\n",
345:     "* The structure of the entire logic is shown, but the information being displayed is specifically focused on the last operation (the `TopK` at the bottom of the structure).\n",
346:     "* The operation is ordering by `total_orders` in descending order, then keeping the top 3 entries.\n",
347:     "* There are 6 total expressions that are accessible from `top_asian_countries`, but only 2 of them are included in the answer when executed: `country_name` and `total_orders`.\n",
348:     "\n",
349:     "More can be learned about these expressions included in the answer with `pydough.explain_term`:"
350:    ]
351:   },
352:   {
353:    "cell_type": "code",
354:    "execution_count": null,
355:    "id": "09d02b91-945c-466c-bf14-b182ad324ae4",
356:    "metadata": {},
357:    "outputs": [],
358:    "source": [
359:     "%%pydough\n",
360:     "\n",
361:     "print(pydough.explain_term(top_asian_countries, country_name, verbose=True))"
362:    ]
363:   },
364:   {
365:    "cell_type": "markdown",
366:    "id": "7abd494f-1a46-4da8-bc76-6b3f1d3986fd",
367:    "metadata": {},
368:    "source": [
369:     "Here, we get the structure of everything done up until this point, and information specifically about `country_name`. In this case, we learn it is the result of claling `LOWER` on `name`. Calling `explain_term(top_asian_countries, name)` would more-or-less display the same information as `explain_term(nations, name)`. Instead, here is the result using `explain_term` to learn about `total_orders`:"
370:    ]
371:   },
372:   {
373:    "cell_type": "code",
374:    "execution_count": null,
375:    "id": "218da407-ee00-4bf2-af15-5bcb624efb6b",
376:    "metadata": {},
377:    "outputs": [],
378:    "source": [
379:     "%%pydough\n",
380:     "\n",
381:     "print(pydough.explain_term(top_asian_countries, total_orders, verbose=True))"
382:    ]
383:   },
384:   {
385:    "cell_type": "markdown",
386:    "id": "c5254776-e8de-41ba-b7d2-a48399105c20",
387:    "metadata": {},
388:    "source": [
389:     "Here, we learn that `total_orders` counts how many records of `customers.orders` exist for each record of `nations`. Now, `explain_terms` is used to learn more about the argument to `COUNT`:"
390:    ]
391:   },
392:   {
393:    "cell_type": "code",
394:    "execution_count": null,
395:    "id": "3280c08a-cc2c-45da-929a-83cf53613de8",
396:    "metadata": {},
397:    "outputs": [],
398:    "source": [
399:     "%%pydough\n",
400:     "\n",
401:     "print(pydough.explain_term(asian_countries, orders_1995, verbose=True))"
402:    ]
403:   },
404:   {
405:    "cell_type": "markdown",
406:    "id": "387e7750-ef2c-405a-b446-650be64b6ef3",
407:    "metadata": {},
408:    "source": [
409:     "Here, we learn that `customers.orders` invokes a child of the current context (`nations.WHERE(region.name == 'ASIA')`) by accessing the `customers` subcollection, then accessing its `orders` collection, then filtering it on the conedition `YEAR(order_date) == 1995`. \n",
410:     "\n",
411:     "We also know that this resulting child is plural with regards to the context, meaning that `asian_countries.CALCULATE(asian_countries.order_date)` would be illegal, but `asian_countries.CALCULATE(MAX(asian_countries.order_date))` is legal.\n",
412:     "\n",
413:     "More combinations of `pydough.explain` and `pydough.explain_terms` can be done to learn more about what each of these components does."
414:    ]
415:   },
416:   {
417:    "cell_type": "code",
418:    "execution_count": null,
419:    "id": "f2017556-2f87-45f6-aed1-2e3019efc3b1",
420:    "metadata": {},
421:    "outputs": [],
422:    "source": []
423:   }
424:  ],
425:  "metadata": {
426:   "kernelspec": {
427:    "display_name": "Python 3 (ipykernel)",

429:    "name": "python3"
430:   },
