1163: %%pydough
1164: People.PARTITION(name="groups")
1165: ```
1166: 
1167: **Bad Example #4**: Count how many packages were ordered in each year. Invalid because `YEAR(order_date)` is not allowed to be used as a partition term (it must be placed in a `CALCULATE` so it is accessible as a named reference).
1168: 
1169: ```py
1170: %%pydough
1171: Packages.PARTITION(name="years", by=YEAR(order_date)).CALCULATE(
1172:     n_packages=COUNT(Packages)
1173: )
1174: ```
1175: 
1176: **Bad Example #5**: Count how many people live in each state. Invalid because `current_address.state` is not allowed to be used as a partition term (it must be placed in a `CALCULATE` so it is accessible as a named reference).
1177: 
1178: ```py
1179: %%pydough
1180: People.PARTITION(name="state", by=current_address.state).CALCULATE(
1181:     n_packages=COUNT(People)
1182: )
1183: ```
1184: 
1185: **Bad Example #6**: Invalid version of good example #8 that did not use a `CALCULATE` to make `state` available via down-streaming or to bind `first_name[:1]` to a name, therefore neither can be used as a partition term.
1186: 
1187: ```py
1188: %%pydough
1189: Addresses.current_occupants.PARTITION(name="combinations", by=(state, first_name[:1])).CALCULATE(
1190:     state,
1191:     first_name[:1],
1192:     n_people=COUNT(current_occupants),
1193: ).TOP_K(10, by=n_people.DESC())
1194: ```

1197: 
1198: ```py
1199: %%pydough
1200: People.CALCULATE(birth_year=YEAR(birth_date)).PARTITION(name="years", by=birth_year).CALCULATE(
1201:     birth_year,
1202:     email,

1209: ```py
1210: %%pydough

1212:     birth_year,
1213:     People.email,
1214:     n_people=COUNT(People)

1222: people_info = Addresses.CALCULATE(state).current_occupants.CALCULATE(
1223:     first_letter=first_name[:1],
1224: )

1232: <!-- TOC --><a name="singular"></a>
1233: ### SINGULAR
1234: 
1235: In PyDough, it is required that if we are accessing a sub-collection in a collection context, the collection must be singular with regards to the sub-collection. Certain PyDough operations, such as specific filters, can cause plural data to become singular. In this case, PyDough will still ban the plural data from being treated as singular unless the `.SINGULAR()` modifier is used to tell PyDough that the data should be treated as singular. It is very important that this only be used if the user is certain that the data will be singular, since otherwise it can result in undefined behavior when the PyDough code is executed.
1236: 
1237: **Good Example #1**: Access the package cost of the most recent package ordered by each person. This is valid because even though `.packages` is plural with regards to `People`, the filter done will ensure that there is only one record for each record of `People`, so `.SINGULAR()` is valid. 
1238: 
1239: ```py
1240: %%pydough
1241: most_recent_package = packages.WHERE(
1242:     RANKING(by=order_date.DESC(), per="People") == 1
1243: ).SINGULAR()
1244: People.CALCULATE(
1245:     ssn,
1246:     first_name,
1247:     middle_name,
1248:     last_name,
1249:     most_recent_package_cost=most_recent_package.package_cost
1250: )
1251: ```
1252: 
1253: **Good Example #2**: Access the email of the current occupant of each address that has the name `"John Smith"` (no middle name). This is valid if it is safe to assume that each address only has one current occupant named `"John Smith"` without a middle name.
1254: 
1255: ```py
1256: %%pydough
1257: js = current_occupants.WHERE(
1258:     (first_name == "John") &  
1259:     (last_name == "Smith") & 
1260:     ABSENT(middle_name)
1261: ).SINGULAR()
1262: Addresses.CALCULATE(
1263:     address_id,
1264:     john_smith_email=DEFAULT_TO(js.email, "NO JOHN SMITH LIVING HERE")
1265: )
1266: ```
1267: 
1268: **Bad Example #1**: This is invalid primarily because of two reasons:
1269: 1. Each `Addresses` might have multiple `current_occupants` named `John`, therefore the use of `.SINGULAR()`, though it would not raise an exception, is invalid.
1270: 2. Even if, `current_occupants` were non-plural after using `SINGULAR`, `packages` is a plural sub-collection of `current_occupants`, therefore, the data being accessed would be plural with regards to `Addresses`.
1271: 
1272: 
1273: ```py
1274: %%pydough
1275: Addresses.CALCULATE(
1276:     package_id=current_occupants.WHERE(
1277:         first_name == "John"
1278:     ).SINGULAR().packages.package_id
1279: )
1280: ```
1281: 
1282: <!-- TOC --><a name="best"></a>
1283: ### BEST
1284: 
1285: PyDough supports selecting the optimal record from a collection based on a given metric, evaluated per-record of an ancestor collection. The `BEST` method is called on the collection with a `by` argument used to define the metric(s) for finding the optimal record of the sub-collection. The `by` argument follows the same rules as `PREV`, `NEXT`, `TOP_K`, etc.: it must be either a single collation term, or an iterable of 1+ collation terms. The ancestor that the optimal record is found with regards to is defined via the same optional `per` argument as window functions: a string referring to the name of the ancestor in question (absent if the optimal record globally is to be found instead).
1286: 
1287: Additional keyword arguments can be supplied to `BEST` that change its behavior:
1288: - `allow_ties` (default=False): if True, changes the behavior to keep all records of the sub-collection that share the optimal values of the collation terms. If `allow_ties` is True, the `BEST` clause is no longer singular.
1289: - `n_best=True`(defaults=1): if an integer greater than 1, changes the behavior to keep the top `n_best` values of the sub-collection for each record of the parent collection (fewer if `n_best` records of the sub-collection do not exist). If `n_best` is greater than 1, the `BEST` clause is no longer singular. NOTE: `n_best` cannot be greater than 1 at the same time that `allow_ties` is True.
1290: 
1291: **Good Example #1**: Find the package id & zip code the package was shipped to for every package that was the first-ever purchase for its customer.
1292: 
1293: ```py
1294: %%pydough
1295: Customers.packages.BEST(by=order_date.ASC(), per="Customers").CALCULATE(
1296:     package_id,
1297:     shipping_address.zip_code
1298: )
1299: ```
1300: 
1301: **Good Example #2**: For each customer, list their ssn and the cost of the most recent package they have purchased.
1302: 
1303: ```py
1304: %%pydough
1305: Customers.CALCULATE(
1306:     ssn,
1307:     most_recent_cost=packages.BEST(by=order_date.DESC(), per="Customers").package_cost
1308: )
1309: ```
1310: 
1311: **Good Example #3**: Find the address in the state of New York with the most occupants, ties broken by address id. Note that since `per` is not provided, the best record globally is found.
1312: 
1313: ```py
1314: %%pydough
1315: addr_info = Addresses.WHERE(
1316:     state == "NY"
1317: ).CALCULATE(address_id, n_occupants=COUNT(current_occupants))
1318: addr_info.BEST(by=(n_occupants.DESC(), address_id.ASC()))
1319: ```
1320: 
1321: **Good Example #4**: For each customer, find the number of people currently living in the address that they most recently shipped a package to.
1322: 
1323: ```py
1324: %%pydough
1325: most_recent_package = packages.BEST(by=order_date.DESC(), per="Customers")
1326: Customers.CALCULATE(
1327:     ssn,
1328:     n_occ_most_recent_addr=COUNT(most_recent_package.shipping_address.current_occupants)
1329: )
1330: ```
1331: 
1332: **Good Example #5**: For each address that has occupants, list out the first/last name of the person living in that address who has ordered the most packages, breaking ties in favor of the person with the smaller social security number. Also includes the city/state of the address, the number of people who live there, and the number of packages that person ordered.
1333: 
1334: ```py
1335: %%pydough
1336: Addresses.WHERE(HAS(current_occupants)).CALCULATE(
1337:     city,
1338:     state,
1339:     n_occupants=COUNT(current_occupants),
1340: ).current_occupants.CALCULATE(
1341:     n_orders=COUNT(packages)
1342: ).BEST(
1343:     by=(n_orders.DESC(), ssn.ASC()),
1344:     per="Addresses"
1345: ).CALCULATE(
1346:     first_name,
1347:     last_name,
1348:     n_orders,
1349:     n_living_in_same_addr=n_occupants,
1350:     city=city,
1351:     state=state,
1352: )
1353: ```
1354: 
1355: **Good Example #6**: For each person, find the total value of the 5 most recent packages they ordered.
1356: 
1357: ```py
1358: %%pydough
1359: five_most_recent = packages.BEST(per="People", by=order_date.DESC(), n_best=5)
1360: People.CALCULATE(
1361:     ssn,
1362:     value_most_recent_5=SUM(five_most_recent.package_cost)
1363: )
1364: ```
1365: 
1366: **Good Example #7**: For each address, find the package most recently ordered by one of the current occupants of that address, including the email of the occupant who ordered it and the address' id.
1367: 
1368: ```py
1369: %%pydough
1370: packages_from_occupants = current_occupants.CALCULATE(email).packages
1371: most_recent_package = packages_from_occupants.BEST(by=order_date.DESC(), per="Adresses")
1372: Addresses.CALCULATE(address_id).most_recent_package.CALCULATE(
1373:     address_id,
1374:     email,
1375:     package_id=package_id,
1376:     order_date=order_date,
1377: )
1378: ```
1379: 
1380: **Good Example #8**: Find all addresses where the most recently purchased package by any current occupant of the address was sent to the same address.
1381: 
1382: ```py
1383: %%pydough
1384: most_recent_package = current_occupants.packages.BEST(per="Addresses", by=order_date.DESC())
1385: Addresses.WHERE(most_recent_package.shipping_address.address_id == address_id)
1386: ```
1387: 
1388: **Good Example #9**: Find each person whose most recently purchased package was shipped to their current address.
1389: 
1390: ```py
1391: %%pydough
1392: most_recent_package = packages.BEST(per="current_occupants", by=order_date.DESC())
1393: people_info = Addresses.CALCULATE(home_id=address_id).current_occupants
1394: people_info.WHERE(most_recent_package.shipping_address.address_id == home_id)
1395: ```
1396: 
1397: **Bad Example #1**: For each person find their best email. This is invalid because `email` is not a sub-collection of `People` (it is a scalar attribute, so there is only 1 `email` per-person).
1398: 
1399: ```py
1400: %%pydough
1401: People.CALCULATE(first_name, email.BEST(by=birth_date.DESC()))
1402: ```
1403: 
1404: **Bad Example #2**: For each person find their best package. This is invalid because the `by` argument is missing.
1405: 
1406: ```py
1407: %%pydough
1408: People.packages.BEST(per="People")
1409: ```
1410: 
1411: **Bad Example #3**: For each person find their best package. This is invalid because the `by` argument is empty
1412: 
1413: ```py
1414: %%pydough
1415: People.packages.BEST(by=(), per="People")
1416: ```
1417: 
1418: **Bad Example #4**: For each person find the 5 most recent packages they have ordered, allowing ties. This is invalid because `n_best` is greater than 1 at the same time that `allow_ties` is True.
1419: 
1420: ```py
1421: %%pydough
1422: People.packages.BEST(by=order_date.DESC(), per="People", n_best=5, allow_ties=True)
1423: ```
1424: 
1425: **Bad Example #5**: For each person, find the package cost of their 10 most recent packages. This is invalid because `n_best` is greater than 1, which means that the `BEST` clause is non-singular so its terms cannot be accessed in the `CALCULATE` without aggregating.
1426: 
1427: ```py
1428: %%pydough
1429: best_packages = packages.BEST(by=order_date.DESC(), per="People", n_best=10)
1430: People.CALCULATE(first_name, best_cost=best_packages.package_cost)
1431: ```
1432: 
1433: **Bad Example #6**: For each person, find the package cost of their most expensive package(s), allowing ties. This is invalid because `allow_ties` is True, which means that the `BEST` clause is non-singular so its terms cannot be accessed in the `CALCULATE` without aggregating.
1434: 
1435: ```py
1436: %%pydough
1437: best_packages = packages.BEST(by=package_cost.DESC(), per="People", allow_ties=True)
1438: People.CALCULATE(first_name, best_cost=best_packages.package_cost)
1439: ```
1440: 
1441: **Bad Example #7**: For each address, find the package most recently ordered by one of the current occupants of that address, including the address id of the address. This is invalid because `address_id` is used despite not being down-streamed from `Addresses`.
1442: 
1443: ```py
1444: %%pydough
1445: most_recent_package = current_occupants.packages.BEST(by=order_date.DESC(), per="Addresses")
1446: Addresses.most_recent_package.CALCULATE(
1447:     address_id=address_id,
1448:     package_id=package_id,
1449:     order_date=order_date,
1450: )
1451: ```
1452: 
1453: **Bad Example #8**: For each address find the oldest occupant. This is invalid because the `BEST` clause is placed in the `CALCULATE` without accessing any of its attributes.
1454: 
1455: ```py
1456: %%pydough
1457: Addresses.CALCULATE(address_id, oldest_occupant=current_occupants.BEST(by=birth_date.ASC(), per="Addresses"))
1458: ```
1459: 
1460: **Bad Example #9**: For each person find their most recent package. This is invalid because the `per` argument is not the name of one of the ancestors of `packages`.
1461: 
1462: ```py
1463: %%pydough
1464: People.packages.BEST(by=order_date.DESC(), per="packages")
1465: ```

1558: <!-- TOC --><a name="example-3-email-of-oldest-non-customer-resident"></a>
1559: ### Example 3: Email of Oldest Non-Customer Resident
1560: 
1561: **Question**: For every city/state, find the email of the oldest resident of that city/state who has never ordered a package (break ties in favor of the lower social security number). Also include the zip code of that occupant. Order alphabetically by state, followed by city.
1562: 
1563: **Answer**:
1564: ```py
1565: %%pydough
1566: 
1567: # Partition every address by the city/state

1573: 
1574: # For each city, find the oldest occupant out of any address in that city
1575: # and include the desired information about that occupant.
1576: oldest_occupants = cities.BEST(
1577:     addrs.current_occupants.WHERE(HASNOT(packages)),
1578:     by=(birth_date.ASC(), ssn.ASC()),
1579: ).CALCULATE(
1580:     state,
1581:     city,
1582:     email,
1583:     zip_code
1584: )
1585: 
1586: # Sort the output by state, followed by city
1587: result = oldest_occupants.ORDER_BY(
1588:     state.ASC(),
1589:     city.ASC(),
1590: )
1591: ```
1592: 
1593: <!-- TOC --><a name="example-4-outlier-packages-per-month-of-2017"></a>
1594: ### Example 4: Outlier Packages Per Month Of 2017
1595: 
1596: **Question**: For every month of the year 2017, identify the percentage of packages ordered in that month that are at least 10x the average value of all packages ordered in 2017. Order the results by month.
1597: 
1598: **Answer**:
1599: ```py
1600: %%pydough
1601: # Contextless expression: identifies is a package was ordered in 2017
1602: is_2017 = YEAR(order_date) == 2017
1603: 
1604: # Identify the average package cost of all packages ordered in 2017
1605: global_info = GRAPH.CALCULATE(
1606:     avg_package_cost=AVG(Packages.WHERE(is_2017).package_cost)
1607: )
1608: 
1609: # Identify all packages ordered in 2017, but where the ancestor is global_info
1610: # instead of GRAPH, so `avg_package_cost` gets down-streamed.
1611: selected_package = global_info.Packages.WHERE(is_2017)
1612: 
1613: # For each such package, identify the month it was ordered, and add a term to
1614: # indicate if the cost of the package is at least 10x the average for all such
1615: # packages.
1616: packages = selected_packages.CALCULATE(
1617:     month=MONTH(order_date),
1618:     is_10x_avg=package_cost >= (10.0 * avg_package_cost)
1619: )
1620: 
1621: # Partition the packages by the month they were ordered, and for each month
1622: # calculate the ratio between the number of packages where is_10x_avg is True
1623: # versus all packages ordered that month, multiplied by 100 to get a percentage.

1632: 
1633: # Order the output by month
1634: result = months.ORDER_BY(month.ASC())
1635: ```
1636: 

1656: 
1657: # Obtain the global average of the year (x-coordinate) and
1658: # n_orders (y-coordinate). These correspond to `x-bar` and `y-bar`.
1659: global_info = GRAPH.CALCULATE(
1660:     avg_x = AVG(yearly_data.year),
1661:     avg_y = AVG(yearly_data.n_orders),
1662: )
1663: 
1664: # Contextless expression: corresponds to `x - x-bar` with regards to yearly_data
1665: # inside of global_info
1666: dx = n_orders - avg_x
1667: 
1668: # Contextless expression: corresponds to `y - y-bar` with regards to yearly_data
1669: # inside of global_info
1670: dy = year - avg_y
1671: 
1672: # Contextless expression: derive the slope with regards to global_info
1673: regression_data = yearly_data(value=(dx * dy) / (dx * dx))
1674: slope = SUM(regression_data.value)
1675: 
1676: # Identify the (chronologically) last record from yearly_data.
1677: # Could also write as `last_year = packs.WHERE(RANKING(by=year.DESC()) == 1).SINGULAR()`
1678: last_year = BEST(packs, by=year.DESC())
1679: 
1680: # Use a loop to derive a pair of terms for each of the 3 next years:
1681: # 1. The year itself
1682: # 2. The predicted number of orders (should be the last year's orders + slope * number of years)
1683: # This is allowed since calcs can operate via keyword arguments, whether real
1684: # or passed in via a dictionary with ** syntax.
1685: results = {}
1686: for n in range(1, 4):
1687:     results[f"year_{n}"] = last_year.year + n
1688:     results[f"year_{n}_prediction"] = last_year.n_orders + (n * slope)
1689: result = global_info.CALCULATE(**results)
1690: ```

  98: 
  99: <!-- TOC --><a name="binary-operators"></a>
 100: 
 101: ## Binary Operators
 102: 
 103: Below is each binary operator currently supported in PyDough.
 104: 
 105: <!-- TOC --><a name="arithmetic"></a>
 106: 
 107: ### Arithmetic
 108: 
 109: Supported mathematical operations: addition (`+`), subtraction (`-`), multiplication (`*`), division (`/`), exponentiation (`**`).
 110: 
 111: ```py
 112: Lineitems.CALCULATE(value = (extended_price * (1 - (discount ** 2)) + 1.0) / part.retail_price)
 113: ```
 114: 
 115: > [!WARNING]
 116: > The behavior when the denominator is `0` depends on the database being used to evaluate the expression.
 117: 
 118: <!-- TOC --><a name="comparisons"></a>
 119: 
 120: ### Comparisons
 121: 
 122: Expression values can be compared using standard comparison operators: `<=`, `<`, `==`, `!=`, `>` and `>=`:
 123: 
 124: ```py
 125: Customers.CALCULATE(
 126:     in_debt = acctbal < 0,
 127:     at_most_12_orders = COUNT(orders) <= 12,
 128:     is_european = nation.region.name == "EUROPE",
 129:     non_german = nation.name != "GERMANY",
 130:     non_empty_acct = acctbal > 0,
 131:     at_least_5_orders = COUNT(orders) >= 5,
 132: )
 133: ```
 134: 
 135: > [!WARNING]
 136: > Chained inequalities, like `a <= b <= c`, can cause undefined/incorrect behavior in PyDough. Instead, use expressions like `(a <= b) & (b <= c)`, or the [MONOTONIC](#monotonic) function.
 137: 
 138: <!-- TOC --><a name="logical"></a>
 139: 
 140: ### Logical
 141: 
 142: Multiple boolean expression values can be logically combined with `&`, `|` and `~` being used as logical AND, OR and NOT, respectively:
 143: 
 144: ```py
 145: is_asian = nation.region.name == "ASIA"
 146: is_european = nation.region.name == "EUROPE"
 147: in_debt = acctbal < 0
 148: Customers.CALCULATE(
 149:     is_eurasian = is_asian | is_european,
 150:     is_not_eurasian = ~(is_asian | is_european),
 151:     is_european_in_debt = is_european & in_debt
 152: )
 153: ```
 154: 
 155: > [!WARNING]
 156: > Do **NOT** use the builtin Python syntax `and`, `or`, or `not` on PyDough node. Using these instead of `&`, `|` or `~` can result in undefined incorrect results.
 157: 
 158: <!-- TOC --><a name="unary-operators"></a>
 159: 
 160: ## Unary Operators
 161: 
 162: Below is each unary operator currently supported in PyDough.
 163: 
 164: <!-- TOC --><a name="negation"></a>
 165: 
 166: ### Negation
 167: 
 168: A numerical expression's sign can be flipped by prefixing it with the `-` operator:
 169: 
 170: ```py
 171: Lineitems.CALCULATE(lost_value = extended_price * (-discount))
 172: ```
 173: 
 174: <!-- TOC --><a name="other-operators"></a>
 175: 
 176: ## Other Operators
 177: 
 178: Below are all other operators currently supported in PyDough that use other syntax besides function calls:
 179: 
 180: <!-- TOC --><a name="slicing"></a>
 181: 
 182: ### Slicing
 183: 
 184: A string expression can have a substring extracted with Python string slicing syntax `s[a:b:c]`.
 185: The implementation is based on Python slicing semantics. PyDough supports negative slicing, but currently, it does not support providing step values other than 1.
 186: 
 187: ```py
 188: Customers.CALCULATE(
 189:     country_code = phone[:3],
 190:     name_without_first_char = name[1:],
 191:     last_digit = phone[-1:],
 192:     name_without_start_and_end_char = name[1:-1]
 193:     phone_without_last_5_chars = phone[:-5]
 194:     name_second_to_last_char = name[-2:-1]
 195: )
 196: ```
 197: 
 198: > [!WARNING]
 199: > PyDough currently only supports combinations of `string[start:stop:step]` where `step` is either 1 or omitted, and both `start` and `stop` are either non-negative values or omitted.
 200: 
 201: <!-- TOC --><a name="string-functions"></a>
 202: 
 203: ## String Functions
 204: 
 205: Below is each function currently supported in PyDough that operates on strings.
 206: 
 207: <!-- TOC --><a name="lower"></a>
 208: 
 209: ### LOWER
 210: 
 211: Calling `LOWER` on a string converts its characters to lowercase:
 212: 
 213: ```py
 214: Customers.CALCULATE(lowercase_name = LOWER(name))
 215: ```
 216: 
 217: <!-- TOC --><a name="upper"></a>
 218: 
 219: ### UPPER
 220: 
 221: Calling `UPPER` on a string converts its characters to uppercase:
 222: 
 223: ```py
 224: Customers.CALCULATE(uppercase_name = UPPER(name))
 225: ```
 226: 
 227: <!-- TOC --><a name="length"></a>
 228: 
 229: ### LENGTH
 230: 
 231: Calling `length` on a string returns the number of characters it contains:
 232: 
 233: ```py
 234: Suppliers.CALCULATE(n_chars_in_comment = LENGTH(comment))
 235: ```
 236: 
 237: <!-- TOC --><a name="startswith"></a>
 238: 
 239: ### STARTSWITH
 240: 
 241: The `STARTSWITH` function checks if its first argument begins with its second argument as a string prefix:
 242: 
 243: ```py
 244: Parts.CALCULATE(begins_with_yellow = STARTSWITH(name, "yellow"))
 245: ```
 246: 
 247: <!-- TOC --><a name="endswith"></a>
 248: 
 249: ### ENDSWITH
 250: 
 251: The `ENDSWITH` function checks if its first argument ends with its second argument as a string suffix:
 252: 
 253: ```py
 254: Parts.CALCULATE(ends_with_chocolate = ENDSWITH(name, "chocolate"))
 255: ```
 256: 
 257: <!-- TOC --><a name="contains"></a>
 258: 
 259: ### CONTAINS
 260: 
 261: The `CONTAINS` function checks if its first argument contains its second argument as a substring:
 262: 
 263: ```py
 264: Parts.CALCULATE(is_green = CONTAINS(name, "green"))
 265: ```
 266: 
 267: <!-- TOC --><a name="like"></a>
 268: 
 269: ### LIKE
 270: 
 271: The `LIKE` function checks if the first argument matches the SQL pattern text of the second argument, where `_` is a 1 character wildcard and `%` is an 0+ character wildcard.
 272: 
 273: ```py
 274: Orders.CALCULATE(is_special_request = LIKE(comment, "%special%requests%"))
 275: ```
 276: 
 277: [This link](https://www.w3schools.com/sql/sql_like.asp) explains how these SQL pattern strings work and provides some examples.
 278: 
 279: <!-- TOC --><a name="join_strings"></a>
 280: 
 281: ### JOIN_STRINGS
 282: 
 283: The `JOIN_STRINGS` function concatenates all its string arguments, using the first argument as a delimiter between each of the following arguments (like the `.join` method in Python):
 284: 
 285: ```py
 286: Regions.CALCULATE(
 287:    region_name=name
 288: ).nations.CALCULATE(
 289:    nation_name=name
 290: ).customers.CALCULATE(
 291:    fully_qualified_name = JOIN_STRINGS("-", region_name, nation_name, name)
 292: )
 293: ```
 294: 
 295: For instance, `JOIN_STRINGS("; ", "Alpha", "Beta", "Gamma)` returns `"Alpha; Beta; Gamma"`.
 296: 
 297: <!-- TOC --><a name="lpad"></a>
 298: ### LPAD
 299: 
 300: The `LPAD` function pads an expression on the left side with a specified padding character until it is the desired length. It takes three arguments:
 301: 
 302: 1. The input string to pad.
 303: 2. The desired final length of the expression. It should be a positive integer literal.
 304: 3. The single character literal to use for padding.
 305: 
 306: The function behaves as follows:
 307: 
 308: - If the input expression is shorter than the desired length, it adds padding characters on the left until reaching the desired length. 
 309: - If the input expression is longer than the desired length, it truncates the expression by removing characters from the right side until it matches the desired length.
 310: - If the desired length is 0, it returns an empty string.
 311: - If the desired length is negative, it raises an error.
 312: - If the padding argument is not a single character, it raises an error.
 313: 
 314: ```py
 315: Customers.CALCULATE(left_padded_name = LPAD(name, 30, "*"))
 316: ```
 317: 
 318: Here are examples on how it pads on string literals:
 319: | Input | Output |
 320: |-------|--------|
 321: | `LPAD("123", 6, "0")` | `"000123"` |
 322: | `LPAD("123", 5, "#")` | `"##123"` |
 323: | `LPAD("123", 3, "0")` | `"123"` |
 324: | `LPAD("123", 2, "0")` | `"12"` |
 325: | `LPAD("123", 0, "0")` | `""` |
 326: 
 327: <!-- TOC --><a name="rpad"></a>
 328: ### RPAD
 329: 
 330: The `RPAD` function pads an expression on the right side with a specified padding character until it is the desired length. It takes three arguments:
 331: 
 332: 1. The input string to pad.
 333: 2. The desired final length of the expression. It should be a positive integer literal.
 334: 3. The single character literal to use for padding.
 335: 
 336: The function behaves as follows:
 337: 
 338: - If the input expression is shorter than the desired length, it adds padding characters on the right until reaching the desired length.
 339: - If the input expression is longer than the desired length, it truncates the expression by removing characters from the right side until it matches the desired length.
 340: - If the desired length is 0, it returns an empty string
 341: - If the desired length is negative, it raises an error
 342: - If the padding argument is not a single character, it raises an error
 343: 
 344: ```py
 345: Customers.CALCULATE(right_padded_name = RPAD(name, 30, "*"))
 346: ```
 347: 
 348: Here are examples on how it pads on string literals:
 349: | Input | Output |
 350: |-------|--------|
 351: | `RPAD("123", 6, "0")` | `"123000"` |
 352: | `RPAD("123", 5, "#")` | `"123##"` |
 353: | `RPAD("123", 3, "0")` | `"123"` |
 354: | `RPAD("123", 2, "0")` | `"12"` |
 355: | `RPAD("123", 0, "0")` | `""` |
 356: 
 357: <!-- TOC --><a name="find"></a>
 358: 
 359: ### FIND
 360: 
 361: The `FIND` function returns the position (0-indexed) of the first occurrence of a substring within a string, or -1 if the substring is not found. The first argument is the string to search within, and the second argument is the substring to search for.
 362: 
 363: ```py
 364: Customers.WHERE(name == "Alex Rodriguez")
 365:          .CALCULATE(
 366:             idx_Alex = FIND(name, "Alex"), # 0
 367:             idx_Rodriguez = FIND(name, "Rodriguez"), # 5
 368:             idx_bob = FIND(name, "bob"), # -1
 369:             idx_e = FIND(name, "e"), # 2
 370:             idx_space = FIND(name, " "), # 4
 371:             idx_of_R = FIND(name, "R"), # 5
 372:             idx_of_Alex_Rodriguez = FIND(name, "Alex Rodriguez"), # 0
 373: )
 374: ```
 375: 
 376: <!-- TOC --><a name="strip"></a>
 377: 
 378: ### STRIP
 379: 
 380: The `STRIP` function returns the first argument with all leading and trailing whitespace removed, including newlines, tabs, and spaces.
 381: If the second argument is provided, it is used as the set of characters to remove from the leading and trailing ends of the first argument.
 382: It continues removing characters until it encounters a character that is not in the set.
 383: This function is equivalent to python's `str.strip()` method.
 384: Note: This function is case-sensitive.
 385: 
 386: ```py
 387: Customers.CALCULATE(stripped_name = STRIP(name)) # removes all leading and trailing whitespace
 388: Customers.CALCULATE(stripped_name = STRIP(name, "aeiou")) # removes all leading and trailing vowels
 389: ```
 390: 
 391: | **Input String (X)**       | **STRIP(X, Y)**                    | **Result**          |
 392: |-----------------------------|---------------------------------------|---------------------|
 393: | `'abcXYZcba'`              | `STRIP('abcXYZcba','abc')`        | `'XYZ'`            |
 394: | `'$$Hello$$'`              | `STRIP('$$Hello$$','$$')`          | `'Hello'`          |
 395: | `'---Test-String---'`      | `STRIP('---Test-String---','-')`  | `'Test-String'`    |
 396: | `'123456Hello654321'`      | `STRIP('123456Hello654321','123456')` | `'Hello'`         |
 397: 
 398: <!-- TOC --><a name="datetime-functions"></a>
 399: 
 400: ## Datetime Functions
 401: 
 402: Below is each function currently supported in PyDough that operates on date/time/timestamp values.
 403: 
 404: <!-- TOC --><a name="datetime"></a>
 405: ### DATETIME
 406: 
 407: The `DATETIME` function is used to build/augment date/timestamp values. The first argument is the base date/timestamp, and it can optionally take in a variable number of modifier arguments.
 408: 
 409: The base argument can be one of the following:
 410: 
 411: - A string literal indicating that the current timestamp should be built, which has to be one of the following: `now`, `current_date`, `current_timestamp`, `current date`, `current timestamp`, `currentdate` or `currenttimestamp`. All of these aliases are equivalent, case-insensitive, and ignore leading/trailing whitespace.
 412: - A string literal representing datetime data (e.g. `"2024-01-01"` or `199-12-31 12:59:30`).
 413: - A datetime literal (e.g. `datetime.date`, `datetime.datetime`, or a `pd.Timestamp` from pandas).
 414: - A column of datetime data.
 415: 
 416: > [!NOTE]
 417: > Other datetime functions ([DATEDIFF](#datediff), [YEAR](#year), [QUARTER](#quarter), [MONTH](#month), [DAY](#day), [HOUR](#hour), [MINUTE](#minute) or [SECOND](#second)) also allow any of the base arguments above as datetime values. For example, you can call `YEAR("now")`, `DATEDIFF("months", dt, pd.Timestamp("2024-03-14")))`, `MONTH("1999-06-13")`, or `DATEDIFF("days", datetime.date(2025, 1, 1), "now")`.
 418: 
 419: The modifier arguments can be the following (all of the options are case-insensitive and ignore leading/trailing/extra whitespace):
 420: - A string literal in the format `start of <UNIT>` indicating to truncate the datetime value to a certain unit, which can be the following:
 421:   - **Years**: Supported aliases are `"years"`, `"year"`, and `"y"`.
 422:   - **Quarters**: Supported aliases are `"quarters"`, `"quarter"`, and `"q"`.
 423:   - **Months**: Supported aliases are `"months"`, `"month"`, and `"mm"`.
 424:   - **Days**: Supported aliases are `"days"`, `"day"`, and `"d"`.
 425:   - **Weeks**: Supported aliases are `"weeks"`, `"week"`, and `"w"`.
 426:   - **Hours**: Supported aliases are `"hours"`, `"hour"`, and `"h"`.
 427:   - **Minutes**: Supported aliases are `"minutes"`, `"minute"`, and `"m"`.
 428:   - **Seconds**: Supported aliases are `"seconds"`, `"second"`, and `"s"`.
 429: - A string literal in the form `±<AMT> <UNIT>` indicating to add/subtract a date/time interval to the datetime value. The sign can be `+` or `-`, and if omitted the default is `+`. The amount must be an integer. The unit must be one of the same unit strings allowed for truncation.
 430: 
 431: For example, `"Days"`, `"DAYS"`, and `"d"` are all treated the same due to case insensitivity.
 432: 
 433: If there are multiple modifiers, they operate left-to-right.
 434: 
 435: ```py
 436: # Returns the following datetime moments:
 437: # 1. The current timestamp
 438: # 2. The start of the current month
 439: # 3. Exactly 12 hours from now
 440: # 4. The last day of the previous year
 441: # 5. The current day, at midnight
 442: # 6. The first day after the start of the current quarter
 443: TPCH.CALCULATE(
 444:    ts_1=DATETIME('now'),
 445:    ts_2=DATETIME('NoW', 'start of month'),
 446:    ts_3=DATETIME(' CURRENT_DATE ', '12 hours'),
 447:    ts_4=DATETIME('Current Timestamp', 'start of y', '- 1 D'),
 448:    ts_5=DATETIME('NOW', '  Start  of  Day  '),
 449:    ts_6=DATETIME('now', 'start of quarter', '+1 d'),
 450: )
 451: 
 452: # For each order, truncates the order date to the first day of the year
 453: Orders.CALCULATE(order_year=DATETIME(order_year, 'START OF Y'))
 454: ```
 455: 
 456: <!-- TOC --><a name="year"></a>
 457: 
 458: ### YEAR
 459: 
 460: Calling `YEAR` on a date/timestamp extracts the year it belongs to:
 461: 
 462: ```py
 463: Orders.WHERE(YEAR(order_date) == 1995)
 464: ```
 465: 
 466: <!-- TOC --><a name="quarter"></a>
 467: 
 468: ### QUARTER
 469: 
 470: Calling `QUARTER` on a date/timestamp extracts the quarter of the year it belongs to. The range of output is from 1-4. Months 1-3 are part of quarter 1, months 4-6 are part of quarter 2, months 7-9 are part of quarter 3, and months 10-12 are part of quarter 4.
 471: 
 472: ```py
 473: Orders.WHERE(QUARTER(order_date) == 1)
 474: ```
 475: 
 476: <!-- TOC --><a name="month"></a>
 477: 
 478: ### MONTH
 479: 
 480: Calling `MONTH` on a date/timestamp extracts the month of the year it belongs to:
 481: 
 482: ```py
 483: Orders.CALCULATE(is_summer = (MONTH(order_date) >= 6) & (MONTH(order_date) <= 8))
 484: ```
 485: 
 486: <!-- TOC --><a name="day"></a>
 487: 
 488: ### DAY
 489: 
 490: Calling `DAY` on a date/timestamp extracts the day of the month it belongs to:
 491: 
 492: ```py
 493: Orders.CALCULATE(is_first_of_month = DAY(order_date) == 1)
 494: ```
 495: 
 496: <!-- TOC --><a name="hour"></a>
 497: 
 498: ### HOUR
 499: 
 500: Calling `HOUR` on a date/timestamp extracts the hour it belongs to. The range of output
 501: is from 0-23:
 502: 
 503: ```py
 504: Orders.CALCULATE(is_12pm = HOUR(order_date) == 12)
 505: ```
 506: 
 507: <!-- TOC --><a name="minute"></a>
 508: 
 509: ### MINUTE
 510: 
 511: Calling `MINUTE` on a date/timestamp extracts the minute. The range of output
 512: is from 0-59:
 513: 
 514: ```py
 515: Orders.CALCULATE(is_half_hour = MINUTE(order_date) == 30)
 516: ```
 517: 
 518: <!-- TOC --><a name="second"></a>
 519: 
 520: ### SECOND
 521: 
 522: Calling `SECOND` on a date/timestamp extracts the second. The range of output
 523: is from 0-59:
 524: 
 525: ```py
 526: Orders.CALCULATE(is_lt_30_seconds = SECOND(order_date) < 30)
 527: ```
 528: 
 529: <!-- TOC --><a name="datediff"></a>
 530: 
 531: ### DATEDIFF
 532: 
 533: Calling `DATEDIFF` between 2 timestamps returns the difference in one of `years`, `quarters`, `months`, `weeks`, `days`, `hours`, `minutes` or `seconds`.
 534: 
 535: - `DATEDIFF("years", x, y)`: Returns the **number of full years since x that y occurred**. For example, if **x** is December 31, 2009, and **y** is January 1, 2010, it counts as **1 year apart**, even though they are only 1 day apart.
 536: - `DATEDIFF("quarters", x, y)`: Returns the **number of full quarters since x that y occurred**. For example, if **x** is March 31, 2014, and **y** is April 1, 2014, it counts as **1 quarter apart**, even though they are only 1 day apart.
 537: - `DATEDIFF("months", x, y)`: Returns the **number of full months since x that y occurred**. For example, if **x** is January 31, 2014, and **y** is February 1, 2014, it counts as **1 month apart**, even though they are only 1 day apart.
 538: - `DATEDIFF("weeks", x, y)`: Returns the **number of full weeks since x that y occurred**. The dates x and y are first truncated to the start of week (as specified by the `start_of_week` config), then the difference in number of full weeks is calculated (a week is defined as 7 days). For example, if `start_of_week` is set to Saturday:
 539:   ```python
 540:   # If x is "2025-03-18" (Tuesday) and y is "2025-03-31" (Monday)
 541:   DATEDIFF("weeks", x, y) returns 2
 542:   ```
 543:  Please see the [Session Configs](./usage.md#session-configs) documentation for more details and in-depth examples.
 544: - `DATEDIFF("days", x, y)`: Returns the **number of full days since x that y occurred**. For example, if **x** is 11:59 PM on one day, and **y** is 12:01 AM the next day, it counts as **1 day apart**, even though they are only 2 minutes apart.
 545: - `DATEDIFF("hours", x, y)`: Returns the **number of full hours since x that y occurred**. For example, if **x** is 6:59 PM and **y** is 7:01 PM on the same day, it counts as **1 hour apart**, even though the difference is only 2 minutes.
 546: - `DATEDIFF("minutes", x, y)`: Returns the **number of full minutes since x that y occurred**. For example, if **x** is 7:00 PM and **y** is 7:01 PM, it counts as **1 minute apart**, even though the difference is exactly 60 seconds.
 547: - `DATEDIFF("seconds", x, y)`: Returns the **number of full seconds since x that y occurred**. For example, if **x** is at 7:00:01 PM and **y** is at 7:00:02 PM, it counts as **1 second apart**.
 548: 
 549: ```py
 550: # Calculates, for each order, the number of days since January 1st 1992
 551: # that the order was placed:
 552: Orders.CALCULATE( 
 553:    days_since=DATEDIFF("days",datetime.date(1992, 1, 1), order_date)
 554: )
 555: ```
 556: 
 557: The first argument in the `DATEDIFF` function supports the following aliases for each unit of time. The argument is **case-insensitive**, and if a unit is not one of the provided options, an error will be thrown. See [`DATETIME`](#datetime) for the supported units and their aliases. Invalid or unrecognized units will result in an error.
 558: 
 559: <!-- TOC --><a name="dayofweek"></a>
 560: 
 561: ### DAYOFWEEK
 562: 
 563: The `DAYOFWEEK` function returns the day of the week for a given date/timestamp. It takes a single argument, which is a date/timestamp, and returns an integer between 1 and 7, or between 0 and 6, depending on the `start_of_week` config and `start_week_as_zero` config. Please see the [Session Configs](./usage.md#session-configs) documentation for more details and in-depth examples.
 564: 
 565: In other words, `DAYOFWEEK` returns which day of the week is the given date/timestamp, where the first day of the give date/timestamp is decided by the `start_of_week` config.
 566: 
 567: ```py
 568: # Returns the day of the week for the order date
 569: Orders.CALCULATE(day_of_week = DAYOFWEEK(order_date))
 570: ```
 571: 
 572: The following table shows the day of the week for a given date/timestamp, where the first day of the give date/timestamp is decided by the `start_of_week` config and if the week starts at 0 or 1 decided by the `start_week_as_zero` config.
 573: 
 574: | Day of Week  | Start is Sunday, Start at 0 | Start is Sunday, Start at 1 | Start is Monday, Start at 0 | Start is Monday, Start at 1 |
 575: |--------------|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|
 576: | Sunday       | 0                           | 1                           | 6                           | 7                           |
 577: | Monday       | 1                           | 2                           | 0                           | 1                           |
 578: | Tuesday      | 2                           | 3                           | 1                           | 2                           |
 579: | Wednesday    | 3                           | 4                           | 2                           | 3                           |
 580: | Thursday     | 4                           | 5                           | 3                           | 4                           |
 581: | Friday       | 5                           | 6                           | 4                           | 5                           |
 582: | Saturday     | 6                           | 7                           | 5                           | 6                           |
 583: 
 584: 
 585: <!-- TOC --><a name="dayname"></a>
 586: 
 587: ### DAYNAME
 588: 
 589: The `DAYNAME` function returns the name of the day of the week for a given date/timestamp. It takes a single argument, which is a date/timestamp, and returns a string, corresponding to the name of the day of the week. This returns one of the following: `"Monday"`, `"Tuesday"`, `"Wednesday"`, `"Thursday"`, `"Friday"`, `"Saturday"`, or `"Sunday"`.
 590: 
 591: ```py
 592: # Returns the name of the day of the week for the order date
 593: Orders.CALCULATE(day_name = DAYNAME(order_date))
 594: ```
 595: 
 596: <!-- TOC --><a name="conditional-functions"></a>
 597: 
 598: ## Conditional Functions
 599: 
 600: Below is each function currently supported in PyDough that handles conditional logic.
 601: 
 602: <!-- TOC --><a name="iff"></a>
 603: 
 604: ### IFF
 605: 
 606: The `IFF` function cases on the True/False value of its first argument. If it is True, it returns the second argument, otherwise it returns the third argument. In this way, the PyDough code `IFF(a, b, c)` is semantically the same as the SQL expression `CASE WHEN a THEN b ELSE c END`.
 607: 
 608: ```py
 609: qty_from_germany = IFF(supplier.nation.name == "GERMANY", quantity, 0)
 610: Customers.CALCULATE(
 611:     total_quantity_shipped_from_germany = SUM(lines.CALCULATE(q=qty_from_germany).q)
 612: )
 613: ```
 614: 
 615: <!-- TOC --><a name="isin"></a>
 616: 
 617: ### ISIN
 618: 
 619: The `ISIN` function takes in an expression and an iterable of literals and returns whether the expression is a member of provided literals.
 620: 
 621: ```py
 622: Parts.WHERE(ISIN(size, (10, 11, 17, 19, 45)))
 623: ```
 624: 
 625: <!-- TOC --><a name="default_to"></a>
 626: 
 627: ### DEFAULT_TO
 628: 
 629: The `DEFAULT_TO` function returns the first of its arguments that is non-null (e.g. the same as the `COALESCE` function in SQL):
 630: 
 631: ```py
 632: Lineitems.CALCULATE(adj_tax = DEFAULT_TO(tax, 0))
 633: ```
 634: 
 635: <!-- TOC --><a name="present"></a>
 636: 
 637: ### PRESENT
 638: 
 639: The `PRESENT` function checks if its argument is non-null (e.g. the same as `IS NOT NULL` in SQL):
 640: 
 641: ```py
 642: Lineitems.CALCULATE(has_tax = PRESENT(tax))
 643: ```
 644: 
 645: <!-- TOC --><a name="absent"></a>
 646: 
 647: ### ABSENT
 648: 
 649: The `ABSENT` function checks if its argument is null (e.g. the same as `IS NULL` in SQL):
 650: 
 651: ```py
 652: Lineitems.CALCULATE(no_tax = ABSENT(tax))
 653: ```
 654: 
 655: <!-- TOC --><a name="keep_if"></a>
 656: 
 657: ### KEEP_IF
 658: 
 659: The `KEEP_IF` function returns the first function if the second arguments is True, otherwise it returns a null value. In other words, `KEEP_IF(a, b)` is equivalent to the SQL expression `CASE WHEN b THEN a END`.
 660: 
 661: ```py
 662: TPCH.CALCULATE(avg_non_debt_balance = AVG(Customers.CALCULATE(no_debt_bal = KEEP_IF(acctbal, acctbal > 0)).no_debt_bal))
 663: ```
 664: 
 665: <!-- TOC --><a name="monotonic"></a>
 666: 
 667: ### MONOTONIC
 668: 
 669: The `MONOTONIC` function checks if all of its arguments are in ascending order (e.g. `MONOTONIC(a, b, c, d)` is equivalent to `(a <= b) & (b <= c) & (c <= d)`):
 670: 
 671: ```py
 672: Lineitems.WHERE(MONOTONIC(10, quantity, 20) & MONOTONIC(5, part.size, 13))
 673: ```
 674: 
 675: <!-- TOC --><a name="numerical-functions"></a>
 676: 
 677: ## Numerical Functions
 678: 
 679: Below is each numerical function currently supported in PyDough.
 680: 
 681: <!-- TOC --><a name="abs"></a>
 682: 
 683: ### ABS
 684: 
 685: The `ABS` function returns the absolute value of its input. The Python builtin `abs()` function can also be used to accomplish the same thing.
 686: 
 687: ```py
 688: Customers.CALCULATE(acct_magnitude = ABS(acctbal))
 689: # The below statement is equivalent to above.
 690: Customers.CALCULATE(acct_magnitude = abs(acctbal))
 691: ```
 692: 
 693: <!-- TOC --><a name="round"></a>
 694: 
 695: ### ROUND
 696: 
 697: The `ROUND` function rounds its first argument to the precision of its second argument. The rounding rules used depend on the database's round function. The second argument is optional, and if not provided, the first argument is rounded to 0 decimal places. The Python builtin `round()` function can also be used to accomplish the same thing. 
 698: 
 699: ```py
 700: Parts.CALCULATE(rounded_price = ROUND(retail_price, 1))
 701: # The below statement is equivalent to above.
 702: Parts.CALCULATE(rounded_price = round(retail_price, 1))
 703: 
 704: # The below statement takes the default precision as 0.
 705: Parts.CALCULATE(rounded_price = ROUND(retail_price))
 706: # The below statement is equivalent to above.
 707: Parts.CALCULATE(rounded_price = ROUND(retail_price,0))
 708: ```
 709: 
 710: Note: The default precision for builtin `round` method is 0, to be in alignment with the Python implementation. The PyDough `ROUND` function requires the precision to be specified.
 711: 
 712: ```py
 713: # This is legal.
 714: Parts.CALCULATE(rounded_price = round(retail_price))
 715: # This is illegal as precision is not specified.
 716: Parts.CALCULATE(rounded_price = ROUND(retail_price))
 717: ```
 718: 
 719: <!-- TOC --><a name="power"></a>
 720: 
 721: ### POWER
 722: 
 723: The `POWER` function exponentiates its first argument to the power of its second argument.
 724: 
 725: ```py
 726: Parts.CALCULATE(powered_price = POWER(retail_price, 2))
 727: ```
 728: 
 729: <!-- TOC --><a name="sqrt"></a>
 730: 
 731: ### SQRT
 732: 
 733: The `SQRT` function takes the square root of its input. It's equivalent to `POWER(x,0.5)`.
 734: 
 735: ```py
 736: Parts.CALCULATE(sqrt_price = SQRT(retail_price))
 737: ```
 738: 
 739: <!-- TOC --><a name="sign"></a>
 740: 
 741: ### SIGN
 742: 
 743: The `SIGN` function returns the sign of its input. It returns 1 if the input is positive, -1 if the input is negative, and 0 if the input is zero.
 744: 
 745: ```py
 746: Suppliers.CALCULATE(sign_of_acctbal = SIGN(account_balance))
 747: ```
 748: 
 749: <!-- TOC --><a name="smallest"></a>
 750: 
 751: ### SMALLEST
 752: 
 753: The `SMALLEST` function returns the smallest value from the set of values it is called on. It can take in a variable number of arguments, but at least two arguments are required. If any of the arguments are `NULL`, the function will return `NULL`.
 754: 
 755: ```py
 756: TPCH.CALCULATE(
 757:     s1=SMALLEST(20,10,10,-1,-2,100,-200), # Returns -200
 758:     s2=SMALLEST(-0.001,-0.01,-0.0001), # Returns -0.0001
 759:     s3=SMALLEST(datetime.datetime(2025,1,1),datetime.datetime(2024,1,1)), # Returns 2024-01-01
 760:     s4=SMALLEST(1,None,3,4), # Returns NULL
 761: )
 762: # Average gap, in days, for shipments between when they were ordered
 763: # versus when they were expected to arrive (or when they actually arrived,
 764: # if they were early), for shipments done via rail.
 765: delay_info = Lineitems.WHERE(HAS(order) & (ship_mode == "RAIL")).CALCULATE(
 766:    day_gap=DATEDIFF("days", order.order_date, SMALLEST(commit_date, receipt_date))
 767: )
 768: return TPCH.CALCULATE(avg_gap=AVG(delay_info.day_gap))
 769: ```
 770: 
 771: <!-- TOC --><a name="largest"></a>
 772: 
 773: ### LARGEST
 774: 
 775: The `LARGEST` function returns the largest value from the set of values it is called on. It can take in a variable number of arguments, but at least two arguments are required. If any of the arguments are `NULL`, the function will return `NULL`.
 776: 
 777: ```py
 778: TPCH.CALCULATE(
 779:     l1=LARGEST(20,10,10,-1,-2,100,-200), # Returns 100
 780:     l2=LARGEST(-0.001,-0.01,-0.0001), # Returns -0.01
 781:     l3=LARGEST(datetime.datetime(2025,1,1),datetime.datetime(2024,1,1)), # Returns 2025-01-01
 782:     l4=LARGEST(1,None,3,4), # Returns NULL
 783: )
 784: # For each region, what is the average account balance of all
 785: # customers in a hypothetical scenario where all debt was erased
 786: Regions.CALCULATE(
 787:    region_name=name,
 788:    avg_bal_without_debt_erasure=AVG(LARGEST(nations.customers.acctbal, 0)),
 789: )
 790: ```
 791: 
 792: <!-- TOC --><a name="aggregation-functions"></a>
 793: 
 794: ## Aggregation Functions
 795: 
 796: When terms of a plural sub-collection are accessed, those terms are plural with regards to the current collection. For example, if each nation in `Nations` has multiple `customers`, and each customer has a single `acctbal`, then `customers.acctbal` is plural with regards to `Nations` and cannot be used in any calculations when the current context is `Nations`. The exception to this is when `customers.acctbal` is made singular with regards to `Nations` by aggregating it.
 797: 
 798: Aggregation functions are a special set of functions that, when called on their inputs, convert them from plural to singular. Below is each aggregation function currently supported in PyDough.
 799: 
 800: <!-- TOC --><a name="sum"></a>
 801: 
 802: ### SUM
 803: 
 804: The `SUM` function returns the sum of the plural set of numerical values it is called on.
 805: 
 806: ```py
 807: Nations.CALCULATE(total_consumer_wealth = SUM(customers.acctbal))
 808: ```
 809: 
 810: <!-- TOC --><a name="avg"></a>
 811: 
 812: ### AVG
 813: 
 814: The `AVG` function takes the average of the plural set of numerical values it is called on.
 815: 
 816: ```py
 817: Parts.CALCULATE(average_shipment_size = AVG(lines.quantity))
 818: ```
 819: 
 820: <!-- TOC --><a name="median"></a>
 821: 
 822: ### MEDIAN
 823: 
 824: The `MEDIAN` function takes the median of the plural set of numerical values it is called on.
 825: Note: absent records are ignored when deriving the median.
 826: 
 827: ```py
 828: Customers.CALCULATE(
 829:    name,
 830:    median_order_price = MEDIAN(orders.total_price)
 831: )
 832: ```
 833: 
 834: <!-- TOC --><a name="min"></a>
 835: 
 836: ### MIN
 837: 
 838: The `MIN` function returns the smallest value from the set of values it is called on.
 839: 
 840: ```py
 841: Suppliers.CALCULATE(cheapest_part_supplied = MIN(supply_records.supply_cost))
 842: ```
 843: 
 844: <!-- TOC --><a name="max"></a>
 845: 
 846: ### MAX
 847: 
 848: The `MAX` function returns the largest value from the set of values it is called on.
 849: 
 850: ```py
 851: Suppliers.CALCULATE(most_expensive_part_supplied = MAX(supply_records.supply_cost))
 852: ```
 853: 
 854: <!-- TOC --><a name="anything"></a>
 855: 
 856: ### ANYTHING
 857: 
 858: The `ANYTHING` function returns an arbitrary value from the set of values it is called on.
 859: 
 860: ```py
 861: Suppliers.CALCULATE(chosen_part_name = ANYTHING(supply_records.part.name))
 862: ```
 863: 
 864: <!-- TOC --><a name="count"></a>
 865: 
 866: ### COUNT
 867: 
 868: The `COUNT` function returns how many non-null records exist on the set of plural values it is called on.
 869: 
 870: ```py
 871: Customers.CALCULATE(num_taxed_purchases = COUNT(orders.lines.tax))
 872: ```
 873: 
 874: The `COUNT` function can also be called on a sub-collection, in which case it will return how many records from that sub-collection exist.
 875: 
 876: ```py
 877: Nations.CALCULATE(num_customers_in_debt = COUNT(customers.WHERE(acctbal < 0)))
 878: ```
 879: 
 880: <!-- TOC --><a name="ndistinct"></a>
 881: 
 882: ### NDISTINCT
 883: 
 884: The `NDISTINCT` function returns how many distinct values of its argument exist.
 885: 
 886: ```py
 887: Customers.CALCULATE(num_unique_parts_purchased = NDISTINCT(orders.lines.parts.key))
 888: ```
 889: 
 890: <!-- TOC --><a name="has"></a>
 891: 
 892: ### HAS
 893: 
 894: The `HAS` function is called on a sub-collection and returns `True` if at least one record of the sub-collection exists. In other words, `HAS(x)` is equivalent to `COUNT(x) > 0`.
 895: 
 896: ```py
 897: Parts.WHERE(HAS(supply_records.supplier.WHERE(nation.name == "GERMANY")))
 898: ```
 899: 
 900: <!-- TOC --><a name="hasnot"></a>
 901: 
 902: ### HASNOT
 903: 
 904: The `HASNOT` function is called on a sub-collection and returns `True` if no records of the sub-collection exist. In other words, `HASNOT(x)` is equivalent to `COUNT(x) == 0`.
 905: 
 906: ```py
 907: Customers.WHERE(HASNOT(orders))
 908: ```
 909: 
 910: <!-- TOC --><a name="var"></a>
 911: 
 912: ### VAR
 913: 
 914: The `VAR` function returns the variance of the set of numerical values it is called on. This operation supports the `type` keyword argument, which can be used to specify the type of variance to compute. The following variances are supported:
 915: 
 916: - `"population"` (default value): The population variance.
 917: - `"sample"`: The sample variance.
 918: 
 919: ```py
 920: # Compute the population variance
 921: Parts.CALCULATE(variance = VAR(supply_records.supply_cost))
 922: 
 923: # Compute the sample variance
 924: Parts.CALCULATE(variance = VAR(supply_records.supply_cost, type="sample"))
 925: ```
 926: 
 927: <!-- TOC --><a name="std"></a>
 928: 
 929: ### STD
 930: 
 931: The `STD` function returns the standard deviation of the set of numerical values it is called on. This operation supports the `type` keyword argument, which can be used to specify the type of standard deviation to compute. The following standard deviations are supported:
 932: 
 933: - `"population"` (default value): The population standard deviation.
 934: - `"sample"`: The sample standard deviation.
 935: 
 936: ```py
 937: # Compute the population standard deviation
 938: Parts.CALCULATE(std = STD(supply_records.supply_cost))
 939: 
 940: # Compute the sample standard deviation
 941: Parts.CALCULATE(std = STD(supply_records.supply_cost, type="sample"))
 942: ```
 943: 
 944: <!-- TOC --><a name="window-functions"></a>
 945: 
 946: ## Window Functions
 947: 
 948: Window functions are special functions whose output depends on other records in the same context.A common example of this is finding the ranking of each record if all of the records were to be sorted.
 949: 
 950: Window functions in PyDough have an optional `per` argument. If this argument is omitted, it means that the window function applies to all records of the current collection (e.g. rank all customers). If it is provided, it should be a string that describes which ancestor of the current context the window function should be calculated with regards to, and in that case it means that the set of values used by the window function should be per-record of the correspond ancestor (e.g. rank all customers per-nation).
 951: 
 952: For example, if using the `RANKING` window function, consider the following examples:
 953: 
 954: ```py
 955: # Rank every customer relative to all other customers byacctbal
 956: Regions.nations.customers.CALCULATE(r=RANKING(by=acctbal.DESC()))
 957: 
 958: # Rank every customer relative to other customers in the same nation, by acctbal
 959: Regions.nations.customers.CALCULATE(r=RANKING(by=acctbal.DESC(), per="nations"))
 960: 
 961: # Rank every customer relative to other customers in the same region, by acctbal
 962: Regions.nations.customers.CALCULATE(r=RANKING(by=acctbal.DESC(), per="Regions"))
 963: ```
 964: 
 965: If there are multiple ancestors of the current context with the same name, the `per` string should include a suffix `:idx` where `idx` specifies which ancestor with that name to use (`1` = the most recent, `2` = the 2nd most recent, etc.) For example, consider the following:
 966: 
 967: ```py
 968: order_info = Orders.CALCULATE(y=YEAR(order_date), m=MONTH(order_date))
 969: p1 = order_info.PARTITION(name="groups", by=(y, m))
 970: p2 = p1.(name="groups", by=(y))
 971: data = p2.groups.Orders
 972: 
 973: # Ranks each order per year/month by its total price.
 974: # The full ancestry is p2 [name=groups] -> p1 [name=groups] -> order_info [name=Orders],
 975: # So "groups:1" means the window function should be computed with regards to p1
 976: # since it is the most recent ancestor with the name "groups".
 977: data.CALCULATE(r=RANKING(by=total_price.DESC(), per="groups:1"))
 978: 
 979: # Ranks each order per year by its total price.
 980: # The full ancestry is p2 [name=groups] -> p1 [name=groups] -> order_info [name=Orders],
 981: # So "groups:2" means the window function should be computed with regards to p2
 982: # since it is the 2nd most recent ancestor with the name "groups".
 983: data.CALCULATE(r=RANKING(by=total_price.DESC(), per="groups:2"))
 984: ```
 985: 
 986: Below is each window function currently supported in PyDough.
 987: 
 988: <!-- TOC --><a name="ranking"></a>
 989: 
 990: ### RANKING
 991: 
 992: The `RANKING` function returns ordinal position of the current record when all records in the current context are sorted by certain ordering keys. The arguments:
 993: 
 994: - `by`:1+ collation values, either as a single expression or an iterable of expressions, used to order the records of the current context. PyDough provides `collation_default_asc` and `propagate_collation` configs to control the default collation and whether to propagate the collation if the current expression is not a collation expression. Please see the [Session Configs](./usage.md#session-configs) documentation for more details.
 995: - `per` (optional): optional argument (default `None`) for the same `per` argument as all other window functions.
 996: - `allow_ties` (optional): optional argument (default False) specifying to allow values that are tied according to the `by` expressions to have the same rank value. If False, tied values have different rank values where ties are broken arbitrarily.
 997: - `dense` (optional): optional argument (default False) specifying that if `allow_ties` is True and a tie is found, should the next value after the ties be the current ranking value plus 1, as opposed to jumping to a higher value based on the number of ties that were there. For example, with the values `[a, a, b, b, b, c]`, the values with `dense=True` would be `[1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3]`, but with `dense=False` they would be `[1, 1, 3, 3, 3, 6]`.
 998: - `by`: 1+ collation values, either as a single expression or an iterable of expressions, used to order the records of the current context. PyDough provides `collation_default_asc` and `propagate_collation` configs to control the default collation and whether to propagate the collation if the current expression is not a collation expression. Please see the [Session Configs](./usage.md#session-configs) documentation for more details.
 999: 
1000: ```py
1001: # Rank customers per-nation by their account balance
1002: # (highest = rank #1, no ties)
1003: Nations.customers.CALCULATE(r = RANKING(by=acctbal.DESC(), per="Nations"))
1004: 
1005: # For every customer, finds their most recent order
1006: # (ties allowed)
1007: Customers.orders.WHERE(RANKING(by=order_date.DESC(), per="Customers", allow_ties=True) == 1)
1008: ```
1009: 
1010: <!-- TOC --><a name="percentile"></a>
1011: 
1012: ### PERCENTILE
1013: 
1014: The `PERCENTILE` function returns what index the current record belongs to if all records in the current context are ordered then split into evenly sized buckets. The arguments:
1015: 
1016: - `by`: 1+ collation values, either as a single expression or an iterable of expressions, used to order the records of the current context. PyDough provides `collation_default_asc` and `propagate_collation` configs to control the default collation and whether to propagate the collation if the current expression is not a collation expression. Please see the [Session Configs](./usage.md#session-configs) documentation for more details.
1017: - `per` (optional): optional argument (default `None`) for the same `per` argument as all other window functions.
1018: - `n_buckets` (optional): optional argument (default 100) specifying the number of buckets to use. The first values according to the sort order are assigned bucket `1`, and the last values are assigned bucket `n_buckets`.
1019: 
1020: ```py
1021: # Keep the top 0.1% of customers with the highest account balances.
1022: Customers.WHERE(PERCENTILE(by=acctbal.ASC(), n_buckets=1000) == 1000)
1023: 
1024: # For every region, find the top 5% of customers with the highest account balances.
1025: Regions.nations.customers.WHERE(PERCENTILE(by=acctbal.ASC(), per="Regions") > 95)
1026: ```
1027: 
1028: <!-- TOC --><a name="prev"></a>
1029: 
1030: ### PREV
1031: 
1032: The `PREV` function returns the value of an expression from a preceding record in the collection. The arguments:
1033: 
1034: - `expression`: the expression to return the shifted value of.
1035: - `n` (optional): optional argument (default `1`) how many records backwards to look.
1036: - `default` (optional): optional argument (default `None`) the value to output when there is no record `n` before the current record. This must be a valid literal.
1037: - `by`: 1+ collation values, either as a single expression or an iterable of expressions, used to order the records of the current context.
1038: - `per` (optional): optional argument (default `None`) for the same `per` argument as all other window functions.
1039: 
1040: ```py
1041: # Find the 10 customers with at least 5 orders with the largest average time
1042: # gap between their orders, in days.
1043: order_info = orders.CALCULATE(
1044:    day_diff=DATEDIFF("days", PREV(order_date, by=order_date.ASC(), per="Customers"), order_date)
1045: )
1046: Customers.WHERE(COUNT(orders) > 5).CALCULATE(
1047:    name,
1048:    average_order_gap=AVG(order_info.day_diff)
1049: ).TOP_K(10, by=average_order_gap.DESC())
1050: 

1067: 
1068: <!-- TOC --><a name="next"></a>
1069: 
1070: ### NEXT
1071: 
1072: The `NEXT` function returns the value of an expression from a following record in the collection. In other words, `NEXT(expr, n)` is the same as `PREV(expr, -n)`. The arguments:
1073: 
1074: - `expression`: the expression to return the shifted value of.
1075: - `n` (optional): optional argument (default `1`) how many records forward to look.
1076: - `default` (optional): optional argument (default `None`) the value to output when there is no record `n` after the current record. This must be a valid literal.
1077: - `by`: 1+ collation values, either as a single expression or an iterable of expressions, used to order the records of the current context.
1078: - `per` (optional): optional argument (default `None`) for the same `per` argument as all other window functions.
1079: 
1080: 
1081: <!-- TOC --><a name="relsum"></a>
1082: 
1083: ### RELSUM
1084: 
1085: The `RELSUM` function returns the sum of multiple rows of a singular expression within the same collection, e.g. the global sum across all rows, or the sum of rows per an ancestor of a sub-collection. The arguments:
1086: 
1087: - `expression`: the singular expression to take the sum of across multiple rows.
1088: - `per` (optional): optional argument (default `None`) for the same `per` argument as all other window functions.
1089: - `by` (optional): 1+ collation values, either as a single expression or an iterable of expressions, used to order the records of the current context. Can only be provided if `cumulative` is True.
1090: - `cumulative` (optional): optional argument (default `False`) that can only be `True` if the `by` argument is provided. If `True`, then instead of returning the sum of all of the data in the context, returns the cumulative sum of all rows up to and including the current row when sorted according to the keys in the `by` argument.
1091: 
1092: For example:
1093: 
1094: ```py
1095: # Finds the ratio between each customer's account balance and the global
1096: # sum of all customers' account balances.
1097: Customers.CALCULATE(ratio=acctbal / RELSUM(acctbal))
1098: 
1099: # Finds the ratio between each customer's account balance and the sum of all
1100: # all customers' account balances within that nation.
1101: Nations.customers.CALCULATE(ratio=acctbal / RELSUM(acctbal, per="Nations"))
1102: 
1103: # Finds, for each customer, the wealth of that customer combined with all
1104: # poorer customers.
1105: Customers.CALCULATE(cumulative_wealth=RELSUM(acctbal, by=acctbal.ASC(), cumulative=True))
1106: ```
1107: 
1108: 
1109: <!-- TOC --><a name="relavg"></a>
1110: 
1111: ### RELAVG
1112: 
1113: The `RELAVG` function returns the average of multiple rows of a singular expression within the same collection, e.g. the global average across all rows, or the average of rows per an ancestor of a sub-collection. The arguments:
1114: 
1115: - `expression`: the singular expression to take the average of across multiple rows.
1116: - `per` (optional): optional argument (default `None`) for the same `per` argument as all other window functions.
1117: - `by` (optional): 1+ collation values, either as a single expression or an iterable of expressions, used to order the records of the current context. Can only be provided if `cumulative` is True.
1118: - `cumulative` (optional): optional argument (default `False`) that can only be `True` if the `by` argument is provided. If `True`, then instead of returning the average of all of the data in the context, returns the cumulative average of all rows up to and including the current row when sorted according to the keys in the `by` argument.
1119: 
1120: ```py
1121: # Finds all customers whose account balance is above the global average of all
1122: # customers' account balances.
1123: Customers.WHERE(acctbal > RELAVG(acctbal))
1124: 
1125: # Finds all customers whose account balance is above the average of all
1126: # customers' account balances within that nation.
1127: Nations.customers.WHERE(acctbal > RELAVG(acctbal, per="Nations"))
1128: 
1129: # Finds the cumulative average of the total price of orders when sorted by
1130: # order date (breaking ties by the order key).
1131: Orders.CALCULATE(average_price_so_far=RELAVG(total_price, by=(order_date.ASC(), key.ASC()), cumulative=True))
1132: ```
1133: 
1134: 
1135: <!-- TOC --><a name="relcount"></a>
1136: 
1137: ### RELCOUNT
1138: 
1139: The `RELCOUNT` function returns the number of non-null records in multiple rows of a singular expression within the same collection, e.g. the count of all non-null rows, or the number of non-null rows per an ancestor of a sub-collection. The arguments:
1140: 
1141: - `expression`: the singular expression to count the number of non-null entries across multiple rows.
1142: - `per` (optional): optional argument (default `None`) for the same `per` argument as all other window functions.
1143: - `by` (optional): 1+ collation values, either as a single expression or an iterable of expressions, used to order the records of the current context. Can only be provided if `cumulative` is True.
1144: - `cumulative` (optional): optional argument (default `False`) that can only be `True` if the `by` argument is provided. If `True`, then instead of returning the count of all of the data in the context, returns the cumulative count of all rows up to and including the current row when sorted according to the keys in the `by` argument.
1145: 
1146: 
1147: ```py
1148: # Divides each customer's account balance by the total number of positive
1149: # account balances globally.
1150: Customers.CALCULATE(ratio = acctbal / RELCOUNT(KEEP_IF(acctbal, acctbal > 0.0)))
1151: 
1152: # Divides each customer's account balance by the total number of positive
1153: # account balances in the same nation.
1154: Nations.customers.CALCULATE(ratio = acctbal / RELCOUNT(KEEP_IF(acctbal, acctbal > 0.0), per="Nations"))
1155: 
1156: # For each customer, count how many customers are poorer than them but are not
1157: # in debt.
1158: Customers.CALCULATE(n_poorer_non_debt=RELCOUNT(KEEP_IF(acctbal, acctbal >= 0), by=(acctbal.ASC()), cumulative=True) - (acctbal >= 0))
1159: ```
1160: 
1161: 
1162: <!-- TOC --><a name="relsize"></a>
1163: 
1164: ### RELSIZE
1165: 
1166: The `RELSIZE` function returns the number of total records, either globally or the number of sub-collection rows per some ancestor collection. The arguments:
1167: 
1168: - `per` (optional): optional argument (default `None`) for the same `per` argument as all other window functions.
1169: - `by` (optional): 1+ collation values, either as a single expression or an iterable of expressions, used to order the records of the current context. Can only be provided if `cumulative` is True.
1170: - `cumulative` (optional): optional argument (default `False`) that can only be `True` if the `by` argument is provided. If `True`, then instead of returning the number rows in the context, returns the cumulative number of rows up to and including the current row when sorted according to the keys in the `by` argument.
1171: 
1172: 
1173: ```py
1174: # Divides each customer's account balance by
1175: # the number of total customers.
1176: Customers.CALCULATE(ratio = acctbal / RELSIZE())
1177: 
1178: # Divides each customer's account balance by the
1179: # number of total customers in that nation.
1180: Nations.customers.CALCULATE(ratio = acctbal / RELSIZE(per="Nations"))
1181: 
1182: # For each customer, returns the number of customers poorer than them.
1183: Customers.CALCULATE(customers_poorer=RELSIZE(by=(acctbal.ASC()), cumulative=True) - 1)
1184: ```
1185: 
1186: 
1187: <!-- TOC --><a name="casting-functions"></a>
1188: 
1189: ## Casting Functions
1190: 
1191: <!-- TOC --><a name="string"></a>
1192: ### STRING
1193: 
1194: The `STRING` function casts the first argument to a string data type. The first argument can be of any data type. This function also supports formatting of dates. This is possible by placing a date-time format string in the second argument. **Please refer to your underlying database's documentation for the format strings it supports.**
1195: 
1196: 
1197: ```py
1198: Orders.CALCULATE(
1199:    # Casts the key column (numeric type) to a string.
1200:    key_string=STRING(key),
1201:    # Casts the order_date column (date type) to a string
1202:    # with the format YYYY-MM-DD.
1203:    # Please refer to your underlying database's documentation
1204:    # for the format strings it supports.
1205:    # In this case, the database used is SQLite.
1206:    order_date_string=STRING(order_date, "%Y-%m-%d"),
1207: )
1208: ```
1209: 
1210: Here is a list of reference links for the format strings of different databases:
1211: 
1212: - [SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_datefunc.html)
1213: 
1214: <!-- TOC --><a name="integer"></a>
1215: 
1216: ### INTEGER
1217: 
1218: The `INTEGER` function casts the argument to an integer.
1219: 
1220: ```py
1221: Orders.CALCULATE(
1222:    # Casts the total_price column (decimal type) to an integer.
1223:    total_price_int=INTEGER(total_price),
1224:    # Casts the string "2" to an integer.
1225:    discount = INTEGER("2")
1226: )
1227: ```
1228: 
1229: <!-- TOC --><a name="float"></a>
1230: 
1231: ### FLOAT
1232: 
1233: The `FLOAT` function casts the argument to a float.
1234: 
1235: ```py
1236: Orders.CALCULATE(
1237:    # Casts the ship_priority column (integer type) to a float.
1238:    ship_priority_float=FLOAT(ship_priority),
1239:    # Casts the string "2" to a float.
1240:    discount = FLOAT("-2.71")
1241: )
1242: ```
1243: 
1244: ## Banned Python Logic
1245: 
1246: Below is a list of banned python logic (magic methods,etc.) that are not supported in PyDough. Calling these methods will result in an Exception.
1247: 
1248: <!-- TOC --><a name="__bool__"></a>
1249: 
1250: ### \_\_bool\_\_
1251: 
1252: The `__bool__` magic method is not supported in PyDough. PyDough code cannot be treated as booleans.
1253: 
1254: ```py
1255: # Not allowed - will raise PyDoughUnqualifiedException
1256: if Customer and Order:
1257:    print("Available")
1258: 
1259: Customers.WHERE((acctbal > 0) and (nation.name == "GERMANY"))
1260: # Use &`instead of `and`:
1261: # Customers.WHERE((acctbal > 0) & (nation.name == "GERMANY"))
1262: 
1263: Orders.WHERE((discount > 0.05) or (tax > 0.08))
1264: # Use `|` instead of `or` 
1265: # Orders.WHERE((discount > 0.05) | (tax > 0.08))
1266: 
1267: Parts.WHERE(not(retail_price > 1000))
1268: # Use `~` instead of `not`
1269: # Parts.WHERE(~(retail_price > 1000))
1270: ```
1271: 
1272: <!-- TOC --><a name="__call__"></a>
1273: 
1274: ### \_\_call\_\_
1275: 
1276: The `__call__` magic method is not supported in PyDough as it calls PyDough code as if it were a function.
1277: 
1278: ```py
1279: # Not allowed - calls PyDough code as if it were a function
1280: (1 - discount)(extended_price * 0.5)
1281: ```
1282: 
1283: <!-- TOC --><a name="__floor__"></a>
1284: 
1285: ### \_\_floor\_\_
1286: 
1287: The `math.floor` function calls the `__floor__` magic method, which is currently not supported in PyDough.
1288: 
1289: ```py
1290: Customer(age=math.floor(order.total_price))
1291: ```
1292: 
1293: <!-- TOC --><a name="__ceil__"></a>
1294: 
1295: ### \_\_ceil\_\_
1296: 
1297: The `math.ceil` function calls the `__ceil__` magic method, which is currently not supported in PyDough.
1298: 
1299: ```py
1300: # Not allowed currently- will raise PyDoughUnqualifiedException
1301: Customer(age=math.ceil(order.total_price))
1302: ```
1303: 
1304: <!-- TOC --><a name="__trunc__"></a>
1305: 
1306: ### \_\_trunc\_\_
1307: 
1308: The `math.trunc` function calls the `__trunc__` magic method, which is currently not supported in PyDough.
1309: 
1310: ```py
1311: # Not allowed currently- will raise PyDoughUnqualifiedException
1312: Customer(age=math.trunc(order.total_price))
1313: ```
1314: 
1315: <!-- TOC --><a name="__reversed__"></a>
1316: 
1317: ### \_\_reversed\_\_
1318: 
1319: The `reversed` function calls the `__reversed__` magic method, which is currently not supported in PyDough.
1320: 
1321: ```py
1322: # Not allowed currently- will raise PyDoughUnqualifiedException
1323: Regions(backwards_name=reversed(name))
1324: ```
1325: 
1326: <!-- TOC --><a name="__int__"></a>
1327: 
1328: ### \_\_int\_\_
1329: 
1330: Casting to `int` calls the `__int__` magic method, which is not supported in PyDough. This operation is not allowed because the implementation has to return an integer instead of a PyDough object.
1331: 
1332: ```py
1333: # Not allowed currently as it would need to return an int instead of a PyDough object
1334: Orders(limit=int(order.total_price))
1335: ```
1336: 
1337: <!-- TOC --><a name="__float__"></a>
1338: 
1339: ### \_\_float\_\_
1340: 
1341: Casting to `float` calls the `__float__` magic method, which is not supported in PyDough. This operation is not allowed because the implementation has to return a float instead of a PyDough object.
1342: 
1343: ```py
1344: # Not allowed currently as it would need to return a float instead of a PyDough object
1345: Orders(limit=float(order.quantity))
1346: ```
1347: 
1348: <!-- TOC --><a name="__complex__"></a>
1349: 
1350: ### \_\_complex\_\_
1351: 
1352: Casting to `complex` calls the `__complex__` magic method, which is not supported in PyDough. This operation is not allowed because the implementation has to return a complex instead of a PyDough object.
1353: 
1354: ```py
1355: # Not allowed currently as it would need to return a complex instead of a PyDough object
1356: Orders(limit=complex(order.total_price))
1357: ```
1358: 
1359: <!-- TOC --><a name="__index__"></a>
1360: 
1361: ### \_\_index\_\_
1362: 
1363: Using an object as an index calls the `__index__` magic method, which is not supported in PyDough. This operation is not allowed because the implementation has to return an integer instead of a PyDough object.
1364: 
1365: ```py
1366: # Not allowed currently as it would need to return an int instead of a PyDough object
1367: Orders(s="ABCDE"[:order_priority])
1368: ```
1369: 
1370: <!-- TOC --><a name="__nonzero__"></a>
1371: 
1372: ### \_\_nonzero\_\_
1373: 
1374: Using an object in a boolean context calls the `__nonzero__` magic method, which is not supported in PyDough. This operation is not allowed because the implementation has to return an integer instead of a PyDough object.
1375: 
1376: ```py
1377: # Not allowed currently as it would need to return an int instead of a PyDough object
1378: Lineitems(is_taxed=bool(tax))
1379: ```
1380: 
1381: <!-- TOC --><a name="__len__"></a>
1382: 
1383: ### \_\_len\_\_
1384: 
1385: The `len` function calls the `__len__` magic method, which is not supported in PyDough. This operation is not allowed because the implementation has to return an integer instead of a PyDough object. Instead, usage of [LENGTH](#length) function is recommended.
1386: 
1387: ```py
1388: # Not allowed currently as it would need to return an int instead of a PyDough object
1389: Customers(len(customer.name))
1390: ```
1391: 
1392: <!-- TOC --><a name="__contains__"></a>
1393: 
1394: ### \_\_contains\_\_
1395: 
1396: Using the `in` operator calls the `__contains__` magic method, which is not supported in PyDough. This operation is not allowed because the implementation has to return a boolean instead of a PyDough object. Instead, If you need to check if a string is inside another substring, use [CONTAINS](#contains). If you need to check if an expression is a member of a list of literals, use [ISIN](#isin).
1397: 
1398: ```py
1399: # Not allowed currently as it would need to return a boolean instead of a PyDough object
1400: Orders('discount' in order.details)
1401: ```
1402: 
1403: <!-- TOC --><a name="__setitem__"></a>
1404: 
1405: ### \_\_setitem\_\_
1406: 
1407: Assigning to an index calls the `__setitem__` magic method, which is not supported in PyDough. This operation is not allowed.
1408: 
1409: ```py
1410: # Not allowed currently as PyDough objects cannot support item assignment.
1411: Order.details['discount'] = True
1412: ```
1413: 
1414: <!-- TOC --><a name="__iter__"></a>
1415: 
1416: ### \_\_iter\_\_
1417: 
1418: Iterating over an object calls the `__iter__` magic method, which is not supported in PyDough. This operation is not allowed because the implementation has to return an iterator instead of a PyDough object.
1419: 
1420: ```py
1421: # Not allowed currently as implementation has to return an iterator instead of a PyDough object.
1422: for item in customer:
1423:    print(item)
1424: 
1425: [item for item in customer]
1426: 
1427: list(customer)
1428: 
1429: tuple(customer)
1430: ```
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/documentation/metadata.md
````markdown
  1: # PyDough Metadata Spec
  2: 
  3: This page document the exact format that the JSON files containing PyDough metadata must ascribe to. The specification of this format is for the initial release of PyDough, but is intended to change drastically in the near future.
  4: 
  5: <!-- TOC start (generated with https://github.com/derlin/bitdowntoc) -->
  6: 
  7: - [JSON File Structure](#json-file-structure)
  8: - [Collections](#collections)
  9:    * [Collection Type: Simple Table](#collection-type-simple-table)
 10: - [Properties](#properties)
 11:    * [Property Type: Table Column](#property-type-table-column)
 12:    * [Property Type: Simple Join](#property-type-simple-join)
 13:    * [Property Type: General Join](#property-type-general-join)
 14:    * [Property Type: Cartesian Product](#property-type-cartesian-product)
 15:    * [Property Type: Compound Relationship](#property-type-compound-relationship)
