 16: - [PyDough Type Strings](#pydough-type-strings)
 17: - [Metadata Samples](#metadata-samples)
 18:    * [Example: Education](#example-education)
 19:    * [Example: Shipping](#example-shipping)
 20: 
 21: <!-- TOC end -->
 22: 
 23: <!-- TOC --><a name="json-file-structure"></a>
 24: ## JSON File Structure
 25: 
 26: The core components of the JSON file structure are as follows:
 27: 
 28: - Each JSON file for PyDough metadata is a JSON object where the keys are the names of the graphs in the file, and the values are JSON object representing the graphs themselves. The names of the graphs must be valid Python variable names. The graph names should not be duplicated within the file.
 29: - Each graph JSON object has keys that are names of collections, and values that are JSON objects for the collections themselves. The collection names should not be duplicated within the file graph, should not be the same names as the graph itself, and must be valid Python variable names.
 30: - Each collection JSON object can adhere to one of several different types of Collections, but all of these types have two required key-value pairs:
 31:     * `type`: a string indicating what kind of collection this is. The value of this string must be one of the known names of types of collections, and informs what additional key-value pairs the JSON object must have.
 32:     * `properties`: a JSON object of all properties of the collection, where the keys are the names of the properties and the values are JSON objects describing the properties.
 33: - Each properties JSON object can adhere to one of several different types of Properties, but all of these types have one required key-value pair: 
 34:     * `type`: a string indicating what kind of property this is. The value of this string must be one of the known names of types of collections, and informs what additional key-value pairs the JSON object must have.
 35: 
 36: Example of the structure of the metadata for the entire file:
 37: 
 38: ```json
 39: {
 40:     "BankerGraph": {
 41:         "Accounts": {...},
 42:         "Clients": {...},
 43:         "Transactions": {...}
 44:     },
 45:     "GroceryGraph": {
 46:         "FoodItems": {...},
 47:         "Inventories": {...},
 48:         "Stores": {...}
 49:     }
 50: }
 51: ```
 52: 
 53: <!-- TOC --><a name="collections"></a>
 54: ## Collections
 55: 
 56: <!-- TOC --><a name="collection-type-simple-table"></a>
 57: ### Collection Type: Simple Table
 58: 
 59: A collection with this type is essentially just a view of a table stored in whatever database is being used to execute the queries. Collections of this type have a type string of "simple_table" and the following additional key-value pairs in their metadata JSON object:
 60: 
 61: - `table_path`: a string indicating the fully-qualified path to reach the table based on where it is stored, e.g. `<db_name>.<schema_name>.<table_name>`. The table_name here does not need to be the same as the name of the collection.
 62: - `unique_properties`: a list of JSON values indicating which properties are unique within the collection, meaning that no two rows of the table will have the same values. If a value in this list is a string, it means that property is unique within the collection. If a value in the list is a list of strings, it means that every combination of the properties in that list is unique within the collection.
 63: 
 64: The following types of properties are supported on this type of collection:
 65: 
 66: - `table_column`
 67: - `simple_join`
 68: - `cartesian_product`
 69: - `compound`
 70: 
 71: Example of the structure of the metadata for a simple table collection:
 72: 
 73: ```json
 74: "Accounts": {
 75:     "type": "simple_table",
 76:     "table_path": "bank_schema.ACCOUNTS",
 77:     "unique_properties": ["account_id"],
 78:     "properties": {
 79:         "client_id": {...},
 80:         "account_type": {...},
 81:         "account_balance": {...},
 82:         "date_opened": {...}
 83:     }
 84: }
 85: ```
 86: 
 87: <!-- TOC --><a name="properties"></a>
 88: ## Properties
 89: 
 90: <!-- TOC --><a name="property-type-table-column"></a>
 91: ### Property Type: Table Column
 92: 
 93: A property with this type is essentially just a view of a column in a table stored in whatever database is being used to execute the queries. Properties of this type are scalar expression attributes of the collection, as opposed to subcollections. Properties of this type have a type string of "table_column" and have the following additional key-value pairs in their metadata JSON object:
 94: 
 95: - `column_name`: a string indicating the name of the column within the table it comes from, which it can be different from the name of the property itself.
 96: - `data_type`: a string indicating the PyDough type that this column corresponds to.
 97: 
 98: Example of the structure of the metadata for a table column property:
 99: 
100: ```json
101: "first_name": {
102:     "type": "table_column",
103:     "column_name": "firstname",
104:     "data_type": "string"
105: }
106: ```
107: 
108: <!-- TOC --><a name="property-type-simple-join"></a>
109: ### Property Type: Simple Join
110: 
111: A property with this type describes a subcollection of the current collection that is derived from performing an equi-join on two tables (e.g. `SELECT ... FROM T1 JOIN T2 ON T1.a=T2.x AND T1.b = T2.y`). Properties of this type are subcollections of the collection, as opposed to scalar attributes. If a collection has a property of this type, a corresponding property is added to the other collection to describe the reverse of the relationship. Properties of this type have a type string of "simple_join" and have the following additional key-value pairs in their metadata JSON object:
112: 
113: - `other_collection_name`: a string indicating the name of the other collection that this property connects the current collection to. This must be another collection in the same graph that supports simple_join properties.
114: - `singular`: a boolean that is true if each record in the current collection has at most 1 matching record of the subcollection, and false otherwise.
115: - `no_collisions`: a boolean that is true if multiple records from this collection can match onto the same record from the other collection, and false otherwise (true if-and-only-if the reverse relationship is singular).
116: - `keys`: a JSON object indicating the combinations of properties from this collection and the other collection that are compared for equality in order to determine join matches. The keys to this JSON object are the names of properties in the current collection, and the values are a list of 1+ strings that. are the names of properties in the other collection that they must be equal to in order to produce a match. All property names invoked in the keys object must correspond to scalar attributes of the collection, as opposed to being names of its subcollections. This object must be non-empty.
117: - `reverse_relationship_name`: the name of the property that is to be added to the other collection to describe the reverse version of this relationship. This string must be a valid property name but cannot be equal to another existing property name in the other collection.
118: 
119: Example of the structure of the metadata for a simple join property (connects a collection `Clients` to a collection `Accounts` by joining `Clients.id` on `Accounts.client_id`):
120: 
121: ```json
122: "accounts_held": {
123:     "type": "simple_join",
124:     "other_collection_name": "Accounts",
125:     "singular": false,
126:     "no_collisions": true,
127:     "keys": {"id": ["client_id"]},
128:     "reverse_relationship_name": "account_holder"
129: }
130: ```
131: 
132: <!-- TOC --><a name="property-type-general-join"></a>
133: ### Property Type: General Join
134: 
135: This property type is a relationship variant of the simple join is the "general join", which instead of joining on equality of key columns has an arbitrary PyDough expression as a condition. This is useful for more arbitrary join conditions such as interval joins (e.g. `SELECT ... FROM T1 JOIN T2 ON T1.a <= T2.B AND T2.B <= T1.c`). Properties of this type are subcollections of the collection, as opposed to scalar attributes. If a collection has a property of this type, a corresponding property is added to the other collection to describe the reverse of the relationship. Properties of this type have a type string of "general_join" and have the following additional key-value pairs in their metadata JSON object:
136: 
137: - `other_collection_name`: a string indicating the name of the other collection that this property connects the current collection to. This must be another collection in the same graph that supports simple_join properties.
138: - `singular`: a boolean that is true if each record in the current collection has at most 1 matching record of the subcollection, and false otherwise.
139: - `no_collisions`: a boolean that is true if multiple records from this collection can match onto the same record from the other collection, and false otherwise (true if-and-only-if the reverse relationship is singular).
140: - `condition`: a string representing the PyDough code for the condition, where columns from the current collection are referred to as `self.xyz` and columns from the child collection being accessed are referred to as `other.xyz`. This can be any valid PyDough code, with the following caveats:
141:   - The code must be a single Python expression.
142:   - The code must return a PyDough expression, as opposed to a collection.
143:   - The code may call regular PyDough functions, but not window functions.
144:   - The code may not access any sub-collections of either collection.
145: - `reverse_relationship_name`: the name of the property that is to be added to the other collection to describe the reverse version of this relationship. This string must be a valid property name but cannot be equal to another existing property name in the other collection.
146: 
147: Example of the structure of the metadata for a simple join property (connects a collection `Incidents` to a collection `WorkerShifts` by joining on whether `Incidents.incident_timestamp` is between `WorkerShifts.start_of_shift` and `WorkerShifts.end_of_shift`):
148: 
149: ```json
150: "shifts_overlapping_with_incident": {
151:     "type": "general_join",
152:     "other_collection_name": "WorkerShifts",
153:     "singular": false,
154:     "no_collisions": false,
155:     "condition": "MONOTONIC(other.start_of_shift, self.incident_timestamp, other.end_of_shift)",
156:     "reverse_relationship_name": "incidents_during_shift"
157: }
158: ```
159: 
160: <!-- TOC --><a name="property-type-cartesian-product"></a>
161: ### Property Type: Cartesian Product
162: 
163: A property with this type describes a subcollection of the current collection that is derived from performing an cross-join on two collections (e.g. SELECT ... FROM T1, T2). Properties of this type are subcollections of the collection, as opposed to scalar attributes. If a collection has a property of this type, a corresponding property is added to the other collection to describe the reverse of the relationship. Properties of this type have a type string of "cartesian_product" and have the following additional key-value pairs in their metadata JSON object:
164: 
165: - `other_collection_name`: a string indicating the name of the other collection that this property connects the current collection to. This must be another collection in the same graph that supports cartesian_product properties.
166: - `reverse_relationship_name`: the name of the property that is to be added to the other collection to describe the reverse version of this relationship. This string must be a valid property name but cannot be equal to another existing property name in the other collection.
167: 
168: Example of the structure of the metadata for a cartesian product property (connects every record of a collection `CalendarDates` to every record of collection `InventorySnapshots`):
169: 
170: ```json
171: "snapshots": {
172:     "type": "cartesian_product",
173:     "other_collection_name": "InventorySnapshots",
174:     "reverse_relationship_name": "calendar_dates"
175: }
176: ```
177: 
178: <!-- TOC --><a name="property-type-compound-relationship"></a>
179: ### Property Type: Compound Relationship
180: 
181: A property with this type describes a subcollection of the current collection that is derived from combining a relationship from this collection to one of its subcollections with a relationship from that subcollection to one of its subcollections. Properties of this type are subcollections of the collection, as opposed to scalar attributes. If a collection has a property of this type, a corresponding property is added to the other collection to describe the reverse of the relationship, and the subcollection can inherit additional properties from the middle subcollection. Properties of this type have a type string of "compound" and have the following additional key-value pairs in their metadata JSON object:
182: 
183: - `primary_property`: a string indicating the name of a property that connects this collection to a subcollection.
184: - `secondary_property`: a string indicating the name of the property that connects the primary subcollection to one of its subcollections.
185: - `singular`: a boolean that is true if each record in the current collection has at most 1 matching record of the subcollection’s subcollection, and false otherwise.
186: - `no_collisions`: a boolean that is true if multiple records from this collection can match onto the same record from the subcollection’s subcollection, and false otherwise (true if-and-only-if the reverse relationship is singular).
187: - `reverse_relationship_name`: the name of the property that is to be added to the other collection to describe the reverse version of this relationship. This string must be a valid property name but cannot be equal to another existing property name in the other collection.
188: - `inherited_properties`: a JSON object indicating any properties of the primary subcollection that should be accessible from the secondary subcollection. The keys are the string names that the inherited properties are referred to by, which can be a new alias or the original name, and the values are names of the properties of the collection accessed by the primary property. The names used for the inherited properties cannot overlap with any other names of properties of the secondary subcollection, including other inherited properties it could have from other compound relationships. This JSON object can be empty if there are no inherited properties.
189: 
190: Example of the structure of the metadata for a compound relationship property (connects a collection `Regions` to a collection `Customers` by combining `Regions.nations.customers` into a single property, skipping over a middle collection `Nations` but picking up its property `name` under a new name `nation_name):
191: 
192: ```json
193: "customers": {
194:     "type": "compound",
195:     "primary_property": "nations",
196:     "secondary_property": "customers",
197:     "singular": false,
198:     "no_collisions": true,
199:     "inherited_properties": {
200:         "nation_name": "name"
201:     },
202:     "reverse_relationship_name": "region"
203: }
204: ```
205: 
206: <!-- TOC --><a name="pydough-type-strings"></a>
207: ## PyDough Type Strings
208: 
209: The strings used in the type field for certain properties must be one of the following:
210: 
211: - `int8`: an 8-bit integer.
212: - `int16`: a 16-bit integer.
213: - `int32`: a 32-bit integer.
214: - `int64`: a 64-bit integer.
215: - `float32`: a 32-bit float.
216: - `float64`: a 64-bit float.
217: - `decimal[p,s]`: a fixed-point number with precision p (integer between 1 and 38) indicating the number of digits and scale s (integer between 0 and p, exclusive of p) indicating the number of digits to the right hand side of the decimal point.
218: - `bool`: a boolean.
219: - `string`: a string.
220: - `binary`: a bytes format.
221: - `date`: a date without any time component.
222: - `time[p]`: a time of day with a precision p (integer between 0 and 9) indicating the number of sub-second decimal places it can have (e.g. 9 = nanosecond precision).
223: - `timestamp[p]`: a date with a time of day of a precision p (same rules as time).
224: - `timestamp[p,tz]`: a date with a time of day of a precision p (same rules as time) with the timezone described by tz (e.g. `timestamp[9,America/Los_Angeles]`).
225: - `array[t]`: an array of values of type t (where t is another PyDough type). For example: `array[int32]` or `array[array[string]]`.
226: - `map[t1,t2]`: a map of values with keys of type type t1 and values of type t2 (where t1 and t2 are also PyDough types). For example: `map[string,int64]` or `map[string,array[date]]`.
227: - `struct[field1:t1,field2:t2,...]`: a struct of values with fields named field1, field2, etc. with types t1, t2, etc. (which are also PyDough types). For example: `struct[x:int32,y:int32]` or `struct[name:string,birthday:date,car_accidents:array[struct[ts:timestamp[9],report:string]]`. Each field name must be a valid Python identifier.
228: - `unknown`: an unknown type.
229: 
230: <!-- TOC --><a name="metadata-samples"></a>
231: ## Metadata Samples
232: 
233: 
234: <!-- TOC --><a name="example-education"></a>
235: ### Example: Education
236: 
237: The knowledge graph is for the following information about tables in a schema called `education`:
238: - `PEOPLE` is a table referring to each known person. Each row in this table has the following information:
239:     - `p_ssn`: the social security number used to uniquely identify the person.
240:     - `p_name`: the name of the person.
241: - `SCHOOLS` is a table referring to each known school. Each row in this table has the following information:
242:     - `s_id`: the identifying number used to uniquely identify the school.
243:     - `s_name`: the name of the school.
244: - `ATTENDANCE` is a table referring to every known instance of a person attending a school (assuming a person could have attended multiple schools, but attended each school at most once). Each row in this table has the following information:
245:     - `a_ssn`: the social security number of the person attending the school.
246:     - `a_id`: the id of the school being attended.
247:     - `a_gpa`: the GPA that the person had while attending the school.
248:     - `a_graddate`: the date that the person graduated from the school.
249:     - `a_degree`: the degree the person earned from teh school.
250: - Records in `PEOPLE` and `ATTENDANCE` can be joined on the social security number.
251: - Records in `SCHOOLS` and `ATTENDANCE` can be joined on the school id.
252: 
253: ```json
254: {
255:   "Education": {
256:     "People": {
257:       "type": "simple_table",
258:       "table_path": "education.PEOPLE",
259:       "unique_properties": ["p_ssn"],
260:       "properties": {
261:         "ssn": {
262:           "type": "table_column",
263:           "column_name": "p_ssn",
264:           "data_type": "string"
265:         },
266:         "name": {
267:           "type": "table_column",
268:           "column_name": "p_name",
269:           "data_type": "string"
270:         },
271:         "attendances": {
272:           "type": "simple_join",
273:           "other_collection_name": "Attendance",
274:           "singular": false,
275:           "no_collisions": true,
276:           "keys": {
277:             "p_ssn": ["a_ssn"]
278:           },
279:           "reverse_relationship_name": "person"
280:         },
281:         "schools_attended": {
282:           "type": "compound",
283:           "primary_property": "attendances",
284:           "secondary_property": "school",
285:           "singular": false,
286:           "no_collisions": false,
287:           "inherited_properties": {
288:             "gpa": "gpa",
289:             "graduation_date": "graduation_date",
290:             "degree": "degree"
291:           },
292:           "reverse_relationship_name": "students"
293:         }
294:       }
295:     },
296:     "Schools": {
297:       "type": "simple_table",
298:       "table_path": "education.SCHOOLS",
299:       "unique_properties": ["school_id"],
300:       "properties": {
301:         "school_id": {
302:           "type": "table_column",
303:           "column_name": "s_id",
304:           "data_type": "string"
305:         },
306:         "name": {
307:           "type": "table_column",
308:           "column_name": "s_name",
309:           "data_type": "string"
310:         },
311:         "attendances": {
312:           "type": "simple_join",
313:           "other_collection_name": "Attendance",
314:           "singular": false,
315:           "no_collisions": true,
316:           "keys": {
317:             "school_id": ["school_id"]
318:           },
319:           "reverse_relationship_name": "school"
320:         }
321:       }
322:     },
323:     "Attendance": {
324:       "type": "simple_table",
325:       "table_path": "education.ATTENDANCE",
326:       "unique_properties": ["person_ssn", "school_id"],
327:       "properties": {
328:         "person_ssn": {
329:           "type": "table_column",
330:           "column_name": "a_ssn",
331:           "data_type": "string"
332:         },
333:         "school_id": {
334:           "type": "table_column",
335:           "column_name": "a_id",
336:           "data_type": "string"
337:         },
338:         "gpa": {
339:           "type": "table_column",
340:           "column_name": "a_gpa",
341:           "data_type": "float64"
342:         },
343:         "graduation_date": {
344:           "type": "table_column",
345:           "column_name": "a_graddate",
346:           "data_type": "date"
347:         },
348:         "degree": {
349:           "type": "table_column",
350:           "column_name": "a_degree",
351:           "data_type": "string"
352:         }
353:       }
354:     }
355:   }
356: }
357: ```
358: 
359: The PyDough metadata representation shown in this JSON file corresponds to the following set of collections:
360: - `People` (corresponds to `education.PEOPLE`; records are unique per unique value of `ssn`). Has the following properties:
361:     - `ssn` (scalar property)
362:     - `name` (scalar property)
363:     - `attendances` (sub-collection connecting to `Attendances`)
364:     - `schools` (sub-collection connecting to `Schools` by going through `Attendances`)
365: - `Schools` (corresponds to `education.SCHOOLS`; records are unique per unique value of `school_id`). Has the following properties:
366:     - `school_id` (scalar property)
367:     - `school_name` (scalar property)
368:     - `attendances` (sub-collection connecting to `Attendances`)
369:     - `students` (sub-collection connecting to `People` by going through `Attendances`, reverse of `People.schools`)
370: - `Attendances` (corresponds to `education.ATTENDANCES`; records are unique per unique combination of `person_ssn` & `school_id`). Has the following properties:
371:     - `person_ssn` (scalar property)
372:     - `school_id` (scalar property)
373:     - `gpa` (scalar property)
374:     - `graduation_date` (scalar property)
375:     - `degree` (scalar property)
376:     - `person` (sub-collection connecting to `People`, reverse of `People.attendances`)
377:     - `school` (sub-collection connecting to `School`, reverse of `Schools.attendances`)
378:

380: ### Example: Shipping
381: 
382: The knowledge graph is for the following information about tables in a schema called `shipping`:
383: - `PEOPLE` is a table referring to each known person. Each row in this table has the following information:
384:     - `ssn`: the social security number used to uniquely identify the person.
385:     - `first`: the first name of the person.
386:     - `middle`: the middle name of the person, if they have one.
387:     - `last`: the last name of the person.
388:     - `bdate`: the date that the person was born.
389:     - `email`: the email of the person.
390:     - `ca_id`: the id of the person's current address, if they have one.
391: - `PACKAGES` is a table referring to each known package. Each row in this table has the following information:
392:     - `pid`: the identifying number used to uniquely identify the package.
393:     - `cust_ssn`: the social security number of the person who ordered the package.
394:     - `ship_id`: the address id of the address the package was shipped to.
395:     - `bill_id`: the address id of the address the package was billed to.
396:     - `order_date`: the date that the package was ordered.
397:     - `arrival_date`: the date that the package arrived, if it has.
398:     - `cost`: the total cost of the package.
399: - `ADDRESSES` is a table referring to every known address. Each row in this table has the following information:
400:     - `aid`: the identifying number used to uniquely identify the address.
401:     - `number`: the street number of the address.
402:     - `street`: the name of the street of the the address.
403:     - `apartment`: the name of the apartment, if the address has one.
404:     - `zip`: the zip code of the address.
405:     - `city`: the city containing the address.
406:     - `state`: the state containing the address.
407: - Records in `PEOPLE` and `PACKAGES` can be joined on the social security number.
408: - Records in `PEOPLE` and `ADDRESSES` can be joined on the address id.
409: - Records in `PACKAGES` and `ADDRESSES` can be joined on either the shipping address id or the billing address id.

  1: # PyDough Usage Guide
  2: 
  3: This document describes how to set up & interact with PyDough. For instructions on how to write PyDough code, see the [PyDough DSL](dsl.md) or the [list of PyDough builtin functions](functions.md).
  4: 
  5: <!-- TOC start (generated with https://github.com/derlin/bitdowntoc) -->
  6: 
  7: - [Setting Up in Jupyter Notebooks](#setting-up-in-jupyter-notebooks)

 10:    * [Session Configs](#session-configs)
 11:    * [Session Database](#session-database)
 12:    * [Session Knowledge Graph](#session-knowledge-graph)
 13: - [Evaluation APIs](#evaluation-apis)
 14:    * [`pydough.to_sql`](#pydoughto_sql)
 15:    * [`pydough.to_df`](#pydoughto_df)
 16: - [Exploration APIs](#exploration-apis)
 17:    * [`pydough.explain_structure`](#pydoughexplain_structure)
 18:    * [`pydough.explain`](#pydoughexplain)
 19:    * [`pydough.explain_term`](#pydoughexplain_term)
 20: - [Logging] (#logging)
 21: 
 22: <!-- TOC end -->
 23: 
 24: <!-- TOC --><a name="setting-up-in-jupyter-notebooks"></a>
 25: ## Setting Up in Jupyter Notebooks
 26: 
 27: Once you have uv set up, you can run the command `uv run jupyter lab` from the PyDough directory to boot up a Jupyter lab process that will have access to PyDough. If you have installed PyDough via pip, you should be able to directly boot up a Jupyter lab process and it will have access to the PyDough module.
 28: 
 29: Once JupyterLab is running, you can either navigate to an existing notebook file or create a new one. In that notebook file, follow these steps in the notebook cells to work with PyDough:
 30: 
 31: 1. Run `import pydough` to import the PyDough module.
 32: 2. Run `%load_ext pydough.jupyter_extensions` to load the PyDough Jupyter extension.
 33: 3. Connect to the metadata graph you wish to use. The metadata should be in a JSON file that can be accessed from the notebook. If the file is located at `<path>`, and the name of the graph within the file that you wish to use is `<graphname>`, then the connection command is `pydough.active_session.load_metadata_graph(<path>, <graphname>)`.
 34: 4. (optional) Connect to the database you wish to use to evaluate your analytical questions. If your database is sqlite and is located at `<path>`, the connection command is `pydough.active_session.connect_database("sqlite", database=<path>)`
 35: 
 36: To summarize, your notebook should start with a cell like this, which you need to run before proceeding with any other tasks:
 37: 
 38: ```py
 39: import pydough
 40: %load_ext pydough.jupyter_extensions
 41: pydough.active_session.load_metadata_graph("knowledge_graphs.json", "MyGraph")
 42: pydough.active_session.connect_database("sqlite", "mydata.db")
 43: ```
 44: 
 45: Once you have done all of these steps, you can run PyDough in any cell of the notebook by prepending the cell with `%%pydough`. For example:
 46: 
 47: ```py
 48: %%pydough
 49: result = nations.WHERE(region.name == "ASIA").CALCULATE(name, n_cust=COUNT(customers))
 50: pydough.to_df(result)
 51: ```
 52: 
 53: Within the contents of a PyDough cell, the following is True:
 54: - Any undefined variable is presumed to be either a function or an access to a collection/property described within the knowledge graph. This presumption is not checked until the code is fully evaluated by calling `pydough.to_df`.
 55:     - For instance, in the example above, the following are all undefined variables that the PyDough cell resolves: `nations`, `region`, `name`, `COUNT`, `customers`.
 56: - Any variables defined outside the current cell are still accessible inside the current cell.
 57: - Any variables defined inside the cell are usable outside the cell.
 58: 
 59: <!-- TOC --><a name="session-apis"></a>
 60: ## Session APIs
 61: 
 62: This section describes various APIs you can use to interact with the PyDough session.
 63: 
 64: <!-- TOC --><a name="pydough-session"></a>
 65: ### PyDough Session
 66: 
 67: A `PyDoughSession` object encapsulates information about the knowledge graph being used, the configuration settings that have been enabled, the database connection being used, and any associated SQL dialect-specific settings.
 68: 
 69: A new `PyDoughSession` object can be created as follows:
 70: 
 71: ```py
 72: from pydough.configs import PyDoughSession
 73: session = PyDoughSession()
 74: ```
 75: 
 76: There exists a special session object `pydough.active_session` used to describe the settings for PyDough by default, unless alternate values are passed in to specific APIs. The active session can be swapped out for another session to keep track of multiple at once:
 77: 
 78: ```py
 79: import pydough
 80: from pydough.configs import PyDoughSession
 81: # Create a new session
 82: session_a = PyDoughSession()
 83: # Capture the original active session
 84: session_b = pydough.active_session
 85: # Replace the active session
 86: pydough.active_session = session_a
 87: # Restore the original active session
 88: pydough.active_session = session_b
 89: ```
 90: 
 91: Each `PyDoughSession` has the following notable fields, each of which can be accessed or switched out:
 92: - `metadata`: the knowledge graph used by PyDough to identify collections/properties. By default, there is no knowledge graph until one is attached to the session. [See here](#session-knowledge-graph) for more details.
 93: - `config`: the miscellaneous configurations used by the PyDough session. By default, each configuration is set to its default value. [See here](#session-configs) for more details.
 94: - `database`: the database context used by PyDough to determine which version of SQL to translate into and used to execute queries in a database. By default, there is no database connection until one is attached to the session. [See here](#session-database) for more details.
 95: 
 96: <!-- TOC --><a name="session-knowledge-graph"></a>
 97: ### Session Knowledge Graph
 98: 
 99: The knowledge graph contains all of the metadata used by PyDough to identify every known collection and all of its properties, including both scalar attributes and sub-collection relationships. The metadata itself is stored in an ancillary file, which currently is only allowed to be a [JSON file in the supported format](metadata.md).
100: 
101: There are two ways to load a knowledge graph into a session:
102: 1. Parse the graph with `parse_json_metadata_from_file` then set `session.graph` to the returned value.
103: 2. Use `session.load_metadata_graph`.
104: 
105: Both examples are shown below. For these examples, assume there is a made-up JSON file located at `hello/world/graphs.json` and that the specific graph that should be used from this file is called `Food` (since the file could contain multiple graphs).
106: 
107: ```py
108: import pydough
109: from pydough import parse_json_metadata_from_file
110: 
111: # First approach
112: my_graph = parse_json_metadata_from_file("hello/world/graphs.json", "Food")
113: pydough.active_session.graph = my_graph
114: 
115: # Second approach
116: my_graph = pydough.active_session.load_metadata_graph("hello/world/graphs.json", "Food")
117: ```
118: 
119: Notice that both `parse_json_metadata_from_file` and `load_metadata_graph` also return the graph metadata. This is useful in case the graphs need to be switched around just like sessions. However, the graphs themselves are not intended to be examined by users except via [the exploration APIs](#exploration-apis), some of which require access to the graph object.
120: 
121: <!-- TOC --><a name="session-configs"></a>
122: ### Session Configs
123: 
124: The miscellaneous configuration settings in PyDough are controlled by a `PyDoughConfigs` object. Each `PyDoughConfigs` contains several fields used at different points in the execution of PyDough to control ambiguous decisions where more than one option is valid. Each of these fields has a default value, but can also be manually controlled by a user replacing the value.
125: 
126: The configurations of a session object can be accessed with the `.config` field of the session object. A new configuration object can be created & subbed-in as follows:
127: 
128: ```py
129: import pydough
130: from pydough.configs import PyDoughConfigs
131: # Create a new session
132: new_configs = PyDoughConfigs()
133: # Capture the original configs of the active session
134: old_configs = pydough.active_session.config
135: # Replace the configs of the active session
136: pydough.active_session.config = new_configs
137: # Restore the original configs of the active session
138: pydough.active_session.config = old_configs
139: ```
140: 
141: Each `PyDoughConfigs` currently encapsulates the following configurations:
142: 1. `sum_default_zero` (default=True): if True, then `SUM` will always return `0` instead of `NULL` when there are no records to be summed (e.g. summing over an empty sub-collection). If False, then the behavior will depend on the database being used to execute (though this nearly always means returning `NULL`).
143: 2. `avg_default_zero` (default=False): if True, then `AVG` will always return `0` instead of `NULL` when there are no records to be summed (e.g. taking the average from an empty sub-collection). If False, then the behavior will depend on the database being used to execute (though this nearly always means returning `NULL`).
144: 
145: For example, consider this PyDough snippet:
146: 
147: ```py
148: %%pydough
149: selected_customers = customers.WHERE(CONTAINS(name, '2468'))
150: result = Nations.CALCULATE(
151:     name,
152:     total_bal=SUM(selected_customers.acctbal),
153:     average_bal=AVG(selected_customers.acctbal),
154: )
155: pydough.to_df(result)
156: ```
157: 
158: Not every nation has at least 1 customer with a name containing the substring `2468`. For these rows in the result, the value of `total_bal` and `average_bal` will depend on whether `sum_default_zero` and `avg_default_zero` are True or not. Below is an example of accessing & switching out these values.
159: 
160: ```py
161: import pydough
162: # Capture the configs of the active session
163: configs = pydough.active_session.config
164: # Access the original value of sum_default_zero (which should be True)
165: old_sum_behavior = configs.sum_default_zero
166: # Toggle the value of sum_default_zero to False
167: configs.sum_default_zero = False
168: ```
169: 
170: The following configs are used in the behavior of `PERCENTILE`, `RANKING`, `ORDER_BY` and `TOP_K` where a collation(`ASC` or `DESC`) is not explicitly specified:
171: 
172: 3. `collation_default_asc` (default=True): if True, then the default collation is ascending. If False, then the default collation is descending.
173: 4. `propagate_collation` (default=False): if True, then the collation of the current expression, which does not have a collation, uses the most recent available collation in the nodes of the term. If there is no recent available collation, then the default collation is used as specified by `collation_default_asc`. If False, the expression uses the default collation as specified by `collation_default_asc`.
174: 
175: For example, consider the following PyDough code:
176: 
177: ```py
178: %%pydough
179: 
180: import pydough
181: # The configs of the active session
182: configs = pydough.active_session.config
183: 
184: # The collations are not explicitly specified for few of the terms.
185: Suppliers.ORDER_BY(
186:   COUNT(lines),
187:   nation.name.ASC(),
188:   COUNT(supply_records),
189:   account_balance.DESC(),
190:   key,
191: )
192: 
193: # Let's see the behavior of the terms with different configurations
194: # With the default settings (collation_default_asc=True and propagate_collation=False)
195: Suppliers.ORDER_BY(
196:   COUNT(lines).ASC(),
197:   nation.name.ASC(),
198:   COUNT(supply_records).ASC(),
199:   account_balance.DESC(),
200:   key.ASC(),
201: )
202: 
203: # With collation_default_asc=False and propagate_collation=True
204: configs.collation_default_asc = False
205: configs.propagate_collation = True
206: Suppliers.ORDER_BY(
207:   COUNT(lines).DESC(),
208:   nation.name.ASC(),
209:   COUNT(supply_records).DESC(),
210:   account_balance.DESC(),
211:   key.DESC(),
212: )
213: 
214: # With collation_default_asc=False and propagate_collation=False
215: configs.collation_default_asc = False
216: configs.propagate_collation = False
217: Suppliers.ORDER_BY(
218:   COUNT(lines).DESC(),
219:   nation.name.ASC(),
220:   COUNT(supply_records).DESC(),
221:   account_balance.DESC(),
222:   key.DESC(),
223: )
224: 
225: # With collation_default_asc=True and propagate_collation=True
226: configs.collation_default_asc = True
227: configs.propagate_collation = True
228: Suppliers.ORDER_BY(
229:   COUNT(lines).ASC(),
230:   nation.name.ASC(),
231:   COUNT(supply_records).ASC(),
232:   account_balance.DESC(),
233:   key.DESC(),
234: )
235: ```
236: 
237: The following configs are used in the behavior of `DAYOFWEEK`, `DATETIME`, and `DATEDIFF`:
238: 
239: 5. `start_of_week` (default=`DayOfWeek.SUNDAY`): Determines which day is considered the first day of the week. This affects the following functions:
240: - `DAYOFWEEK` : A function that returns the number of days since the start of the week. Start of week is relative to the `start_of_week` config.
241: - `DATETIME` : This function also supports the `start of week` unit, which is relative to the `start_of_week` config.
242: - `DATEDIFF` : This function also supports difference between two dates in terms of weeks, which is relative to the `start_of_week` config.
243: 
244: The value must be one of the following `DayOfWeek` enum values:
245: 
246:    - `DayOfWeek.SUNDAY` (default)
247:    - `DayOfWeek.MONDAY`  
248:    - `DayOfWeek.TUESDAY`
249:    - `DayOfWeek.WEDNESDAY`
250:    - `DayOfWeek.THURSDAY`
251:    - `DayOfWeek.FRIDAY`
252:    - `DayOfWeek.SATURDAY`
253: 
254:    The `DayOfWeek` enum is defined in the `pydough.configs` module.
255: 6. `start_week_as_zero` (default=True): if True, then the first day of the week is considered to be 0. If False, then the first day of the week is considered to be 1. This config is used by  `DAYOFWEEK` function.
256: 
257: ```py
258: import pydough
259: from pydough.configs import DayOfWeek
260: 
261: # The configs of the active session
262: configs = pydough.active_session.config
263: 
264: # Understanding the behavior of DAYOFWEEK
265: # Set the start of the week to Monday
266: configs.start_of_week = DayOfWeek.MONDAY
267: # Set start of week to be 1
268: configs.start_week_as_zero = False
269: # This would return dow = 4, as March 20, 2025 is a Thursday and is the 4th day 
270: # of the week when the start of week is considered to be Monday
271: TPCH.calculate(dow = DAYOFWEEK("2025-03-20")) # dow = 4
272: # If start_week_as_zero is set to True (configs.start_week_as_zero = True), 
273: # then DAYOFWEEK("2025-03-20") = 3
274: configs.start_week_as_zero = True
275: TPCH.calculate(dow = DAYOFWEEK("2025-03-20")) # dow = 3
276: 
277: # Now, start_of_week is set to Thursday,
278: configs.start_of_week = DayOfWeek.Thursday
279: configs.start_week_as_zero = False
280: # This would return dow = 1, as March 20, 2025 is a Thursday and is the 1st day
281: # of the week when the start of week is considered to be Thursday.
282: TPCH.calculate(dow = DAYOFWEEK("2025-03-20")) # dow = 1
283: # If start_week_as_zero is set to True (configs.start_week_as_zero = True), 
284: # then DAYOFWEEK("2025-03-20") = 0
285: configs.start_week_as_zero = True
286: TPCH.calculate(dow = DAYOFWEEK("2025-03-20")) # dow = 0
287: 
288: 
289: # Understanding the behavior of DATETIME with `start of week`
290: # Set the start of the week to Monday
291: configs.start_of_week = DayOfWeek.MONDAY
292: # This would set `dt` to the start of the week for March 20, 2025 (Wednesday)
293: # to be March 17, 2025 (recent Monday)
294: TPCH.calculate(dt = DATETIME("2025-03-20", "start of week")) # dt = 2025-03-17
295: 
296: # start_of_week is set to Thursday,
297: configs.start_of_week = DayOfWeek.Thursday
298: # This would set `dt` to the start of the week for March 20, 2025 (Thursday)
299: # to be March 20, 2025 (recent Thursday)
300: TPCH.calculate(dt = DATETIME("2025-03-20", "start of week")) # dt = 2025-03-20
301: # Note: DATETIME function related to week does not depend on the 
302: # `start_week_as_zero` config.
303: 
304: 
305: # Understanding the behavior of DATEDIFF with `start of week`
306: # Set the start of the week to Monday
307: configs.start_of_week = DayOfWeek.MONDAY
308: # This would return 0, as the difference between March 20, 2025(Thursday) and 
309: # March 17, 2025(Monday) is 0 weeks when the start of week is considered to be 
310: # Monday. This is because both these dates fall on the same week.
311: TPCH.calculate(diff = DATEDIFF("2025-03-17", "2025-03-20", "week")) # diff = 0
312: 
313: # Set the start of the week to Thursday
314: configs.start_of_week = DayOfWeek.Thursday
315: # This would return 1, as the difference between March 20, 2025 (Thursday)
316: # and March 17, 2025 (Monday) is 1 week when the start of week is considered 
317: # to be Thursday. This is because March 17, 2025 belongs to the week starting
318: # from March 13, 2025 (the recent Thursday for it) and March 20, 2025 belongs 
319: # to the week starting from March 20, 2025 (the recent Thursday).
320: TPCH.calculate(diff = DATEDIFF("2025-03-17", "2025-03-20", "week")) # diff = 1
321: # Note: DATEDIFF function related to week does not depend on the 
322: # `start_week_as_zero` config.
323: ```
324: 
325: <!-- TOC --><a name="session-database"></a>
326: ### Session Database
327: 
328: The final core piece encapsulated by the session is the database context. A database context currently includes a connection to an actual database and an enum indicating which dialect to use.
329: 
330: By default, the database context contains an empty connection (which cannot be used to execute queries, but can be used to translate to SQL) and the ANSI dialect.
331: 
332: Just like the knowledge graph & miscellaneous configurations, the database context can also be accessed from the session and/or swapped out for another value. The APIs for creating a new database context currently take in the name of which database to use, as well as keyword arguments used by that database connector API's connection method.
333: 
334: Below is a list of all supported values for the database name:
335: - `sqlite`: uses a SQLite database. [See here](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.connect) for details on the connection API and what keyword arguments can be passed in.
336: 
337: Below are examples of how to access the context and switch it out for a newly created one, either by manually setting it or by using `session.load_database`. These examples assume that there are two different sqlite database files located at `db_files/education.db` and `db_files/shakespeare.db`.
338: 
339: ```py
340: import pydough
341: from pydough.database_connectors import load_database_context
342: 
343: # Capture the original context of the active session (empty)
344: old_context = pydough.active_session.database
345: 
346: # Create a new sqlite context & set it as the database of the active session
347: education_context = load_database_context("sqlite", database="db_files/education.db")
348: pydough.active_session.database = education_context
349: 
350: # Same but for another database & with a different method
351: shakespeare_context  = pydough.active_session.load_database("sqlite", database="db_files/education.db")
352: ```
353: 
354: Notice that both APIs `load_database_context` and `sesion.load_database` take in the name of the databse type first and all the connection keyword arguments, and also return the context object.
355: 
356: It is important to ensure that the correct database context is being used for several reasons:
357: - It controls what SQL dialect is used when translating from PyDough to SQL.
358: - The context's database connection is used to execute queries once translated to SQL.
359: 
360: <!-- TOC --><a name="evaluation-apis"></a>
361: ## Evaluation APIs
362: 
363: This sections describes various APIs you can use to execute PyDough code. 
364: 
365: <!-- TOC --><a name="pydoughto_sql"></a>
366: ### `pydough.to_sql`
367: 
368: The `to_sql` API takes in PyDough code and transforms it into SQL query text without executing it on a database. The first argument it takes in is the PyDough node for the collection being converted to SQL. It can optionally take in the following keyword arguments:
369: 
370: - `columns`: which columns to include in the answer if what names to call them by (if omitted, uses the names/ordering from the last `CALCULATE` clause). This can either be a non-empty list of column name strings, or a non-empty dictionary where the values are column name strings, and the keys are the strings of the aliases they should be named as.
371: - `metadata`: the PyDough knowledge graph to use for the conversion (if omitted, `pydough.active_session.metadata` is used instead).
372: - `config`: the PyDough configuration settings to use for the conversion (if omitted, `pydough.active_session.config` is used instead).
373: - `database`: the database context to use for the conversion (if omitted, `pydough.active_session.database` is used instead). The database context matters because it controls which SQL dialect is used for the translation.
374: 
375: Below is an example of using `pydough.to_sql` and the output (the SQL output may be outdated if PyDough's SQL conversion process has been updated):
376: 
377: ```py
378: %%pydough
379: european_countries = nations.WHERE(region.name == "EUROPE")
380: result = european_countries.CALCULATE(name, n_custs=COUNT(customers))
381: pydough.to_sql(result, columns=["name", "n_custs"])
382: ```
383: 
384: ```sql
385: SELECT name, COALESCE(agg_0, 0) AS n_custs
386: FROM (
387:     SELECT name, agg_0
388:     FROM (
389:         SELECT name, key
390:         FROM (
391:             SELECT _table_alias_0.name AS name, _table_alias_0.key AS key, _table_alias_1.name AS name_3
392:             FROM (
393:                 SELECT n_name AS name, n_nationkey AS key, n_regionkey AS region_key FROM main.NATION
394:             ) AS _table_alias_0
395:             LEFT JOIN (
396:                 SELECT r_name AS name, r_regionkey AS key
397:                 FROM main.REGION
398:             ) AS _table_alias_1
399:             ON region_key = _table_alias_1.key
400:         )
401:         WHERE name_3 = 'EUROPE'
402:     )
403:     LEFT JOIN (
404:         SELECT nation_key, COUNT() AS agg_0
405:         FROM (
406:             SELECT c_nationkey AS nation_key
407:             FROM main.CUSTOMER
408:         )
409:         GROUP BY nation_key
410:     )
411:     ON key = nation_key
412: )
413: ```
414: 
415: See the [demo notebooks](../demos/README.md) for more instances of how to use the `to_sql` API.
416: 
417: <!-- TOC --><a name="pydoughto_df"></a>
418: ### `pydough.to_df`
419: 
420: The `to_df` API does all the same steps as the [`to_sql` API](#pydoughto_sql), but goes a step further and executes the query using the provided database connection, returning the result as a pandas DataFrame.  The first argument it takes in is the PyDough node for the collection being converted to SQL. It can optionally take in the following keyword arguments:
421: 
422: 
423: - `columns`: which columns to include in the answer if what names to call them by (if omitted, uses the names/ordering from the last `CALCULATE` clause). This can either be a non-empty list of column name strings, or a non-empty dictionary where the values are column name strings, and the keys are the strings of the aliases they should be named as.
424: - `metadata`: the PyDough knowledge graph to use for the conversion (if omitted, `pydough.active_session.metadata` is used instead).
425: - `config`: the PyDough configuration settings to use for the conversion (if omitted, `pydough.active_session.config` is used instead).
426: - `database`: the database context to use for the conversion (if omitted, `pydough.active_session.database` is used instead). The database context matters because it controls which SQL dialect is used for the translation.
427: - `display_sql`: displays the sql before executing in a logger.
428: 
429: Below is an example of using `pydough.to_df` and the output, attached to a sqlite database containing data for the TPC-H schema:
430: 
431: ```py
432: %%pydough
433: european_countries = nations.WHERE(region.name == "EUROPE")
434: result = european_countries.CALCULATE(n=COUNT(customers))
435: pydough.to_df(result, columns={"name": "name", "n_custs": "n"})
436: ```
437: 
438: <div>
439: <table border="1">
440:   <thead>
441:     <tr style="text-align: right;">
442:       <th></th>
443:       <th>name</th>
444:       <th>n_custs</th>
445:     </tr>
446:   </thead>
447:   <tbody>
448:     <tr>
449:       <th>0</th>
450:       <td>FRANCE</td>
451:       <td>6100</td>
452:     </tr>
453:     <tr>
454:       <th>1</th>

457:     </tr>
458:     <tr>
459:       <th>2</th>
460:       <td>RUSSIA</td>
461:       <td>6078</td>
462:     </tr>
463:     <tr>
464:       <th>3</th>
465:       <td>UNITED KINGDOM</td>
466:       <td>6011</td>
467:     </tr>

476: 
477: See the [demo notebooks](../demos/notebooks/1_introduction.ipynb) for more instances of how to use the `to_df` API.

479: <!-- TOC --><a name="exploration-apis"></a>
480: ## Exploration APIs
481: 
482: This sections describes various APIs you can use to explore PyDough code and figure out what each component is doing without having PyDough fully evaluate it. The following APIs take an optional `config` argument which can be used to specify the PyDough configuration settings to use for the exploration.
483: 
484: See the [demo notebooks](../demos/notebooks/2_exploration.ipynb) for more instances of how to use the exploration APIs.
485: 
486: <!-- TOC --><a name="pydoughexplain_structure"></a>
487: ### `pydough.explain_structure`
488: 
489: The `explain_structure` API can be called on a PyDough knowledge graph object returned from `load_metadata_graph` or `parse_json_metadata_from_file`. It displays information about a the metadata graph, including the names of each collection in the graph, the names of all scalar and sub-collection properties for each collection, and some details of the sub-collection properties.
490: 
491: Below is an example that displays information about the TPC-H schema, truncated to only include nations, regions and customers.
492: 
493: ```py
494: import pydough
495: graph = pydough.parse_json_metadata_from_file("insert_path_here.json", "TPCH")
496: pydough.explain_structure(graph)
497: ```
498: 
499: ```
500: Structure of PyDough graph: TPCH
501: 
502:   customers
503:   ├── acctbal
504:   ├── address
505:   ├── comment
506:   ├── key
507:   ├── mktsegment
508:   ├── name
509:   ├── nation_key
510:   ├── phone
511:   ├── nation [one member of nations] (reverse of nations.customers)
512:   └── orders [multiple orders] (reverse of orders.customer)
513: 
514:   nations
515:   ├── comment
516:   ├── key
517:   ├── name
518:   ├── region_key
519:   ├── customers [multiple customers] (reverse of customers.nation)
520:   ├── region [one member of regions] (reverse of regions.nations)
521:   └── suppliers [multiple suppliers] (reverse of suppliers.nation)
522: 
523:   regions
524:   ├── comment
525:   ├── key
526:   ├── name
527:   └── nations [multiple nations] (reverse of nations.region)
528: 
529: ...
530: ```
531: 
532: Notice how for each collection, the scalar properties are listed first without any information, followed by the sub-collections which include information about the sub-collection they connect to, the cardinality of the connection, and the reverse property.
533: 
534: <!-- TOC --><a name="pydoughexplain"></a>
535: ### `pydough.explain`
536: 
537: The `explain` API is a more generic explanation interface that can be called on different things to display different information:
538: 
539: - A metadata graph object
540: - A specific collection within a metadata graph object (can be accessed as `graph["collection_name"]`)
541: - A specific property within a specific collection within a metadata graph object (can be accessed as `graph["collection_name"]["property_name"]`)
542: - The PyDough code for a collection that could have `to_sql` or `to_df` called on it.
543: 
544: The `explain` API also has an optional `verbose` argument (default=False) that enables displaying additional information.
545: 
546: Below are examples of each of these behaviors, using a knowledge graph for the TPCH schema.
547: 
548: 1. Calling `explain` on the graph metadata.
549: 
550: ```py
551: import pydough
552: graph = pydough.parse_json_metadata_from_file("insert_path_here.json", "TPCH")
553: pydough.explain(graph, verbose=True)
554: ```
555: 
556: ```
557: PyDough graph: TPCH
558: Collections:
559:   customers
560:   lines
561:   nations
562:   orders
563:   parts
564:   regions
565:   suppliers
566:   supply_records
567: Call pydough.explain(graph[collection_name]) to learn more about any of these collections.
568: Call pydough.explain_structure(graph) to see how all of the collections in the graph are connected.
569: ```
570: 
571: 2. Calling `explain` on a collection's metadata.
572: 
573: ```py
574: import pydough
575: graph = pydough.parse_json_metadata_from_file("insert_path_here.json", "TPCH")
576: pydough.explain(graph["nations"], verbose=True)
577: ```
578: 
579: ```
580: PyDough collection: nations
581: Table path: main.NATION
582: Unique properties of collection: ['key']
583: Scalar properties:
584:   comment
585:   key
586:   name
587:   region_key
588: Subcollection properties:
589:   customers
590:   region
591:   suppliers
592: Call pydough.explain(graph['nations'][property_name]) to learn more about any of these properties
593: ```
594: 
595: 3a. Calling `explain` on a property's metadata (scalar attribute).
596: 
597: ```py
598: import pydough
599: graph = pydough.parse_json_metadata_from_file("insert_path_here.json", "TPCH")
600: pydough.explain(graph["nations"]["name"], verbose=True)
601: ```
602: 
603: ```
604: PyDough property: nations.name
605: Column name: main.NATION.n_name
606: Data type: string
607: ```
608: 
609: 3b. Calling `explain` on a property's metadata (sub-collection).
610: 
611: ```py
612: import pydough
613: graph = pydough.parse_json_metadata_from_file("insert_path_here.json", "TPCH")
614: pydough.explain(graph["nations"]["customers"], verbose=True)
615: ```
616: 
617: ```
618: PyDough property: nations.customers
619: This property connects collection nations to customers.
620: Cardinality of connection: One -> Many
621: Is reversible: yes
622: Reverse property: customers.nation
623: The subcollection relationship is defined by the following join conditions:
624:     nations.key == customers.nation_key
625: ```
626: 
627: 4a. Calling `explain` on PyDough code for a collection (example 1: entire graph).
628: 
629: ```py
630: %%pydough
631: result = TPCH
632: pydough.explain(result, verbose=True)
633: ```
634: 
635: ```
636: PyDough collection representing the following logic:
637:   TPCH
638: 
639: This node is a reference to the global context for the entire graph. An operation must be done onto this node (e.g. a CALCULATE or accessing a collection) before it can be executed.
640: 
641: The collection does not have any terms that can be included in a result if it is executed.
642: 
643: The collection has access to the following collections:
644:   customers, lines, nations, orders, parts, regions, suppliers, supply_records
645: 
646: Call pydough.explain_term(collection, term) to learn more about any of these
647: expressions or collections that the collection has access to.
648: ```
649: 
650: 4b. Calling `explain` on PyDough code for a collection (example 2: single collection).
651: 
652: ```py
653: %%pydough
654: result = nations
655: pydough.explain(result, verbose=True)
656: ```
657: 
658: ```
659: PyDough collection representing the following logic:
660:   ──┬─ TPCH
661:     └─── TableCollection[nations]
662: 
663: This node, specifically, accesses the collection nations.
664: Call pydough.explain(graph['nations']) to learn more about this collection.
665: 
666: The following terms will be included in the result if this collection is executed:
667:   comment, key, name, region_key
668: 
669: The collection has access to the following expressions:
670:   comment, key, name, region_key
671: 
672: The collection has access to the following collections:
673:   customers, region, suppliers
674: 
675: Call pydough.explain_term(collection, term) to learn more about any of these
676: expressions or collections that the collection has access to.
677: ```
678: 
679: 4c. Calling `explain` on PyDough code for a collection (example 3: filtering).
680: 
681: ```py
682: %%pydough
683: result = nations.WHERE(region.name == "EUROPE")
684: pydough.explain(result, verbose=True)
685: ```
686: 
687: ```
688: PyDough collection representing the following logic:
689:   ──┬─ TPCH
690:     ├─── TableCollection[nations]
691:     └─┬─ Where[$1.name == 'EUROPE']
692:       └─┬─ AccessChild
693:         └─── SubCollection[region]
694: 
695: This node first derives the following children before doing its main task:
696:   child $1:
697:     └─── SubCollection[region]
698: 
699: The main task of this node is to filter on the following conditions:
700:   $1.name == 'EUROPE', aka region.name == 'EUROPE'
701: 
702: The following terms will be included in the result if this collection is executed:
703:   comment, key, name, region_key
704: 
705: The collection has access to the following expressions:
706:   comment, key, name, region_key
707: 
708: The collection has access to the following collections:
709:   customers, region, suppliers
710: 
711: Call pydough.explain_term(collection, term) to learn more about any of these
712: expressions or collections that the collection has access to.
713: ```
714: 
715: 4d. Calling `explain` on PyDough code for a collection (example 4: CALCULATE).
716: 
717: ```py
718: %%pydough
719: result = nations.WHERE(region.name == "EUROPE").CALCULATE(name, n_custs=COUNT(customers))
720: pydough.explain(result, verbose=True)
721: ```
722: 
723: ```
724: PyDough collection representing the following logic:
725:   ──┬─ TPCH
726:     ├─── TableCollection[nations]
727:     ├─┬─ Where[$1.name == 'EUROPE']
728:     │ └─┬─ AccessChild
729:     │   └─── SubCollection[region]
730:     └─┬─ Calculate[name=name, n_custs=COUNT($1)]
731:       └─┬─ AccessChild
732:         └─── SubCollection[customers]
733: 
734: This node first derives the following children before doing its main task:
735:   child $1:
736:     └─── SubCollection[customers]
737: 
738: The main task of this node is to calculate the following additional expressions that are added to the terms of the collection:
739:   n_custs <- COUNT($1), aka COUNT(customers)
740:   name <- name (propagated from previous collection)
741: 
742: The following terms will be included in the result if this collection is executed:
743:   n_custs, name
744: 
745: The collection has access to the following expressions:
746:   comment, key, n_custs, name, region_key
747: 
748: The collection has access to the following collections:
749:   customers, region, suppliers
750: 
751: Call pydough.explain_term(collection, term) to learn more about any of these
752: expressions or collections that the collection has access to.
753: ```
754: 
755: <!-- TOC --><a name="pydoughexplain_term"></a>
756: ### `pydough.explain_term`
757: 
758: The `explain` API is limited in that it can only be called on complete PyDough collections that can be passed to `to_sql` or `to_df`. For example, it would be illegal to call `explain_term` on `name` or `nations.name` because neither is a collection, unlike `nations` or `nations.customers` which are collections.
759: 
760: To handle cases where you need to learn about a term within a collection, you can use the `explain_term` API. The first argument to `explain_term` is PyDough code for a collection, which can have `explain` called on it, and the second is PyDough code for a term that can be evaluated within the context of that collection (e.g. a scalar term of the collection, or one of its sub-collections).
761: 
762: The `explain_term` API also has a `verbose` keyword argument (default False) to specify whether to include a more detailed explanation, as opposed to a more compact summary.
763: 
764: Below are examples of using `explain_term`, using a knowledge graph for the TPCH schema. For each of these examples, `european_countries` is the "context" collection, which could have `to_sql` or `to_df` called on it, and `term` is the term being explained with regards to `european_countries`.
765: 
766: 1. Calling `explain_term` on a scalar attribute of a collection.
767: 
768: ```py
769: %%pydough
770: european_countries = nations.WHERE(region.name == "EUROPE")
771: term = name
772: pydough.explain_term(european_countries, term, verbose=True)
773: ```
774: 
775: ```
776: Collection:
777:   ──┬─ TPCH
778:     ├─── TableCollection[nations]
779:     └─┬─ Where[$1.name == 'EUROPE']
780:       └─┬─ AccessChild
781:         └─── SubCollection[region]
782: 
783: The term is the following expression: name
784: 
785: This is column 'name' of collection 'nations'
786: 
787: This term is singular with regards to the collection, meaning it can be placed in a CALCULATE of a collection.
788: For example, the following is valid:
789:   TPCH.nations.WHERE(region.name == 'EUROPE').CALCULATE(name)
790: ```
791: 
792: 2. Calling `explain_term` on a sub-collection of a collection.
793: 
794: ```py
795: %%pydough
796: european_countries = nations.WHERE(region.name == "EUROPE")
797: term = customers
798: pydough.explain_term(european_countries, term, verbose=True)
799: ```
800: 
801: ```
802: Collection:
803:   ──┬─ TPCH
804:     ├─── TableCollection[nations]
805:     └─┬─ Where[$1.name == 'EUROPE']
806:       └─┬─ AccessChild
807:         └─── SubCollection[region]
808: 
809: The term is the following child of the collection:
810:   └─┬─ AccessChild
811:     └─── SubCollection[customers]
812: 
813: This child is plural with regards to the collection, meaning its scalar terms can only be accessed by the collection if they are aggregated.
814: For example, the following are valid:
815:   TPCH.nations.WHERE(region.name == 'EUROPE').CALCULATE(COUNT(customers.acctbal))
816:   TPCH.nations.WHERE(region.name == 'EUROPE').WHERE(HAS(customers))
817:   TPCH.nations.WHERE(region.name == 'EUROPE').ORDER_BY(COUNT(customers).DESC())
818: 
819: To learn more about this child, you can try calling pydough.explain on the following:
820:   TPCH.nations.WHERE(region.name == 'EUROPE').customers
821: ```
822: 
823: 3. Calling `explain_term` on a plural expression.
824: 
825: ```py
826: %%pydough
827: european_countries = nations.WHERE(region.name == "EUROPE")
828: term = customers.acctbal
829: pydough.explain_term(european_countries, term, verbose=True)
830: ```
831: 
832: ```
833: Collection:
834:   ──┬─ TPCH
835:     ├─── TableCollection[nations]
836:     └─┬─ Where[$1.name == 'EUROPE']
837:       └─┬─ AccessChild
838:         └─── SubCollection[region]
839: 
840: The evaluation of this term first derives the following additional children to the collection before doing its main task:
841:   child $1:
842:     └─── SubCollection[customers]
843: 
844: The term is the following expression: $1.acctbal
845: 
846: This is a reference to expression 'acctbal' of child $1
847: 
848: This expression is plural with regards to the collection, meaning it can be placed in a CALCULATE of a collection if it is aggregated.
849: For example, the following is valid:
850:   TPCH.nations.WHERE(region.name == 'EUROPE').CALCULATE(COUNT(customers.acctbal))
851: ```
852: 
853: 4. Calling `explain_term` on an aggregation function call.
854: 
855: ```py
856: %%pydough
857: european_countries = nations.WHERE(region.name == "EUROPE")
858: term = AVG(customers.acctbal)
859: pydough.explain_term(european_countries, term, verbose=True)
860: ```
861: 
862: ```
863: Collection:
864:   ──┬─ TPCH
865:     ├─── TableCollection[nations]
866:     └─┬─ Where[$1.name == 'EUROPE']
867:       └─┬─ AccessChild
868:         └─── SubCollection[region]
869: 
870: The evaluation of this term first derives the following additional children to the collection before doing its main task:
871:   child $1:
872:     └─── SubCollection[customers]
873: 
874: The term is the following expression: AVG($1.acctbal)
875: 
876: This expression calls the function 'AVG' on the following arguments, aggregating them into a single value for each record of the collection:
877:   customers.acctbal
878: 
879: Call pydough.explain_term with this collection and any of the arguments to learn more about them.
880: 
881: This term is singular with regards to the collection, meaning it can be placed in a CALCULATE of a collection.
882: For example, the following is valid:
883:   TPCH.nations.WHERE(region.name == 'EUROPE').CALCULATE(AVG(customers.acctbal))
884: ```
885: ## Logging
886: 
887: Logging is enabled and set to INFO level by default. We can change the log level by setting the environment variable `PYDOUGH_LOG_LEVEL` to the standard levels: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL.
888: 
889: A new `logger` object can be created using `get_logger`.
890: This function configures and returns a logger instance. It takes the following arguments:
891: 
892: - `name` : The logger's name, typically the module name (`__name__`).
893: - `default_level` : The default logging level if not set externally via environment variable `PYDOUGH_LOG_LEVEL`. Defaults to `logging.INFO`.
894: - `fmt` : An optional log message format compatible with Python's logging. The default format is `"%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(name)s: %(message)s"`.
895: - `handlers` : An optional list of logging handlers to attach to the logger.
896: 
897: It returns a configured `logging.Logger` instance.
898: Here is an example of basic usage. We have not set the environment variable, hence the default level of logging is INFO.
899: 
900: ```py
901: from pydough import get_logger
902: pyd_logger = get_logger(__name__)
903: 
904: logger.info("This is an info message.")
905: logger.error("This is an error message.")
906: ```
907: 
908: We can also set the level of logging via a function argument. Note that if `PYDOUGH_LOG_LEVEL` is available, the default_level argument is overridden. 
909: 
910: ```python
911: # Import the function
912: from pydough import get_logger
913: 
914: # Get logger with a custom name and level
915: logger = get_logger(name="custom_logger", default_level=logging.DEBUG)
916: 
917: # Log messages
918: logger.debug("This is a debug message.")
919: logger.warning("This is a warning message.")
920: ```
921: We can also attach other handlers in addition to the default handler(`logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)`), by sending a list of handlers.
922: 
923: ```python
924: import logging
925: from pydough import get_logger
926: 
927: # Create a file handler
928: file_handler = logging.FileHandler("logfile.log")
929: 
930: # Get logger with custom file handler
931: logger = get_logger(handlers=[file_handler])
932: 
933: # Log messages
934: logger.info("This message will go to the console and the file.")
935: ```
````
