## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/meta_visualizer/public/js/graph/renderers/nodeRenderer.js
````javascript
  1: // Node Renderer - Renders node elements (collection boxes)
  2: 
  3: // --- Layout Constants ---
  4: const paddingX = 20;
  5: const nodeTitleY = 35;
  6: const tablePathY = 60;
  7: const dividingLineY = 70;
  8: const propertiesHeaderY = 90;
  9: const columnStartY = 110; // Y position of the first column item
 10: const subcollectionHeaderYOffset = 20; // Vertical distance from last column item to subcollection header
 11: const subcollectionStartYOffset = 20; // Vertical distance from subcollection header to first subcollection item
 12: const lineHeight = 22; // Vertical distance between lines (columns/subcollections)
 13: const bottomPadding = 15; // Space below last item, including tooltip indicator
 14: const tooltipOffset = 20; // Offset for tooltip from bottom-right corner
 15: const minHeight = 150; // Minimum node height
 16: // --- End Layout Constants ---
 17: 
 18: /**
 19:  * Calculate the required height for a node based on its content.
 20:  * @param {Object} d - The node data object.
 21:  * @returns {number} The calculated height.
 22:  */
 23: function calculateNodeHeight(d) {
 24:   // Start with the Y position of the "Properties:" header
 25:   let lastElementY = propertiesHeaderY;
 26: 
 27:   // Calculate Y position of the baseline of the last column item
 28:   if (d.columns.length > 0) {
 29:     // Baseline of the first column is columnStartY, last is offset by (length-1)*lineHeight
 30:     lastElementY = columnStartY + (d.columns.length - 1) * lineHeight;
 31:   }
 32: 
 33:   // Calculate Y position of the baseline of the last subcollection item
 34:   if (d.subcollections.length > 0) {
 35:     // Y position of the subcollection header
 36:     const subcollectionHeaderBaseY =
 37:       d.columns.length > 0
 38:         ? columnStartY + d.columns.length * lineHeight // Below last column
 39:         : propertiesHeaderY; // Below "Properties:" if no columns
 40:     const subcollectionHeaderY =
 41:       subcollectionHeaderBaseY + subcollectionHeaderYOffset;
 42: 
 43:     // Y position of the first subcollection item's baseline
 44:     const firstSubcollectionItemY =
 45:       subcollectionHeaderY + subcollectionStartYOffset;
 46: 
 47:     // Y position of the last subcollection item's baseline
 48:     lastElementY =
 49:       firstSubcollectionItemY + (d.subcollections.length - 1) * lineHeight;
 50:   }
 51: 
 52:   // Calculate total height: baseline of last element + padding below it
 53:   // Adding roughly half a line height adjusts from baseline to approximate bottom of text.
 54:   let calculatedHeight = lastElementY + lineHeight / 2 + bottomPadding;
 55: 
 56:   // Ensure minimum height is respected
 57:   return Math.max(calculatedHeight, minHeight);
 58: }
 59: 
 60: /**
 61:  * Create nodes for the graph
 62:  * @param {Object} g - The SVG group element
 63:  * @param {Array} nodes - The array of nodes
 64:  * @param {Object} tooltipHandlers - Object containing tooltip handlers and tooltip element
 65:  * @returns {Object} The D3 selection of nodes
 66:  */
 67: export function createNodes(g, nodes, tooltipHandlers) {
 68:   const {
 69:     tooltip,
 70:     showNodeTooltip,
 71:     hideTooltip,
 72:     isMouseOverTooltip,
 73:     clearHoverElement,
 74:     scheduleHide,
 75:     cancelHide,
 76:   } = tooltipHandlers || {};
 77: 
 78:   // Calculate required height for each node before creating elements
 79:   nodes.forEach((d) => {
 80:     // Store original height if needed, otherwise overwrite or use a new property
 81:     d.calculatedHeight = calculateNodeHeight(d);
 82:   });
 83: 
 84:   // Create the node containers
 85:   const node = g
 86:     .selectAll(".node")
 87:     .data(nodes)
 88:     .enter()
 89:     .append("g")
 90:     .attr("class", "node")
 91:     .attr("id", (d) => `node-${d.id}`);
 92: 
 93:   // Add rectangles for the collection boxes
 94:   node
 95:     .append("rect")
 96:     .attr("width", (d) => d.width)
 97:     .attr("height", (d) => d.calculatedHeight)
 98:     .attr("rx", 10)
 99:     .attr("ry", 10);
100: 
101:   // Add collection titles
102:   node
103:     .append("text")
104:     .attr("x", paddingX)
105:     .attr("y", nodeTitleY)
106:     .attr("class", "node-title")
107:     .style("font-size", "18px")
108:     .style("font-weight", "bold")
109:     .text((d) => d.name);
110: 
111:   // Add table path
112:   node
113:     .append("text")
114:     .attr("x", paddingX)
115:     .attr("y", tablePathY)
116:     .attr("class", "table-path")
117:     .style("font-size", "13px")
118:     .text((d) => d.tablePath);
119: 
120:   // Add dividing line
121:   node
122:     .append("line")
123:     .attr("x1", paddingX)
124:     .attr("y1", dividingLineY)
125:     .attr("x2", (d) => d.width - paddingX)
126:     .attr("y2", dividingLineY)
127:     .attr("stroke", "#333")
128:     .attr("stroke-width", 1);
129: 
130:   // Add properties header
131:   addPropertiesHeader(node);
132: 
133:   // Add columns
134:   addColumnsList(node);
135: 
136:   // Add subcollections header and list
137:   addSubcollectionsList(node);
138: 
139:   // Add tooltip indicator in bottom right corner with event handlers
140:   const tooltipIndicator = node
141:     .append("g")
142:     .attr("class", "tooltip-indicator-group")
143:     // Position tooltip relative to calculated height and width
144:     .attr(
145:       "transform",
146:       (d) =>
147:         `translate(${d.width - tooltipOffset}, ${
148:           d.calculatedHeight - tooltipOffset
149:         })`
150:     );
151: 
152:   // Only add event handlers if tooltip handlers are provided
153:   if (
154:     tooltip &&
155:     showNodeTooltip &&
156:     hideTooltip &&
157:     isMouseOverTooltip &&
158:     clearHoverElement &&
159:     scheduleHide &&
160:     cancelHide
161:   ) {
162:     tooltipIndicator
163:       .on("mouseover", function (event, d) {
164:         // Cancel any pending hide operations
165:         cancelHide();
166:         // Show tooltip for this indicator
167:         const nodeId = `node-${d.id}`;
168:         showNodeTooltip(tooltip, d, event, nodeId);
169:       })
170:       .on("mouseout", function (event, d) {
171:         const nodeId = `node-${d.id}`;
172:         // Schedule tooltip to hide after a short delay
173:         // Tooltip mouseover will cancel this if the mouse moves onto it.
174:         scheduleHide(tooltip, nodeId, 100); // 100ms delay
175:       });
176:   }
177: 
178:   tooltipIndicator
179:     .append("circle")
180:     .attr("class", "tooltip-indicator")
181:     .attr("r", 8)
182:     .attr("fill", "#1f77b4")
183:     .attr("opacity", 0.7);
184: 
185:   // Add question mark in the indicator
186:   tooltipIndicator
187:     .append("text")
188:     .attr("class", "tooltip-indicator-text")
189:     .attr("text-anchor", "middle")
190:     .attr("dy", "0.35em")
191:     .attr("fill", "white")
192:     .attr("font-size", "12px")
193:     .attr("font-weight", "bold")
194:     .text("?");
195: 
196:   return node;
197: }
198: 
199: /**
200:  * Add the properties header to nodes
201:  * @param {Object} node - The D3 selection of nodes
202:  */
203: function addPropertiesHeader(node) {
204:   node
205:     .append("text")
206:     .attr("x", paddingX)
207:     .attr("y", propertiesHeaderY)
208:     .attr("class", "properties-header")
209:     .style("font-size", "15px")
210:     .style("font-weight", "bold")
211:     .text("Properties:");
212: }
213: 
214: /**
215:  * Add the columns list to nodes
216:  * @param {Object} node - The D3 selection of nodes
217:  */
218: function addColumnsList(node) {
219:   node
220:     .selectAll(".column-item")
221:     .data((d) => d.columns.map((column) => ({ column, parent: d })))
222:     .enter()
223:     .append("text")
224:     .attr("x", paddingX + 10) // Indent properties slightly
225:     .attr("y", (d, i) => columnStartY + i * lineHeight)
226:     .attr("class", "column-item")
227:     .style("font-size", "13px")
228:     .text((d) => `${d.column.name} (${d.column.dataType})`);
229: }
230: 
231: /**
232:  * Add the subcollections header and list to nodes
233:  * @param {Object} node - The D3 selection of nodes
234:  */
235: function addSubcollectionsList(node) {
236:   // Add subcollections header
237:   node
238:     .append("text")
239:     .attr("x", paddingX)
240:     .attr("y", (d) => {
241:       // Calculate Y position based on whether there are columns
242:       const baseY =
243:         d.columns.length > 0
244:           ? columnStartY + d.columns.length * lineHeight // Below last column
245:           : propertiesHeaderY; // Below "Properties:" if no columns
246:       return baseY + subcollectionHeaderYOffset;
247:     })
248:     .attr("class", "properties-header") // Reuse class for styling consistency
249:     .style("font-size", "15px")
250:     .style("font-weight", "bold")
251:     .text("Subcollections:");
252: 
253:   // Add subcollection items
254:   node
255:     .selectAll(".subcollection-item")
256:     .data((d) => d.subcollections.map((subcol) => ({ subcol, parent: d })))
257:     .enter()
258:     .append("text")
259:     .attr("x", paddingX + 10) // Indent subcollections slightly
260:     .attr("y", (d, i) => {
261:       const parent = d.parent;
262:       // Calculate Y position for subcollection header based on column count
263:       const subcollectionHeaderBaseY =
264:         parent.columns.length > 0
265:           ? columnStartY + parent.columns.length * lineHeight
266:           : propertiesHeaderY;
267:       const subcollectionHeaderY =
268:         subcollectionHeaderBaseY + subcollectionHeaderYOffset;
269:       // Calculate Y position for this subcollection item
270:       const currentItemY =
271:         subcollectionHeaderY + subcollectionStartYOffset + i * lineHeight;
272:       return currentItemY;
273:     })
274:     .attr(
275:       "class",
276:       (d) =>
277:         `subcollection-item subcollection-${d.subcol.type} ${
278:           d.subcol.isReverse ? "subcollection-reverse" : ""
279:         }`
280:     )
281:     .style("font-size", "13px")
282:     .text((d) => {
283:       // Always show relationships as outgoing (→) to indicate they can be accessed from this node
284:       return `${d.subcol.name} → ${d.subcol.target}`;
285:     });
286: }
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/meta_visualizer/public/js/graph/renderers/README.md
````markdown
 1: # Graph Renderers
 2: 
 3: This directory contains modules responsible for creating the visual SVG elements of the graph based on the processed data.
 4: 
 5: ## Files
 6: 
 7: - `nodeRenderer.js`: Creates the visual representation for each node (collection). It builds an SVG group containing a rectangle, title text, table path text, property/column lists, subcollection list, and a tooltip indicator.
 8: - `linkRenderer.js`: Creates the visual representation for each link (relationship). It builds an SVG group containing a path element (the line connecting nodes) with an appropriate arrowhead marker and a text label displaying the relationship name along the path.
 9: - `markerRenderer.js`: Defines reusable SVG `<marker>` elements (arrowheads) used by `linkRenderer.js` to indicate relationship direction and type (e.g., `simple_join`, `cartesian_product`, `highlighted`).
10: 
11: ## Responsibilities
12: 
13: - Translating node data (name, path, columns, subcollections) into structured SVG elements (rectangles, text, lines).
14: - Translating link data (source, target, name, type) into SVG paths and text labels.
15: - Defining and applying appropriate markers (arrowheads) to links based on relationship type and interaction state.
16: - Structuring the SVG output within the main graph group (`<g>`) provided by `graphCreator.js`.
17: - Setting up basic element attributes (IDs, classes) for styling and interaction handling.
18: 
19: ## Rendering Process
20: 
21: 1. `markerRenderer.js` (`setupMarkers`) is called first by `graphCreator.js` to define the SVG arrowheads in the `<defs>` section.
22: 2. `nodeRenderer.js` (`createNodes`) is called to generate the SVG groups and internal elements for all nodes.
23: 3. `linkRenderer.js` (`createLinks`) is called to generate the SVG groups, paths, and labels for all links, referencing the pre-defined markers.
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/meta_visualizer/public/js/graph/styles/README.md
````markdown
 1: # Graph Styles
 2: 
 3: This directory contains the styling definitions for the graph visualization.
 4: 
 5: ## Files
 6: 
 7: - `graphStyles.js`: Defines and injects CSS rules for all visual components of the graph, including nodes, links, markers, tooltips, and interaction states.
 8: 
 9: ## Responsibilities
10: 
11: - Defining the visual appearance of nodes (rectangles, text, titles, properties sections) in various states (default, highlighted, primary, faded).
12: - Styling links based on type (forward, reverse) and state (default, highlighted), including line style, color, thickness, and labels.
13: - Styling arrow markers for links.
14: - Defining the appearance and layout of tooltips.
15: - Using CSS transitions for smooth visual feedback during interactions.
16: - Ensuring a consistent and readable visual language for the graph.
17: 
18: ## Key Styling Areas
19: 
20: - **Nodes:** Base appearance, text formatting (title, headers, items), state-based highlighting (stroke, fill, font size changes).
21: - **Links:** Distinguishing forward (solid blue) and reverse (dashed orange) relationships, highlighting (thicker green), label appearance and positioning.
22: - **Tooltips:** Background, border, padding, font sizes, layout for titles and content sections, hints.
23: - **Interaction States:** Styles for `.node-highlighted`, `.node-primary`, `.node-faded`, `.link-highlighted`, `.arrowhead-highlighted`, `.link-label-highlighted`.
24: - **Transitions:** Smooth visual changes for properties like stroke, fill, opacity, font-size, etc.
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/meta_visualizer/public/js/graph/utils/geometryUtils.js
````javascript
  1: // Geometry Utils - Utility functions for geometric calculations
  2: 
  3: /**
  4:  * Calculate the intersection point of a line with a rectangle
  5:  * @param {Object} node - The node (rectangle)
  6:  * @param {number} targetX - The target x coordinate
  7:  * @param {number} targetY - The target y coordinate
  8:  * @returns {Object} The intersection point {x, y}
  9:  */
 10: export function calculateIntersection(node, targetX, targetY) {
 11:   const centerX = node.x + node.width / 2;
 12:   const centerY = node.y + node.height / 2;
 13: 
 14:   // Calculate angle between center of node and target point
 15:   const angle = Math.atan2(targetY - centerY, targetX - centerX);
 16: 
 17:   // Calculate intersection point on rectangle border
 18:   let x, y;
 19: 
 20:   if (Math.abs(Math.cos(angle)) > Math.abs(Math.sin(angle))) {
 21:     // Intersect with left or right edge
 22:     x = node.x + (Math.cos(angle) > 0 ? node.width : 0);
 23:     y = centerY + Math.tan(angle) * (x - centerX);
 24:   } else {
 25:     // Intersect with top or bottom edge
 26:     y = node.y + (Math.sin(angle) > 0 ? node.height : 0);
 27:     x = centerX + (y - centerY) / Math.tan(angle);
 28:   }
 29: 
 30:   return { x, y };
 31: }
 32: 
 33: /**
 34:  * Calculate the distance between two points
 35:  * @param {number} x1 - The x coordinate of the first point
 36:  * @param {number} y1 - The y coordinate of the first point
 37:  * @param {number} x2 - The x coordinate of the second point
 38:  * @param {number} y2 - The y coordinate of the second point
 39:  * @returns {number} The distance between the points
 40:  */
 41: export function calculateDistance(x1, y1, x2, y2) {
 42:   return Math.sqrt(Math.pow(x2 - x1, 2) + Math.pow(y2 - y1, 2));
 43: }
 44: 
 45: /**
 46:  * Calculate the center point of a node
 47:  * @param {Object} node - The node
 48:  * @returns {Object} The center point {x, y}
 49:  */
 50: export function calculateCenter(node) {
 51:   return {
 52:     x: node.x + node.width / 2,
 53:     y: node.y + node.height / 2,
 54:   };
 55: }
 56: 
 57: /**
 58:  * Calculate the midpoint between two points
 59:  * @param {number} x1 - The x coordinate of the first point
 60:  * @param {number} y1 - The y coordinate of the first point
 61:  * @param {number} x2 - The x coordinate of the second point
 62:  * @param {number} y2 - The y coordinate of the second point
 63:  * @returns {Object} The midpoint {x, y}
 64:  */
 65: export function calculateMidpoint(x1, y1, x2, y2) {
 66:   return {
 67:     x: (x1 + x2) / 2,
 68:     y: (y1 + y2) / 2,
 69:   };
 70: }
 71: 
 72: /**
 73:  * Calculate the SVG path string for a link between two nodes,
 74:  * ensuring the path connects to the node boundaries accurately.
 75:  * Also calculates a parallel path for potential reverse links.
 76:  *
 77:  * @param {Object} sourceNode - The source node object.
 78:  * @param {Object} targetNode - The target node object.
 79:  * @param {number} [offset=10] - The perpendicular distance between forward and reverse paths.
 80:  * @returns {{forward: string, reverse: string}|{forward: string, reverse: string}} Path strings or empty strings if nodes invalid.
 81:  */
 82: export function calculateLinkPath(sourceNode, targetNode, offset = 10) {
 83:   if (!sourceNode || !targetNode) {
 84:     console.warn("CalculateLinkPath: Invalid source or target node provided.");
 85:     return { forward: "", reverse: "" }; // Return empty paths
 86:   }
 87: 
 88:   // Get centers
 89:   const sourceCenter = calculateCenter(sourceNode);
 90:   const targetCenter = calculateCenter(targetNode);
 91: 
 92:   // Calculate intersection points
 93:   const sourceIntersection = calculateIntersection(
 94:     sourceNode,
 95:     targetCenter.x,
 96:     targetCenter.y
 97:   );
 98:   const targetIntersection = calculateIntersection(
 99:     targetNode,
100:     sourceCenter.x,
101:     sourceCenter.y
102:   );
103: 
104:   // Calculate the angle for offsetting
105:   const angle = Math.atan2(
106:     targetIntersection.y - sourceIntersection.y,
107:     targetIntersection.x - sourceIntersection.x
108:   );
109:   const perpAngle = angle + Math.PI / 2; // Perpendicular angle
110:   const offsetX = Math.cos(perpAngle) * offset;
111:   const offsetY = Math.sin(perpAngle) * offset;
112: 
113:   // Define source and target points for the path calculation
114:   const sx = sourceIntersection.x;
115:   const sy = sourceIntersection.y;
116:   const tx = targetIntersection.x;
117:   const ty = targetIntersection.y;
118: 
119:   // Return both forward and reverse paths with offset
120:   return {
121:     forward: `M${sx + offsetX},${sy + offsetY}L${tx + offsetX},${ty + offsetY}`,
122:     reverse: `M${tx - offsetX},${ty - offsetY}L${sx - offsetX},${sy - offsetY}`, // Note: Reverse direction for reverse path
123:   };
124: }
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/meta_visualizer/public/js/graph/utils/README.md
````markdown
 1: # Graph Utilities
 2: 
 3: This directory contains reusable utility functions supporting various calculations needed for the graph visualization.
 4: 
 5: ## Files
 6: 
 7: - `geometryUtils.js`: Provides helper functions for common geometric calculations related to node positions, link paths, and distances.
 8: 
 9: ## Responsibilities
10: 
11: - Encapsulating common mathematical or geometric operations used by other graph modules (renderers, layouts, interactions).
12: - Providing clean interfaces for calculations like finding intersection points, distances, centers, and midpoints.
13: 
14: ## Provided Utilities (`geometryUtils.js`)
15: 
16: - `calculateIntersection(node, targetX, targetY)`: Computes the intersection point between the edge of a rectangular node and a line segment extending from the node's center towards a target point (`targetX`, `targetY`). Used for drawing links precisely to the node boundary.
17: - `calculateDistance(x1, y1, x2, y2)`: Calculates the distance between two points.
18: - `calculateCenter(node)`: Returns the center coordinates (`{x, y}`) of a given node rectangle.
19: - `calculateMidpoint(x1, y1, x2, y2)`: Computes the midpoint between two points.
20: - `calculateLinkPath(sourceNode, targetNode, offset)`: Calculates the SVG path string for a link between two nodes, connecting to their boundaries, and includes an offset path for reverse links.
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/meta_visualizer/public/js/graph/README.md
````markdown
 1: # Graph Visualization Component
 2: 
 3: This directory contains the JavaScript modules responsible for creating and managing the interactive graph visualization component of MetaViewer. It leverages D3.js for rendering and interaction.
 4: 
 5: ## Directory Structure
 6: 
 7: - **`core/`**: Handles the overall initialization, data processing, and orchestration of the graph creation.
 8: 
 9:   - `graphInitializer.js`: Sets up the UI (file load button), handles JSON file input, parses data, and calls `graphCreator`.
10:   - `dataProcessor.js`: Transforms the raw JSON metadata into `nodes` and `links` arrays suitable for D3, processing collections, properties, and relationships (including reverse links).
11:   - `graphCreator.js`: The main orchestrator that sets up the SVG canvas, calls renderers, initializes layouts and interactions, and manages the main D3 simulation loop.
12: 
13: - **`renderers/`**: Modules focused on creating the visual SVG elements.
14: 
15:   - `nodeRenderer.js`: Renders nodes as SVG groups (rect, text for title/path/columns/subcollections, tooltip indicator).
16:   - `linkRenderer.js`: Renders links as SVG groups (path with markers, text label).
17:   - `markerRenderer.js`: Defines SVG arrowheads (`<marker>`) for different link types and states.
18: 
19: - **`layouts/`**: Algorithms for positioning nodes and links.
20: 
21:   - `forceLayout.js`: Implements the default force-directed layout using D3 simulation forces.
22:   - `treeLayout.js`: Implements a hierarchical tree layout triggered by node clicks, arranging nodes based on outgoing links from a root.
23: 
24: - **`interactions/`**: Modules handling user input and visual feedback.
25: 
26:   - `dragHandler.js`: Enables node dragging and updates fixed positions (`fx`, `fy`).
27:   - `highlightHandler.js`: Manages highlighting of related nodes/links on hover and click, triggers tree layout.
28:   - `zoomHandler.js`: Implements zoom/pan functionality with UI controls.
29:   - `tooltipHandler.js`: Manages the display of informative tooltips on hover.
30: 
31: - **`styles/`**: Styling definitions for the graph.
32: 
33:   - `graphStyles.js`: Injects CSS rules to style nodes, links, tooltips, and interaction states (highlighted, faded, etc.).
34: 
35: - **`utils/`**: Reusable utility functions.
36:   - `geometryUtils.js`: Provides geometric calculation helpers (intersections, distances, centers).
37: 
38: ## Initialization and Data Flow
39: 
40: The visualization is bootstrapped by `main.js`, which calls `initGraphVisualization` from `core/graphInitializer.js`.
41: 
42: 1.  `graphInitializer.js` sets up the "Load JSON File" button and waits for user input.
43: 2.  When a user selects a valid JSON file, it's read and parsed.
44: 3.  The parsed data object is passed to `createGraph` in `core/graphCreator.js`.
45: 4.  `graphCreator.js` calls `processMetadata` (from `core/dataProcessor.js`) to get `nodes` and `links`.
46: 5.  `graphCreator.js` then initializes the D3 simulation (`layouts/forceLayout.js`), sets up SVG markers (`renderers/markerRenderer.js`), renders nodes (`renderers/nodeRenderer.js`) and links (`renderers/linkRenderer.js`), applies styles (`styles/graphStyles.js`), and sets up interactions (`interactions/` handlers).
47: 6.  The force simulation automatically positions nodes, and interaction handlers provide zoom, pan, drag, highlight, and tooltip features.
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/meta_visualizer/DEVELOPER_DOCS.md
````markdown
  1: # MetaViewer - Developer Documentation
  2: 
  3: This document provides a deeper dive into the core data structures and internal workings of the MetaViewer graph visualization component, intended for developers looking to understand or extend the functionality.
  4: 
  5: ## D3.js Background Knowledge
  6: 
  7: This project heavily utilizes D3.js (Data-Driven Documents) for its graph visualization capabilities. Understanding the following core D3.js concepts is crucial for working with the MetaViewer codebase:
  8: 
  9: - **Nodes and Links Data Structure**: D3's force simulation expects data as arrays of `nodes` (representing entities) and `links` (representing relationships). MetaViewer's `dataProcessor.js` prepares data in this specific format.
 10: - **Force Simulation (`d3.forceSimulation`)**: This is the physics engine D3 uses to position nodes and links based on forces like charge repulsion and link attraction. It's central to MetaViewer's graph layout (`forceLayout.js`) and dynamically updates node properties like `x`, `y`, `vx`, and `vy`.
 11: - **Selections (`d3.select`, `d3.selectAll`)**: D3 uses a powerful selection mechanism to find and manipulate DOM elements (primarily SVG elements in this project). MetaViewer uses selections to target visual elements for creation, styling, and updates.
 12: - **Data Binding (`.data()`, `.enter()`, `.append()`, `.join()`)**: This is D3's declarative method for joining an array of data (our `nodes` and `links`) to a selection of DOM elements. The `.enter()` selection handles new data points (creating new SVG elements). `nodeRenderer.js` and `linkRenderer.js` extensively use data binding.
 13: - **SVG Manipulation**: D3 is used to create and modify Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG)(HTML elements). MetaViewer renders nodes as SVG `<rect>` elements, links as `<path>` elements, and labels using `<text>` and `<textPath>`. Attributes like `transform` (for positioning) and `d` (for path definitions) are key. An important SVG element is the group element (`<g>`), which is used to group other SVG elements. Transformations (like translation or rotation) applied to a `<g>` element affect all its children, making it useful for composite objects like our nodes (which might consist of a rectangle and text) or link groups (path and label).
 14: - **Simulation Tick Event (`simulation.on("tick", ...)`):** The force simulation emits a "tick" event at each step of its calculation. `graphCreator.js` listens to this event to update the positions of SVG nodes and links, visually reflecting the simulation's current state.
 15: - **Fixed Positioning (`fx`, `fy`)**: D3 allows nodes to have their positions "fixed" using `fx` and `fy` properties, which override the simulation's calculations. MetaViewer uses this for user-initiated dragging (`dragHandler.js`) and for the hierarchical tree layout (`treeLayout.js`).
 16: - **Event Handling (`.on()`)**: D3 can attach event listeners (e.g., `click`, `mouseover`, `drag`) to SVG elements. This enables interactivity in MetaViewer, such as highlighting connections, showing tooltips (`tooltipHandler.js`), and drag-and-drop.
 17: 
 18: For a deeper understanding of these concepts and D3.js in general, the following resources are recommended:
 19: 
 20: - **[D3.js Official Website](https://d3js.org/)**: The primary source for documentation, official examples, and API references.
 21: 
 22: ## Core Data Structures (`nodes` and `links`)
 23: 
 24: The heart of the visualization lies in two key arrays generated by `dataProcessor.js`: `nodes` and `links`. These arrays conform to the structure expected by D3.js's force simulation and are used throughout the rendering and interaction logic.
 25: 
 26: ### 1. Node Object Structure
 27: 
 28: Each element in the `nodes` array represents a collection (table/entity) from the input metadata. Here's a breakdown of its key properties:
 29: 
 30: - **`id`** (String): Unique identifier for the node, typically the collection name. Used by D3 simulation to link nodes.
 31: - **`name`** (String): Display name for the node (usually same as `id`).
 32: - **`columns`** (Array): List of objects representing table columns/attributes within the collection. Each object typically contains `name`, `columnName`, and `dataType`. Used by `nodeRenderer.js` to display properties.
 33: - **`subcollections`** (Array): List of objects representing relationships originating _from_ this node. Each object details the relationship (`name`, `type`, `target` ID, `singular`, `noCollisions`, `isForward`/`isReverse`, `propertyData`). Used by `nodeRenderer.js` to list outgoing connections and by `dataProcessor.js` to create links.
 34: - **`tablePath`** (String): The source path provided in the metadata. Displayed by `nodeRenderer.js`.
 35: - **`uniqueProperties`** (Array): List of unique property names/combinations. Displayed by `tooltipHandler.js`.
 36: - **`width`, `height`** (Number): Calculated dimensions for the node's visual representation (the rectangle). `width` is currently fixed, while `height` is dynamically calculated by `nodeRenderer.js` (using `calculateNodeHeight`) based on the number of displayed columns and subcollections to ensure content fits. Used by `nodeRenderer.js` and `forceCollide`.
 37: - **`x`, `y`** (Number): _Added/Modified by D3 Simulation_. Current calculated horizontal and vertical position of the node center. Updated on every simulation "tick". `nodeRenderer.js` uses these via the `tick` handler in `graphCreator.js` to set the node group's `transform` attribute.
 38: - **`vx`, `vy`** (Number): _Added/Modified by D3 Simulation_. Current velocity of the node. Used internally by the simulation.
 39: - **`fx`, `fy`** (Number | null): _Set by Drag/Tree Layout_. Fixed position coordinates. If non-null, the simulation will not modify `x` or `y`. `dragHandler.js` sets these on drag end to keep nodes in place. `treeLayout.js` sets these to arrange nodes hierarchically, overriding the force simulation.
 40: - **`treeLevel`** (Number | null): _Set by `treeLayout.js`_. The depth level of the node in the current tree view (0 for the root). Null if not in tree view or not part of the current tree.
 41: - **`treePosition`** (Number | null): _Set by `treeLayout.js`_. The calculated horizontal position within its level in the tree view.
 42: - **`treeParent`** (String | null): _Set by `treeLayout.js`_. The `id` of the parent node in the current tree view hierarchy.
 43: 
 44: ### Understanding Node Position Properties (x/y, fx/fy, vx/vy)
 45: 
 46: The D3 force simulation adds several properties to each node object in the `nodes` array to manage its position and movement. Understanding their roles is key:
 47: 
 48: - **`x`, `y` (Current Position):** These represent the node's calculated coordinates at the current simulation tick. The simulation updates these values based on applied forces (links, repulsion, centering, collision) and the node's velocity. The visual position of the SVG node group (`<g class="node">`) is typically updated in the `tick` event handler to match these `x` and `y` values using a `transform="translate(x, y)"` attribute.
 49: 
 50: - **`vx`, `vy` (Velocity):** These represent the node's current velocity along the x and y axes. The simulation calculates these based on the forces acting on the node. In the next simulation step, the node's `x` and `y` will be updated based on `vx` and `vy` (factoring in simulation constraints like friction/damping). Developers typically don't directly manipulate `vx`/`vy`, but they drive the node's movement during the simulation's settling process.
 51: 
 52: - **`fx`, `fy` (Fixed Position):** These properties allow you to **fix** a node's position. If `fx` is set to a non-null numerical value, the simulation will **ignore** its own calculations for the node's x-position and velocity (`x`, `vx`) and hold the node's `x` coordinate at the `fx` value. The same applies to `fy` for the y-position. This provides a mechanism to override the simulation's positioning.
 53:   - **Use Case 1 (Dragging):** `dragHandler.js` sets `fx` and `fy` to the node's current `x` and `y` during the drag (`dragstarted`, `dragged`) and keeps them set at the end (`dragended`). This pins the node where the user dropped it.
 54:   - **Use Case 2 (Tree Layout):** `treeLayout.js` calculates specific positions for nodes in the hierarchy and sets their `fx` and `fy` values accordingly. This forces the nodes into the desired tree structure, regardless of the physics simulation forces.
 55: 
 56: In summary: `x`/`y` show where a node _is_, `vx`/`vy` determine how it's _moving_ according to the simulation, and `fx`/`fy` _override_ the simulation to pin the node in place.
 57: 
 58: ### 2. Link Object Structure
 59: 
 60: Each element in the `links` array represents a relationship between two collections.
 61: 
 62: - **`source`** (Object): _Reference_ to the source node object (element from the `nodes` array). D3 simulation uses this reference.
 63: - **`target`** (Object): _Reference_ to the target node object (element from the `nodes` array). D3 simulation uses this reference.
 64: - **`name`** (String): The name of the relationship (property name from the source collection's metadata). Displayed as the link label by `linkRenderer.js`.
 65: - **`type`** (String): The type of relationship (e.g., `simple_join`, `cartesian_product`, `general_join`). Used for styling and potentially by the simulation or renderers.
 66: - **`condition`** (String | null): _Specific to `general_join`_. The join condition string provided in the metadata. Displayed by `tooltipHandler.js`.
 67: - **`singular`** (Boolean): Metadata flag indicating a one-to-one type relationship. Used in tooltips.
 68: - **`noCollisions`** (Boolean): Metadata flag. Used in tooltips.
 69: - **`isForward`** (Boolean): Flag indicating if this link represents a relationship defined directly in the source node's metadata.
 70: - **`isReverse`** (Boolean): Flag indicating if this link represents a reverse relationship added by `dataProcessor.js` for bidirectionality. Used for styling (e.g., dashed lines).
 71: - **`propertyData`** (Object): Reference to the original property data object from the input JSON for this relationship.
 72: 
 73: _Initial state_: `dataProcessor.js` initially creates links where `source` and `target` might be string IDs. `linkRenderer.js` (or sometimes the simulation setup) resolves these IDs to actual object references before rendering/simulation starts.
 74: 
 75: ## Data Processing Flow (`dataProcessor.js`)
 76: 
 77: 1.  **Node Creation**: Iterates through collections in the raw JSON data. For each collection, it creates a node object, extracting `table_path`, `unique_properties`, processing `properties` into `columns` and `subcollections` (only forward relationships initially). Initial `width` is fixed, and `height` is dynamically calculated by `nodeRenderer.js` (`calculateNodeHeight`) based on content. Initial `x`/`y` positions are often set in a simple grid pattern but are quickly overridden by the simulation.
 78: 2.  **Reverse Relationship Processing**: Iterates through all created nodes and their `subcollections`. For each _forward_ relationship found (A -> B) that has a `reverse_relationship_name` defined, it finds the target node (B) and adds a corresponding _reverse_ subcollection (B -> A) to the target node's `subcollections` list, flipping relevant flags (`singular`/`noCollisions`).
 79: 3.  **Link Creation**: Iterates through all nodes again. For every relationship listed in a node's `subcollections` (both forward and reverse), it creates a link object, initially setting `source` and `target` to the respective node IDs.
 80: 
 81: ## Rendering Interaction (`graphCreator.js`, `renderers/`)
 82: 
 83: - `graphCreator.js` receives the `nodes` and `links` arrays.
 84: - It calls `createNodes(g, nodes, ...)` from `nodeRenderer.js`. `nodeRenderer` uses D3's data binding (`.data(nodes).enter().append('g')...`) to create an SVG group (`<g class="node">`) for each node object. Inside this group, it appends SVG elements (`<rect>`, `<text>`, etc.) whose attributes (size, text content) are determined by the bound node data (`d`).
 85: - It calls `createLinks(g, links, nodes)` from `linkRenderer.js`. `linkRenderer` binds the `links` data to create SVG groups (`<g class="link-group">`). Inside, it appends a `<path>` and a `<text>` with `<textPath>`. The path's `d` attribute (defining its shape) is calculated in the simulation `tick` handler based on the `source` and `target` node positions. The `textPath` uses the path to display the link `name`. It references markers defined by `markerRenderer.js` (e.g., `arrowhead-simple_join`, `arrowhead-general_join`).
 86: 
 87: ## Layout Interaction (`graphCreator.js`, `layouts/`)
 88: 
 89: - `setupForceSimulation(nodes, links, ...)` from `forceLayout.js` initializes the D3 simulation, providing it the `nodes` and `links` arrays. The simulation internally calculates forces and updates the `x`, `y`, `vx`, `vy` properties of each object _in the `nodes` array_ on each simulation step ("tick").
 90: - `graphCreator.js` sets up a listener for the simulation's `"tick"` event: `simulation.on("tick", ticked);`.
 91: - The `ticked` function (within `graphCreator.js`) iterates through the D3 selections of node and link SVG groups.
 92:   - For each node group, it updates the `transform` attribute: `node.attr("transform", d => \`translate(\${d.x}, \${d.y})\`);`. This visually moves the node according to the simulation's calculated `x`, `y`.
 93:   - For each link group's path, it recalculates and updates the `d` attribute based on the _current_ `x`, `y` of its referenced `source` and `target` node objects.
 94: - When `treeLayout.js`'s `createTreeLayout` is called (via `highlightHandler`), it directly modifies the `fx` and `fy` properties of the node objects _in the `nodes` array_. It then restarts the simulation (`simulation.alpha(1).restart()`), forcing it to respect these fixed positions and trigger the `tick` handler to update the SVG positions.
 95: 
 96: ## User Interaction (`graphCreator.js`, `interactions/`)
 97: 
 98: - Event listeners (`.on("mouseover", ...), .on("click", ...), .call(drag)`) are attached directly to the D3 selections of the SVG elements (e.g., `node` selection from `nodeRenderer`, `link` selection from `linkRenderer`).
 99: - When an event occurs (e.g., mouseover on a node group), the attached handler function receives the event object and, crucially, the data bound to that element (`d`). This `d` is the corresponding object from the `nodes` or `links` array.
100: - Interaction handlers (e.g., `highlightConnections`, `showNodeTooltip`, `dragstarted`) use this bound data `d` to identify the specific node/link being interacted with (e.g., `d.id`, `d.source.id`).
101: - Handlers then perform actions like:
102:   - Adding/removing CSS classes (`.classed("node-highlighted", true)`) to the SVG elements for styling changes.
103:   - Calling `tooltipHandler` functions with the data `d` to display relevant info (e.g., `showLinkTooltip` includes the `condition` for `general_join` links).
104:   - Modifying the data object itself (e.g., `dragHandler` setting `d.fx = event.x`).
105:   - Calling layout functions (e.g., `highlightHandler` calling `createTreeLayout(d)` on click).
106:   - Modifying simulation state (e.g., `dragHandler` changing `simulation.alphaTarget()`).
107: 
108: ## Styling (`styles/graphStyles.js`)
109: 
110: The visual appearance of the graph is controlled by CSS rules injected by `applyGraphStyles()` in `public/js/graph/styles/graphStyles.js`. Key classes include:
111: 
112: - **Nodes:**
113:   - `.node`: Base styles for the node group.
114:   - `.node rect`: Styles for the background rectangle.
115:   - `.node text`: Base text styles.
116:   - `.node-title`, `.properties-header`, `.column-item`, `.subcollection-item`: Specific text element styles.
117:   - `.node-highlighted`, `.node-primary`, `.node-faded`: Classes applied during interactions (hover, click, tree view) to modify node appearance (stroke, fill, opacity, font size).
118: - **Links:**
119:   - `.link-group`: Container for path and label.
120:   - `.link`: Base styles for the path element.
121:   - `.link-forward`, `.link-reverse`, `.link-cartesian_product`, `.link-general_join`: Type-specific path styles (stroke color, dasharray). `general_join` typically uses an orange stroke (`#ff7f0e`).
122:   - `.link-highlighted`: Applied on hover/tree view, usually changing stroke color (dark green) and width.
123:   - `.link-label`: Styles for the text label on the link.
124:   - `.link-label-forward`, `.link-label-reverse`: Color for labels based on direction.
125:   - `.link-label-highlighted`: Applied on hover/tree view, changing fill color and font size.
126: - **Markers:**
127:   - `.arrowhead`: Base style for arrowheads.
128:   - `.arrowhead-cartesian_product`, `.arrowhead-general_join`: Type-specific fill colors (purple, orange).
129:   - `.arrowhead-highlighted`: Fill color for highlighted state (dark green).
130: - **Tooltips:**
131:   - `.tooltip`: Main tooltip container styles.
132:   - `.tooltip-title`, `.tooltip-table`, `.tooltip-label`, etc.: Styles for internal tooltip elements.
133: 
134: The key takeaway is the central role of the `nodes` and `links` arrays. They hold the state, are manipulated by the simulation and layouts, drive the rendering process, and provide context to interaction handlers via D3's data binding.
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/meta_visualizer/README.md
````markdown
 1: # MetaViewer - Graph Visualization Tool
 2: 
 3: MetaViewer is a web-based graph visualization tool designed to display and explore relationships between collections defined in a user-provided JSON metadata schema. It provides an interactive interface using D3.js for navigating complex data relationships.
 4: 
 5: ## Getting Started
 6: 
 7: ### For Users
 8: 
 9: 1.  Clone the repository.
10: 2.  Install dependencies:
11:     ```bash
12:     npm install
13:     ```
14: 3.  Start the server:
15:     ```bash
16:     ./serve.sh
17:     ```
18: 4.  Visit `http://localhost:8000` (or the port specified in `serve.sh`) in your browser.
19: 5.  Click the "Load JSON File" button and select your first metadata JSON file. The graph will be displayed. The metada JSON file should adhere to the schema defined in [metadata](https://github.com/bodo-ai/PyDough/blob/main/documentation/metadata.md).
20: 6.  To load more graphs, click "Load JSON File" again and select another file.
21: 7.  To switch between loaded graphs, click the hamburger icon (☰) in the header and select the desired graph filename from the dropdown.
22: 
23: ### For Developers
24: 
25: 1.  Clone the repository.
26: 2.  Install dependencies:
27:     ```bash
28:     npm install
29:     ```
30: 3.  Start the development server (which typically includes live reloading):
31:     ```bash
32:     npm start
33:     ```
34: 4.  Visit `http://localhost:3000` (or the port configured for the development server) in your browser.
35: 5.  The application will load. Use the "Load JSON File" button as described in the user section.
36: 
37: ## Features
38: 
39: - **Load Multiple Graphs**: Upload multiple JSON files containing metadata schemas. Each file is treated as a separate graph.
40: - **Switch Between Graphs**: Use the hamburger menu (☰) in the top-left corner to select and view any of the loaded graphs.
41: - **Interactive Graph Visualization**: View collections and their relationships in a force-directed graph for the currently selected graph.
42: - **Tree View**: Click on any node to see a hierarchical tree view of its outgoing connections.
43: - **Relationship Details**: Hover over connections or nodes to see detailed information.
44: - **Zoom and Pan**: Navigate large graphs with zoom (mouse wheel, buttons) and pan (drag background) controls.
45: - **Highlighting**: Hovering highlights connected nodes and links.
46: - **Tooltips**: Detailed information about nodes and links appears on hover over indicators/links.
47: - **Node Dragging**: Manually reposition nodes.
48: 
49: ## Visual Elements
50: 
51: The graph visualization displays the following information:
52: 
53: - **Nodes (Collections)**:
54: 
55:   - Each collection is represented as a rectangular box.
56:   - **Title**: The collection name is shown at the top.
57:   - **Table Path**: The source `table_path` is displayed below the title.
58:   - **Properties (Columns)**: Attributes with `type: "table_column"` are listed under "Properties:".
59:   - **Relationships (Subcollections)**: Outgoing relationships (like `simple_join`, `cartesian_product`) are listed under "Subcollections:".
60:   - **Tooltip Indicator**: A small circle in the bottom-right corner can be hovered over to show a detailed tooltip with all properties.
61: 
62: - **Links (Relationships)**:
63: 
64:   - Each defined relationship between collections is drawn as a line connecting the corresponding nodes.
65:   - **Direction & Type**: An arrowhead indicates the direction and type of relationship (different styles for simple join vs. cartesian product).
66:   - **Label**: The subcollection access name is displayed as a label along the link path.
67:   - **Tooltip**: Hovering directly over the link line shows a tooltip with relationship details.
68: 
69: - **Interactions & Highlighting**:
70:   - **Hover**: Hovering over a node highlights the node, its direct links, and connected nodes. Hovering over a link highlights the link and its source/target nodes.
71:   - **Click (Tree View)**: Clicking a node transitions the layout to a hierarchical tree view, showing only the clicked node (as root) and nodes reachable via outgoing links. Dragging any node again returns to the force layout.
72:   - **Zoom/Pan**: Standard mouse wheel/trackpad controls for zooming, and dragging the background for panning. Buttons are also available.
73: 
74: ## Project Structure
75: 
76: - **`public/`**: Contains all the front-end code and assets.
77:   - **`css/`**: CSS stylesheets.
78:   - **`js/`**: JavaScript code.
79:     - **`graph/`**: Graph visualization components (see below).
80:     - **`main.js`**: Entry point that initializes the graph visualization.
81:   - **`index.html`**: Main HTML file.
82: 
83: ### Graph Visualization Components (`public/js/graph/`)
84: 
85: The graph visualization is implemented as a modular component:
86: 
87: - **`core/`**: Handles initialization, data processing (JSON to nodes/links), and orchestration (`graphCreator`).
88: - **`renderers/`**: Creates SVG elements for nodes, links, and arrow markers.
89: - **`layouts/`**: Implements node positioning algorithms (force-directed, hierarchical tree).
90: - **`interactions/`**: Manages user input (zoom, pan, drag, hover, click) and feedback (highlighting, tooltips, tree view activation).
91: - **`styles/`**: Defines CSS styles injected for visual appearance.
92: - **`utils/`**: Provides utility functions (e.g., geometry calculations).
93: 
94: (See the README.md files in the respective subdirectories for more details.)
95: 
96: ## Dependencies
97: 
98: - D3.js v7.x - Used for DOM manipulation, SVG rendering, force simulation, zoom/drag behaviors, and transitions.
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/configs/pydough_configs.py
````python
  1: """
  2: Definitions of configuration settings for PyDough.
  3: """
  4: 
  5: __all__ = ["DayOfWeek", "PyDoughConfigs"]
  6: 
  7: from enum import Enum
  8: from typing import Any, Generic, TypeVar
  9: 
 10: T = TypeVar("T")
 11: 
 12: 
 13: class DayOfWeek(Enum):
 14:     """
 15:     An enum to represent the day of the week.
 16:     """
 17: 
 18:     SUNDAY = "SUNDAY"
 19:     MONDAY = "MONDAY"
 20:     TUESDAY = "TUESDAY"
 21:     WEDNESDAY = "WEDNESDAY"
 22:     THURSDAY = "THURSDAY"
 23:     FRIDAY = "FRIDAY"
 24:     SATURDAY = "SATURDAY"
 25: 
 26:     @property
 27:     def pandas_dow(self) -> int:
 28:         match self:
 29:             case DayOfWeek.SUNDAY:
 30:                 return 6
 31:             case DayOfWeek.MONDAY:
 32:                 return 0
 33:             case DayOfWeek.TUESDAY:
 34:                 return 1
 35:             case DayOfWeek.WEDNESDAY:
 36:                 return 2
 37:             case DayOfWeek.THURSDAY:
 38:                 return 3
 39:             case DayOfWeek.FRIDAY:
 40:                 return 4
 41:             case DayOfWeek.SATURDAY:
 42:                 return 5
 43: 
 44: 
 45: class ConfigProperty(Generic[T]):
 46:     """
 47:     A type-generic property class to be used as a descriptor inside of the
 48:     PyDoughConfigs class. An invocation of `ConfigProperty` looks as follows:
 49: 
 50:     ```
 51:     class ClassName:
 52:         ...
 53:         foo = ConfigProperty[str]("")
 54:         bar = ConfigProperty[int](0)
 55:     ```
 56: 
 57:     In this example, every instance of the class `ClassName` now has two
 58:     properties: `foo` has type `str` and a default of `""`, and `bar`
 59:     has type `int` and has a default value of `0`. Both properties have
 60:     standard getters and setters usable via `.foo` and `.bar`.
 61:     """
 62: 
 63:     def __init__(self, default: T):
 64:         self._default: T = default
 65: 
 66:     def __set_name__(self, owner, name):
 67:         self._name = name
 68: 
 69:     def __get__(self, instance, owner) -> T:
 70:         if instance is None:
 71:             return self._default
 72:         return instance.__dict__.get(self._name, self._default)
 73: 
 74:     def __set__(self, instance, value: T):
 75:         instance.__dict__[self._name] = value
 76: 
 77:     def __repr__(self) -> str:
 78:         return f"config:{self._name}"
 79: 
 80: 
 81: class PyDoughConfigs:
 82:     """
 83:     Class used to store information about various configuration settings of
 84:     PyDough.
 85:     """
 86: 
 87:     sum_default_zero = ConfigProperty[bool](True)
 88:     """
 89:     If True, then the `SUM` function always defaults to 0 if there are no
 90:     records to be summed up. If False, the output could be `NULL`. The default
 91:     is True.
 92:     """
 93: 
 94:     avg_default_zero = ConfigProperty[bool](False)
 95:     """
 96:     If True, then the `AVG` function always defaults to 0 if there are no
 97:     records to be averaged. If False, the output could be `NULL`. The default
 98:     is False.
 99:     """
100: 
101:     collation_default_asc = ConfigProperty[bool](True)
102:     """
103:     If True, then the collation will default to `ASC`. If False, then the
104:     collation will default to `DESC`. The default is True.
105:     """
106: 
107:     propagate_collation = ConfigProperty[bool](False)
108:     """
109:     If True, each term, which does not have an explicit collation, will inherit
110:     the collation (ASC/DESC) from the previous specified term. If False, terms
111:     without an explicit collation will use the default from
112:     `collation_default_asc`. The default is False.
113:     """
114: 
115:     start_of_week = ConfigProperty[DayOfWeek](DayOfWeek.SUNDAY)
116:     """
117:     The day of the week that is considered the start of the week. The default
118:     is Sunday.
119:     """
120: 
121:     start_week_as_zero = ConfigProperty[bool](True)
122:     """
123:     If True, then the week starts at zero. If False, then the week starts at one.
124:     The default is True.
125:     """
126: 
127:     def __setattr__(self, name: str, value: Any) -> None:
128:         if name not in dir(self):
129:             raise AttributeError(f"Unrecognized PyDough config name: {name}")
130:         super().__setattr__(name, value)
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/configs/README.md
````markdown
 1: # Configs
 2: 
 3: This subdirectory of the PyDough directory deals with the configuration settings for PyDough.
 4: 
 5: The configs module provides functionality to manage various configuration settings that affect the behavior of PyDough.
 6: 
 7: ## Available APIs
 8: 
 9: ### [pydough_configs.py](pydough_configs.py)
10: 
11: - `PyDoughConfigs`: Class used to store information about various configuration settings of PyDough.
12:     - `sum_default_zero`: If True, the `SUM` function always defaults to 0 if there are no records to be summed up. If False, the output could be `NULL`. The default is True.
13:     - `avg_default_zero`: If True, the `AVG` function always defaults to 0 if there are no records to be averaged. If False, the output could be `NULL`. The default is False.
14:     - `collation_default_asc`: If True, the default collation is ascending. If False, the default collation is descending. The default is True.
15:     - `propogate_collation`: If True, the collation of the current expression, which does not have a collation, uses the most recent available collation in the nodes of the term. If False, the expression uses the default collation as specified by `collation_default_asc`. The default is False.
16:     - `start_of_week`: The day of the week that is considered the start of the week. The default is `DayOfWeek.SUNDAY`.
17:     - `start_week_as_zero`: If True, then the first day of the week is considered to be 0. If False, then the first day of the week is considered to be 1. The default is True.
18: - `DayOfWeek`: Enum to represent the day of the week.
19:     - `SUNDAY`: Sunday.
20:     - `MONDAY`: Monday.
21:     - `TUESDAY`: Tuesday.
22:     - `WEDNESDAY`: Wednesday.
23:     - `THURSDAY`: Thursday.
24:     - `FRIDAY`: Friday.
25:     - `SATURDAY`: Saturday.
26: 
27: ### [session.py](session.py)
28: 
29: - `PyDoughSession`: Container class used to define a PyDough session. This includes both a set of properties that can be accessed and modified directly, as well as helper methods to assist with some of the plumbing.
30:     - `metadata`: Property to get or set the active metadata graph.
31:     - `config`: Property to get or set the active PyDough configuration.
32:     - `database`: Property to get or set the active database context.
33:     - `connect_database`: Method to create a new DatabaseContext and register it in the session.
34:     - `load_metadata_graph`: Method to load a metadata graph from a file and register it in the session.
35: 
36: ## Active Session
37: 
38: PyDough maintains an active session that is used to process any user code. The active session can be accessed and modified via the `pydough.active_session` property. By default, most users will modify the active session, but it is also possible to swap out the active session for a new one if needed.
39: 
40: ## Usage
41: 
42: To use the configs module, you can import the necessary classes and call them with the appropriate arguments. For example:
43: 
44: ```python
45: from pydough.configs import PyDoughConfigs, PyDoughSession
46: import pydough
47: 
48: # Create a new configuration object and change its value of the
49: # `sum_default_zero` configuration
50: config = PyDoughConfigs()
51: config.sum_default_zero = False
52: 
53: # Create a new session and set the configuration
54: session = PyDoughSession()
55: session.config = config
56: 
57: # Connect to a database
58: session.connect_database("sqlite", database="path/to/database.db")
59: 
60: # Load a metadata graph
61: session.load_metadata_graph("path/to/graph.json", "graph_name")
62: 
63: # Access the active session
64: active_session = pydough.active_session
65: 
66: # Modify the active session's configuration
67: active_session.config.sum_default_zero = True
68: ```
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/configs/session.py
````python
  1: """
  2: PyDough session configuration used for end to end processing
  3: of PyDough execution or code generation. This session tracks
  4: important information like:
  5: - The active metadata graph.
  6: - Any PyDough configuration for function behavior.
  7: - Backend information (SQL dialect, Database connection, etc.)
  8: 
  9: In the future this session will also contain other information
 10: such as any User Defined registration for additional backend
 11: functionality that should not be merged to main repository.
 12: 
 13: The intended use of a session is that by default the PyDough project
 14: will maintain an active session and will use this information to process
 15: any user code. By default most people will just modify the active session
 16: (via property access syntax or methods), but in some cases users can also
 17: swap out the active session for a brand new one if they want to preserve
 18: existing state.
 19: """
 20: 
 21: from pydough.database_connectors import (
 22:     DatabaseContext,
 23:     DatabaseDialect,
 24:     empty_connection,
 25:     load_database_context,
 26: )
 27: from pydough.metadata import GraphMetadata, parse_json_metadata_from_file
 28: 
 29: from .pydough_configs import PyDoughConfigs
 30: 
 31: 
 32: class PyDoughSession:
 33:     """
 34:     Container class used to define a PyDough session. This includes both
 35:     a set of properties that can be accessed and modified directly, as
 36:     well as helper methods to assist with some of the plumbing.
 37:     """
 38: 
 39:     def __init__(self) -> None:
 40:         self._metadata: GraphMetadata | None = None
 41:         self._config: PyDoughConfigs = PyDoughConfigs()
 42:         # By default we have a backend that cannot execute any SQL but can
 43:         # still generate ANSI SQL, since this doesn't require any database
 44:         # setup. We create a new DatabaseContext each time instead of a
 45:         # singleton since a user may opt to provide their own connection
 46:         # by just swapping the connection attribute.
 47:         self._database: DatabaseContext = DatabaseContext(
 48:             connection=empty_connection, dialect=DatabaseDialect.ANSI
 49:         )
 50: 
 51:     @property
 52:     def metadata(self) -> GraphMetadata | None:
 53:         """
 54:         Get the active metadata graph.
 55: 
 56:         Returns:
 57:             GraphMetadata: The active metadata graph.
 58:         """
 59:         return self._metadata
 60: 
 61:     @metadata.setter
 62:     def metadata(self, graph: GraphMetadata | None) -> None:
 63:         """
 64:         Set the active metadata graph.
 65: 
 66:         Args:
 67:             graph (GraphMetadata | None): The metadata graph to set.
 68:         """
 69:         self._metadata = graph
 70: 
 71:     @property
 72:     def config(self) -> PyDoughConfigs:
 73:         """
 74:         Get the active PyDough configuration.
 75: 
 76:         Returns:
 77:             PyDoughConfigs: The active PyDough configuration.
 78:         """
 79:         return self._config
 80: 
 81:     @config.setter
 82:     def config(self, config: PyDoughConfigs) -> None:
 83:         """
 84:         Set the active PyDough configuration.
 85: 
 86:         Args:
 87:             config (PyDoughConfigs): The PyDough configuration to set.
 88:         """
 89:         self._config = config
 90: 
 91:     @property
 92:     def database(self) -> DatabaseContext:
 93:         """
 94:         Get the active database context.
 95: 
 96:         Returns:
 97:             DatabaseContext: The active database context.
 98:         """
 99:         return self._database
100: 
101:     @database.setter
102:     def database(self, context: DatabaseContext) -> None:
103:         """
104:         Set the active database context.
105: 
106:         Args:
107:             context (DatabaseContext): The database context to set.
108:         """
109:         self._database = context
110: 
111:     def connect_database(self, database_name: str, **kwargs) -> DatabaseContext:
112:         """
113:         Create a new DatabaseContext and register it in the session. This returns
114:         the corresponding context in case the user wants/needs to modify it.
115: 
116:         Args:
117:             database_name (str): The name of the database to connect to.
118:             **kwargs: Additional keyword arguments to pass to the connection.
119:                 All arguments must be accepted using the supported connect API
120:                 for the dialect. Most likely the database path will be required.
121: 
122:         Returns:
123:             DatabaseContext: The newly created database context.
124:         """
125:         context: DatabaseContext = load_database_context(database_name, **kwargs)
126:         self.database = context
127:         return context
128: 
129:     def load_metadata_graph(self, graph_path: str, graph_name: str) -> GraphMetadata:
130:         """
131:         Load a metadata graph from a file and register it in the session.
132:         This returns the corresponding graph for use. If there is already
133:         an existing graph it will be removed from the session, although
134:         the user is free to maintain a reference to it and set the session
135:         property directly later.
136: 
137:         Args:
138:             graph_path (str): The path to load the graph. At this time this must be on
139:                 the user's local file system.
140:             graph_name (str): The name under which to load the graph from the file. This
141:                 is to allow loading multiple graphs from the same json file.
142: 
143:         Returns:
144:             GraphMetadata: The loaded metadata graph.
145:         """
146:         graph: GraphMetadata = parse_json_metadata_from_file(graph_path, graph_name)
147:         self.metadata = graph
148:         return graph
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/conversion/agg_removal.py
````python
  1: """
  2: Logic used to partially transpose aggregates beneath joins when splittable into
  3: a partial aggregation.
  4: """
  5: 
  6: __all__ = ["remove_redundant_aggs"]
  7: 
  8: 
  9: import pydough.pydough_operators as pydop
 10: from pydough.relational import (
 11:     Aggregate,
 12:     CallExpression,
 13:     EmptySingleton,
 14:     Filter,
 15:     Join,
 16:     JoinType,
 17:     Limit,
 18:     LiteralExpression,
 19:     Project,
 20:     RelationalExpression,
 21:     RelationalNode,
 22:     RelationalRoot,
 23:     Scan,
 24: )
 25: from pydough.relational.rel_util import (
 26:     bubble_uniqueness,
 27:     extract_equijoin_keys,
 28: )
 29: from pydough.types import BooleanType, Int64Type
 30: 
 31: 
 32: def delete_aggregation(agg: Aggregate) -> RelationalNode:
 33:     """
 34:     Deletes an aggregation node from the relational plan determined to be
 35:     redundant via uniqueness, and returns the equivalent projection node.
 36: 
 37:     Args:
 38:         `agg`: the aggregation node to be deleted.
 39: 
 40:     Returns:
 41:         The transformed node.
 42:     """
 43:     projection_cols: dict[str, RelationalExpression] = {}
 44:     for name, col in agg.keys.items():
 45:         projection_cols[name] = col
 46:     for name, agg_call in agg.aggregations.items():
 47:         match agg_call.op:
 48:             # For these operators, when called on a single row, just return
 49:             # that row unmodified.
 50:             case (
 51:                 pydop.SUM
 52:                 | pydop.MIN
 53:                 | pydop.MAX
 54:                 | pydop.AVG
 55:                 | pydop.ANYTHING
 56:                 | pydop.MEDIAN
 57:             ):
 58:                 projection_cols[name] = agg_call.inputs[0]
 59:             # If COUNT is called with no arguments, always return 1. If it is
 60:             # called with 1 argument, return 1 if the row is non-null,
 61:             # otherwise 0.
 62:             case pydop.COUNT:
 63:                 if len(agg_call.inputs) == 0:
 64:                     projection_cols[name] = LiteralExpression(1, Int64Type())
 65:                 else:
 66:                     projection_cols[name] = CallExpression(
 67:                         pydop.IFF,
 68:                         Int64Type(),
 69:                         [
 70:                             CallExpression(
 71:                                 pydop.PRESENT, BooleanType(), [agg_call.inputs[0]]
 72:                             ),
 73:                             LiteralExpression(1, Int64Type()),
 74:                             LiteralExpression(0, Int64Type()),
 75:                         ],
 76:                     )
 77:             # If any other aggregations are present besides the supported
 78:             # operators, skip the deletion operation and just return the
 79:             # original aggregation.
 80:             case _:
 81:                 return agg
 82:     return Project(agg.input, projection_cols)
 83: 
 84: 
 85: def deduce_join_uniqueness(
 86:     join: Join, input_unique_sets: list[set[frozenset[str]]]
 87: ) -> set[frozenset[str]]:
 88:     """
 89:     Infers the unique column sets of a join based on its join condition and the
 90:     uniqueness sets of its inputs.
 91:     """
 92:     # Reject unless doing a join on two inputs.
 93:     if len(join.inputs) != 2:
 94:         return set()
 95:     lhs_unique, rhs_unique = input_unique_sets
 96: 
 97:     # If doing a semi/anti join, just use the LHS uniqueness.
 98:     if join.join_types[0] in (JoinType.SEMI, JoinType.ANTI):
 99:         return bubble_uniqueness(
100:             lhs_unique, join.columns, join.default_input_aliases[0]
101:         )
102: 
103:     # Convert the uniqueness sets from sets of column names to sets of tuples
104:     # in the form (is_lhs, column_name) to distinguish the lhs columns from the
105:     # rhs columns. Then, create the `result_pairs` set from the cartesian
106:     # product of all lhs/rhs uniqueness sets.
107:     result_pairs: set[frozenset[tuple[bool, str]]] = set()
108:     lhs_pairs: set[frozenset[tuple[bool, str]]] = {
109:         frozenset({(True, k) for k in unique_set}) for unique_set in lhs_unique
110:     }
111:     rhs_pairs: set[frozenset[tuple[bool, str]]] = {
112:         frozenset({(False, k) for k in unique_set}) for unique_set in rhs_unique
113:     }
114:     for lhs_set in lhs_pairs:
115:         for rhs_set in rhs_pairs:
116:             result_pairs.add(lhs_set | rhs_set)
117: 
118:     # Using the equi-join keys, build remappings from columns in the lhs
119:     # uniqueness sets to corresponding columns in the rhs uniqueness sets, and
120:     # vice versa.
121:     remappings: dict[tuple[bool, str], set[tuple[bool, str]]] = {}
122:     lhs_keys, rhs_keys = extract_equijoin_keys(join)
123:     for lhs_key, rhs_key in zip(lhs_keys, rhs_keys):
124:         remappings[(True, lhs_key.name)] = remappings.get((True, lhs_key.name), set())
125:         remappings[(True, lhs_key.name)].add((False, rhs_key.name))
126:         remappings[(False, rhs_key.name)] = remappings.get((False, rhs_key.name), set())
127:         remappings[(False, rhs_key.name)].add((True, lhs_key.name))
128: 
129:     # Using this mapping, update the uniqueness set by adding each variant of
130:     # a uniqueness set where a column from one side is replaced by a column
131:     # from the other side that it is inferred to e equal to based on the join
132:     # condition.
133:     new_pairs: set[frozenset[tuple[bool, str]]]
134:     for remapping_key in remappings:
135:         new_pairs = set()
136:         for pair_set in result_pairs:
137:             if remapping_key in pair_set:
138:                 for alternate in remappings[remapping_key]:
139:                     new_pairs.add(
140:                         pair_set.difference({remapping_key}).union({alternate})
141:                     )
142:         result_pairs.update(new_pairs)
143: 
144:     # If any of the uniqueness sets are entirely in one side, and are a
145:     # strict superset of the uniqueness keys of that side, add the
146:     # corresponding uniqueness sets from that side (this occurs if the ioin
147:     # did not alter the cardinality of that side).
148:     new_pairs = set()
149:     for pair_set in result_pairs:
150:         if all(is_lhs for is_lhs, _ in pair_set):
151:             for lhs_pair_set in lhs_pairs:
152:                 if pair_set > lhs_pair_set:
153:                     new_pairs.update(lhs_pairs)
154:                     break
155:         if all(not is_lhs for is_lhs, _ in pair_set):
156:             for rhs_pair_set in rhs_pairs:
157:                 if pair_set > rhs_pair_set:
158:                     new_pairs.update(rhs_pairs)
159:                     break
160:     result_pairs.update(new_pairs)
161: 
162:     # Remove any uniqueness sets that are strict supersets of other uniqueness
163:     # sets.
164:     redundant_uniqueness_sets: list[frozenset[tuple[bool, str]]] = [
165:         set_a for set_a in result_pairs for set_b in result_pairs if set_a > set_b
166:     ]
167:     for redundant_set in redundant_uniqueness_sets:
168:         result_pairs.discard(redundant_set)
169: 
170:     # Finally, convert from the tuple form back to just uniqueness sets of
171:     # column names using the output column names of the join. Any uniqueness
172:     # sets that contain columns not present in the outut are discarded.
173:     result: set[frozenset[str]] = set()
174:     for unique_set in result_pairs:
175:         if len(unique_set) == 0:
176:             result.add(frozenset())
177:             continue
178:         # Split the uniqueness set into its columns from the lhs vs rhs, and
179:         # drop the boolean tuple.
180:         lhs_elem_names: set[str] = {k for is_lhs, k in unique_set if is_lhs}
181:         rhs_elem_names: set[str] = {k for is_lhs, k in unique_set if not is_lhs}
182:         # Propagate the columns from the lhs through the join output columns.
183:         # If this is possible, `new_lhs_elems` will be a singleton set whose
184:         # element is all of the lhs columns bubbled through. If not, it will be
185:         # an empty set.
186:         new_lhs_elems: set[frozenset[str]]
187:         if len(lhs_elem_names) > 0:
188:             new_lhs_elems = bubble_uniqueness(
189:                 {frozenset(lhs_elem_names)}, join.columns, join.default_input_aliases[0]
190:             )
191:         else:
192:             new_lhs_elems = set()
193:         # Repeat the same idea for the rhs.
194:         new_rhs_elems: set[frozenset[str]]
195:         if len(rhs_elem_names) > 0:
196:             new_rhs_elems = bubble_uniqueness(
197:                 {frozenset(rhs_elem_names)}, join.columns, join.default_input_aliases[1]
198:             )
199:         else:
200:             new_rhs_elems = set()
201:         # If both sides were able to have their columns bubbled through (or did
202:         # not have columns from that side to begin with), then create the new
203:         # output uniqueness set by combining their output columns from their
204:         # singleton uniqueness sets (or ignoring them if there were no columns
205:         # from that side to begin with)
206:         if len(new_lhs_elems) == len(lhs_elem_names) and len(new_rhs_elems) == len(
207:             rhs_elem_names
208:         ):
209:             assert len(new_lhs_elems) <= 1 and len(new_rhs_elems) <= 1
210:             new_set: frozenset[str] = frozenset()
211:             if len(new_lhs_elems) > 0:
212:                 new_set = new_set.union(new_lhs_elems.pop())
213:             if len(new_rhs_elems) > 0:
214:                 new_set = new_set.union(new_rhs_elems.pop())
215:             result.add(new_set)
216: 
217:     return result
218: 
219: 
220: def aggregation_uniqueness_helper(
221:     node: RelationalNode,
222: ) -> tuple[RelationalNode, set[frozenset[str]]]:
223:     """
224:     Core helper function that runs the aggregation uniqueness removal,
225:     returning the transformed node as well as a set of all sets of column
226:     names that can be used to uniquely identify the rows of the returned
227:     node.
228: 
229:     Args:
230:         `node`: the node to be transformed.
231: 
232:     Returns:
233:         The transformed node and a set of all sets of column names that can
234:         be used to uniquely identify the rows of the returned node.
235:     """
236:     input_uniqueness: set[frozenset[str]]
237:     match node:
238:         # Scans are unchanged, and their uniqueness is based on the unique sets
239:         # of the underlying table.
240:         case Scan():
241:             return node, bubble_uniqueness(node.unique_sets, node.columns, None)
242:         # For filters, projections, limits and roots, the node is unchanged,
243:         # and the uniqueness should be propagated upward through the selected
244:         # columns.
245:         case Filter() | Project() | Limit() | RelationalRoot():
246:             node._input, input_uniqueness = aggregation_uniqueness_helper(node.input)
247:             input_uniqueness = bubble_uniqueness(input_uniqueness, node.columns, None)
248:             return node, input_uniqueness
249:         # For aggregations, the output uniqueness is the aggregation keys.
250:         # However, if this is a superset of any of the unique sets of the input
251:         # then the aggregation should be deleted since it is redundant.
252:         case Aggregate():
253:             node._input, input_uniqueness = aggregation_uniqueness_helper(node.input)
254:             agg_keys: frozenset[str] = frozenset(node.keys)
255:             output_uniqueness: set[frozenset[str]] = {agg_keys}
256:             for unique_set in input_uniqueness:
257:                 if agg_keys.issuperset(unique_set):
258:                     node = delete_aggregation(node)
259:                     # If deleting the aggregation, then the uniqueness of the
260:                     # input is propagated through the new projection.
261:                     output_uniqueness = bubble_uniqueness(
262:                         input_uniqueness, node.columns, None
263:                     )
264:                     break
265:             return node, output_uniqueness
266:         # For joins, gather the uniqueness information from each input, then
267:         # infer the combined uniqueness information after joining.
268:         case Join():
269:             unique_sets: list[set[frozenset[str]]] = []
270:             for idx, input_node in enumerate(node.inputs):
271:                 node.inputs[idx], input_uniqueness = aggregation_uniqueness_helper(
272:                     input_node
273:                 )
274:                 unique_sets.append(input_uniqueness)
275:             final_uniqueness: set[frozenset[str]] = deduce_join_uniqueness(
276:                 node, unique_sets
277:             )
278:             return node, final_uniqueness
279:         # Empty singletons don't have uniqueness information.
280:         case EmptySingleton():
281:             return node, set()
282:         case _:
283:             raise NotImplementedError(
284:                 f"Unsupported node for redundant aggregation removal: {node.__class__.__name__}"
285:             )
286: 
287: 
288: def remove_redundant_aggs(root: RelationalRoot) -> RelationalRoot:
289:     """
290:     Invokes the procedure to delete aggregations that are redundant since the
291:     data they are called on is already unique with regards to the aggregation
292:     keys.
293: 
294:     Args:
295:         `node`: the root node of the relational plan to be transformed.
296: 
297:     Returns:
298:         The transformed relational root. The transformation is also done
299:         in-place.
300:     """
301:     result, _ = aggregation_uniqueness_helper(root)
302:     assert isinstance(result, RelationalRoot)
303:     return result
````
