## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/abstract_node.py
````python
  1: """
  2: This file contains the abstract base classes for the relational
  3: representation. This roughly maps to a Relational Algebra representation
  4: but is not exact because it needs to maintain PyDough traits that define
  5: ordering and other properties of the relational expression.
  6: """
  7: 
  8: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
  9: from typing import Any
 10: 
 11: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import RelationalExpression
 12: 
 13: 
 14: class RelationalNode(ABC):
 15:     """
 16:     The base class for any relational node. This interface defines the basic
 17:     structure of all relational nodes in the PyDough system.
 18:     """
 19: 
 20:     def __init__(self, columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression]) -> None:
 21:         self._columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression] = columns
 22: 
 23:     @property
 24:     @abstractmethod
 25:     def inputs(self) -> list["RelationalNode"]:
 26:         """
 27:         Returns any inputs to the current relational expression.
 28: 
 29:         Returns:
 30:             list["RelationalNode"]: The list of inputs, each of which must
 31:             be a relational expression.
 32:         """
 33: 
 34:     @property
 35:     def default_input_aliases(self) -> list[str | None]:
 36:         """
 37:         Provide the default aliases for each input
 38:         to this node. This is used when remapping the
 39:         names of each input for differentiating columns.
 40:         By default we don't use an alias, which maps to None
 41:         for each input.
 42: 
 43:         Note: The lowering steps are not required to use this alias
 44:         and can choose any name they want.
 45:         """
 46:         return [None for i in range(len(self.inputs))]
 47: 
 48:     @property
 49:     def columns(self) -> dict[str, RelationalExpression]:
 50:         """
 51:         Returns the columns of the relational expression.
 52: 
 53:         Returns:
 54:             dict[str, RelationalExpression]: The columns of the relational expression.
 55:                 This does not have a defined ordering.
 56:         """
 57:         return self._columns
 58: 
 59:     @abstractmethod
 60:     def node_equals(self, other: "RelationalNode") -> bool:
 61:         """
 62:         Determine if two relational nodes are exactly identical,
 63:         excluding column generic column details shared by every
 64:         node. This should be extended to avoid duplicating equality
 65:         logic shared across relational nodes.
 66: 
 67:         Args:
 68:             other (Relational): The other relational node to compare against.
 69: 
 70:         Returns:
 71:             bool: Are the two relational nodes equal.
 72:         """
 73: 
 74:     def equals(self, other: "RelationalNode") -> bool:
 75:         """
 76:         Determine if two relational nodes are exactly identical,
 77:         including column ordering.
 78: 
 79:         Args:
 80:             other (Relational): The other relational node to compare against.
 81: 
 82:         Returns:
 83:             bool: Are the two relational nodes equal.
 84:         """
 85:         return self.node_equals(other) and self.columns == other.columns
 86: 
 87:     def __eq__(self, other: Any) -> bool:
 88:         return isinstance(other, RelationalNode) and self.equals(other)
 89: 
 90:     def make_column_string(self, columns: dict[str, Any], compact: bool) -> str:
 91:         """
 92:         Converts the columns of the relational node to a deterministically
 93:         ordered string (alphabetically).
 94:         """
 95:         pairs: list[str] = []
 96:         for key in sorted(columns):
 97:             expr = columns[key]
 98:             assert isinstance(expr, RelationalExpression)
 99:             pairs.append(f"{key!r}: {columns[key].to_string(compact)}")
100:         return f"{{{', '.join(pairs)}}}"
101: 
102:     @abstractmethod
103:     def to_string(self, compact: bool = False) -> str:
104:         """
105:         Convert the relational node to a string.
106: 
107:         Args:
108:             `compact`: if True, converts to a more minimal string form for the
109:             purposes of conversion to a tree string.
110: 
111:         Returns:
112:             str: A string representation of the relational tree
113:             with this node at the root.
114:         """
115: 
116:     def __repr__(self) -> str:
117:         return self.to_string()
118: 
119:     def to_tree_string(self) -> str:
120:         """
121:         Convert the relational node to a string, including the descendants
122:         of the node.
123: 
124:         Returns:
125:             str: A string representation of the relational tree
126:             with this node at the root.
127:         """
128:         from .tree_string_visitor import TreeStringVisitor
129: 
130:         visitor: TreeStringVisitor = TreeStringVisitor()
131:         self.accept(visitor)
132:         return visitor.make_tree_string()
133: 
134:     @abstractmethod
135:     def accept(self, visitor: "RelationalVisitor") -> None:  # type: ignore # noqa
136:         """
137:         Accept a visitor to traverse the relational tree.
138: 
139:         Args:
140:             visitor (RelationalVisitor): The visitor to traverse the tree.
141:         """
142: 
143:     @abstractmethod
144:     def node_copy(
145:         self,
146:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
147:         inputs: list["RelationalNode"],
148:     ) -> "RelationalNode":
149:         """
150:         Copy the given relational node with the provided columns and/or
151:         inputs. This copy maintains any additional properties of the
152:         given node in the output. Every node is required to implement
153:         this directly.
154: 
155:         Args:
156:             columns (dict[str, RelationalExpression]): The columns
157:                 to copy.
158:             inputs (list[RelationalNode]): The inputs to copy.
159: 
160:         Returns:
161:             Relational: The copied relational node.
162:         """
163: 
164:     def copy(
165:         self,
166:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression] | None = None,
167:         inputs: list["RelationalNode"] | None = None,
168:     ) -> "RelationalNode":
169:         """
170:         Copy the given relational node with the provided columns and/or
171:         inputs. This copy maintains any additional properties of the
172:         given node in the output. If any of the inputs are None, then we
173:         will grab those fields from the current node.
174: 
175:         Args:
176:             columns (dict[str, RelationalExpression] | None): The
177:                 columns to copy.
178:             inputs (list[RelationalNode] | None): The inputs to copy.
179: 
180:         Returns:
181:             Relational: The copied relational node.
182:         """
183:         columns = self.columns if columns is None else columns
184:         inputs = self.inputs if inputs is None else inputs
185:         return self.node_copy(columns, inputs)
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/aggregate.py
````python
 1: """
 2: This file contains the relational implementation for an aggregation. This is our
 3: relational representation for any grouping operation that optionally involves
 4: keys and aggregate functions.
 5: """
 6: 
 7: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import (
 8:     CallExpression,
 9:     ColumnReference,
10:     RelationalExpression,
11: )
12: 
13: from .abstract_node import RelationalNode
14: from .single_relational import SingleRelational
15: 
16: 
17: class Aggregate(SingleRelational):
18:     """
19:     The Aggregate node in the relational tree. This node represents an aggregation
20:     based on some keys, which should most commonly be column references, and some
21:     aggregate functions.
22:     """
23: 
24:     def __init__(
25:         self,
26:         input: RelationalNode,
27:         keys: dict[str, ColumnReference],
28:         aggregations: dict[str, CallExpression],
29:     ) -> None:
30:         total_cols: dict[str, RelationalExpression] = {**keys, **aggregations}
31:         assert len(total_cols) == len(keys) + len(aggregations), (
32:             "Keys and aggregations must have unique names"
33:         )
34:         super().__init__(input, total_cols)
35:         self._keys: dict[str, ColumnReference] = keys
36:         self._aggregations: dict[str, CallExpression] = aggregations
37:         assert all(agg.is_aggregation for agg in aggregations.values()), (
38:             "All functions used in aggregations must be aggregation functions"
39:         )
40: 
41:     @property
42:     def keys(self) -> dict[str, ColumnReference]:
43:         """
44:         The keys for the aggregation operation.
45:         """
46:         return self._keys
47: 
48:     @property
49:     def aggregations(self) -> dict[str, CallExpression]:
50:         """
51:         The aggregation functions for the aggregation operation.
52:         """
53:         return self._aggregations
54: 
55:     def node_equals(self, other: RelationalNode) -> bool:
56:         return (
57:             isinstance(other, Aggregate)
58:             and self.keys == other.keys
59:             and self.aggregations == other.aggregations
60:             and super().node_equals(other)
61:         )
62: 
63:     def to_string(self, compact: bool = False) -> str:
64:         return f"AGGREGATE(keys={self.make_column_string(self.keys, compact)}, aggregations={self.make_column_string(self.aggregations, compact)})"
65: 
66:     def accept(self, visitor: "RelationalVisitor") -> None:  # type: ignore # noqa
67:         visitor.visit_aggregate(self)
68: 
69:     def node_copy(
70:         self,
71:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
72:         inputs: list[RelationalNode],
73:     ) -> RelationalNode:
74:         assert len(inputs) == 1, "Aggregate node should have exactly one input"
75:         # Aggregate nodes don't cleanly map to the existing columns API.
76:         # We still fulfill it as much as possible by mapping all column
77:         # references to the keys since aggregates must be functions.
78:         keys = {}
79:         aggregations = {}
80:         for key, val in columns.items():
81:             if isinstance(val, ColumnReference):
82:                 keys[key] = val
83:             else:
84:                 assert isinstance(val, CallExpression), (
85:                     "All columns must be references or functions"
86:                 )
87:                 aggregations[key] = val
88:         return Aggregate(inputs[0], keys, aggregations)
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/column_pruner.py
````python
  1: """
  2: Module responsible for pruning columns from relational expressions.
  3: """
  4: 
  5: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import (
  6:     ColumnReference,
  7:     ColumnReferenceFinder,
  8:     CorrelatedReference,
  9:     CorrelatedReferenceFinder,
 10:     RelationalExpression,
 11: )
 12: 
 13: from .abstract_node import RelationalNode
 14: from .aggregate import Aggregate
 15: from .empty_singleton import EmptySingleton
 16: from .join import Join, JoinType
 17: from .project import Project
 18: from .relational_expression_dispatcher import RelationalExpressionDispatcher
 19: from .relational_root import RelationalRoot
 20: 
 21: __all__ = ["ColumnPruner"]
 22: 
 23: 
 24: class ColumnPruner:
 25:     def __init__(self) -> None:
 26:         self._column_finder: ColumnReferenceFinder = ColumnReferenceFinder()
 27:         self._correl_finder: CorrelatedReferenceFinder = CorrelatedReferenceFinder()
 28:         # Note: We set recurse=False so we only check the expressions in the
 29:         # current node.
 30:         self._finder_dispatcher = RelationalExpressionDispatcher(
 31:             self._column_finder, recurse=False
 32:         )
 33:         self._correl_dispatcher = RelationalExpressionDispatcher(
 34:             self._correl_finder, recurse=False
 35:         )
 36: 
 37:     def _prune_identity_project(self, node: RelationalNode) -> RelationalNode:
 38:         """
 39:         Remove a projection and return the input if it is an
 40:         identity projection.
 41: 
 42:         Args:
 43:             node (Relational): The node to check for identity projection.
 44: 
 45:         Returns:
 46:             Relational: The new node with the identity projection removed.
 47:         """
 48:         if isinstance(node, Project) and node.is_identity():
 49:             return node.inputs[0]
 50:         else:
 51:             return node
 52: 
 53:     def _prune_node_columns(
 54:         self, node: RelationalNode, kept_columns: set[str]
 55:     ) -> tuple[RelationalNode, set[CorrelatedReference]]:
 56:         """
 57:         Prune the columns for a subtree starting at this node.
 58: 
 59:         Args:
 60:             node (Relational): The node to prune columns from.
 61:             kept_columns (set[str]): The columns to keep.
 62: 
 63:         Returns:
 64:             Relational: The new node with pruned columns. Its input may also
 65:                 be changed if columns were pruned from it.
 66:         """
 67:         # Prune columns from the node.
 68:         if isinstance(node, Aggregate):
 69:             # Avoid pruning keys from an aggregate node. In the future we may
 70:             # want to decouple the keys from the columns so not all keys need to
 71:             # be present in the output.
 72:             required_columns = set(node.keys.keys())
 73:         else:
 74:             required_columns = set()
 75:         columns = {
 76:             name: expr
 77:             for name, expr in node.columns.items()
 78:             if name in kept_columns or name in required_columns
 79:         }
 80: 
 81:         # Update the columns.
 82:         new_node = node.copy(columns=columns)
 83: 
 84:         # Find all the identifiers referenced by the the current node.
 85:         self._finder_dispatcher.reset()
 86:         new_node.accept(self._finder_dispatcher)
 87:         found_identifiers: set[ColumnReference] = (
 88:             self._column_finder.get_column_references()
 89:         )
 90: 
 91:         # Determine which identifiers to pass to each input.
 92:         new_inputs: list[RelationalNode] = []
 93:         # Note: The ColumnPruner should only be run when all input names are
 94:         # still present in the columns.
 95:         # Iterate over the inputs in reverse order so that the source of
 96:         # correlated data is pruned last, since it will need to account for
 97:         # any correlated references in the later inputs.
 98:         correl_refs: set[CorrelatedReference] = set()
 99:         for i, default_input_name in reversed(
100:             list(enumerate(new_node.default_input_aliases))
101:         ):
102:             s: set[str] = set()
103:             input_node: RelationalNode = node.inputs[i]
104:             for identifier in found_identifiers:
105:                 if identifier.input_name == default_input_name:
106:                     s.add(identifier.name)
107:             if (
108:                 isinstance(new_node, Join)
109:                 and i == 0
110:                 and new_node.correl_name is not None
111:             ):
112:                 for correl_ref in correl_refs:
113:                     if correl_ref.correl_name == new_node.correl_name:
114:                         s.add(correl_ref.name)
115:             new_input_node, new_correl_refs = self._prune_node_columns(input_node, s)
116:             new_inputs.append(new_input_node)
117:             if i == len(node.inputs) - 1:
118:                 correl_refs = new_correl_refs
119:             else:
120:                 correl_refs.update(new_correl_refs)
121:         new_inputs.reverse()
122: 
123:         # Find all the correlated references in the new node.
124:         self._correl_dispatcher.reset()
125:         new_node.accept(self._correl_dispatcher)
126:         found_correl_refs: set[CorrelatedReference] = (
127:             self._correl_finder.get_correlated_references()
128:         )
129:         correl_refs.update(found_correl_refs)
130: 
131:         # Determine the new node.
132:         output = new_node.copy(inputs=new_inputs)
133:         output = self._prune_identity_project(output)
134:         # Special case: replace empty aggregation with VALUES () if possible.
135:         if (
136:             isinstance(output, Aggregate)
137:             and len(output.keys) == 0
138:             and len(output.aggregations) == 0
139:         ):
140:             return EmptySingleton(), correl_refs
141:         # Special case: replace join where LHS is VALUES () with the RHS if
142:         # possible.
143:         if (
144:             isinstance(output, Join)
145:             and isinstance(output.inputs[0], EmptySingleton)
146:             and output.join_types in ([JoinType.INNER], [JoinType.LEFT])
147:         ):
148:             return output.inputs[1], correl_refs
149: 
150:         # Special case: replace LEFT join where RHS is unused with LHS (only
151:         # possible if the join is used to bring 1:1 data into the rows of the
152:         # LHS, which is unecessary if no data is being brought).
153:         if isinstance(output, Join) and output.join_types == [JoinType.LEFT]:
154:             uses_rhs: bool = False
155:             for column in output.columns.values():
156:                 if (
157:                     isinstance(column, ColumnReference)
158:                     and column.input_name == output.default_input_aliases[1]
159:                 ):
160:                     uses_rhs = True
161:                     break
162:             if not uses_rhs:
163:                 new_columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression] = {}
164:                 for column_name, column_val in output.columns.items():
165:                     assert isinstance(column_val, ColumnReference)
166:                     new_columns[column_name] = output.inputs[0].columns[column_val.name]
167:                 if isinstance(output.inputs[0], Aggregate):
168:                     for key in output.inputs[0].keys:
169:                         new_columns[key] = output.inputs[0].keys[key]
170:                 output = output.inputs[0].copy(columns=new_columns)
171: 
172:         return output, correl_refs
173: 
174:     def prune_unused_columns(self, root: RelationalRoot) -> RelationalRoot:
175:         """
176:         Prune columns that are unused in each relational expression.
177: 
178:         Args:
179:             root (RelationalRoot): The tree root to prune columns from.
180: 
181:         Returns:
182:             RelationalRoot: The root after updating all inputs.
183:         """
184:         new_root, _ = self._prune_node_columns(root, set(root.columns.keys()))
185:         assert isinstance(new_root, RelationalRoot), "Expected a root node."
186:         return new_root
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/empty_singleton.py
````python
 1: """
 2: This file contains the relational implementation for an dummy relational node
 3: with 1 row and 0 columns.
 4: """
 5: 
 6: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import (
 7:     RelationalExpression,
 8: )
 9: 
10: from .abstract_node import RelationalNode
11: 
12: 
13: class EmptySingleton(RelationalNode):
14:     """
15:     A node in the relational tree representing a constant table with 1 row and
16:     0 columns, for use in cases such as `SELECT 42 as A from (VALUES())`
17:     """
18: 
19:     def __init__(self) -> None:
20:         super().__init__({})
21: 
22:     @property
23:     def inputs(self) -> list[RelationalNode]:
24:         return []
25: 
26:     def node_equals(self, other: RelationalNode) -> bool:
27:         return isinstance(other, EmptySingleton)
28: 
29:     def to_string(self, compact: bool = False) -> str:
30:         return "EMPTYSINGLETON()"
31: 
32:     def accept(self, visitor: "RelationalVisitor") -> None:  # type: ignore # noqa
33:         return visitor.visit_empty_singleton(self)
34: 
35:     def node_copy(
36:         self,
37:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
38:         inputs: list[RelationalNode],
39:     ) -> RelationalNode:
40:         assert len(columns) == 0, "EmptySingleton has no columns"
41:         assert len(inputs) == 0, "EmptySingleton has no inputs"
42:         return EmptySingleton()
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/filter.py
````python
 1: """
 2: This file contains the relational implementation for a "filter". This is our
 3: relational representation statements that map to where, having, or qualify
 4: in SQL.
 5: """
 6: 
 7: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import RelationalExpression
 8: from pydough.types.boolean_type import BooleanType
 9: 
10: from .abstract_node import RelationalNode
11: from .single_relational import SingleRelational
12: 
13: 
14: class Filter(SingleRelational):
15:     """
16:     The Filter node in the relational tree. This generally represents all the possible
17:     locations where filtering can be applied.
18:     """
19: 
20:     def __init__(
21:         self,
22:         input: RelationalNode,
23:         condition: RelationalExpression,
24:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
25:     ) -> None:
26:         super().__init__(input, columns)
27:         assert isinstance(condition.data_type, BooleanType), (
28:             "Filter condition must be a boolean type"
29:         )
30:         self._condition: RelationalExpression = condition
31: 
32:     @property
33:     def condition(self) -> RelationalExpression:
34:         """
35:         The condition that is being filtered on.
36:         """
37:         return self._condition
38: 
39:     def node_equals(self, other: RelationalNode) -> bool:
40:         return (
41:             isinstance(other, Filter)
42:             and self.condition == other.condition
43:             and super().node_equals(other)
44:         )
45: 
46:     def to_string(self, compact: bool = False) -> str:
47:         return f"FILTER(condition={self.condition.to_string(compact)}, columns={self.make_column_string(self.columns, compact)})"
48: 
49:     def accept(self, visitor: "RelationalVisitor") -> None:  # type: ignore # noqa
50:         visitor.visit_filter(self)
51: 
52:     def node_copy(
53:         self,
54:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
55:         inputs: list[RelationalNode],
56:     ) -> RelationalNode:
57:         assert len(inputs) == 1, "Filter node should have exactly one input"
58:         return Filter(inputs[0], self.condition, columns)
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/join_type_relational_visitor.py
````python
 1: """
 2: The visitor pattern for collecting join types from the relational tree.
 3: """
 4: 
 5: from .aggregate import Aggregate
 6: from .empty_singleton import EmptySingleton
 7: from .filter import Filter
 8: from .join import Join, JoinType
 9: from .limit import Limit
10: from .project import Project
11: from .relational_root import RelationalRoot
12: from .relational_visitor import RelationalVisitor
13: from .scan import Scan
14: 
15: __all__ = ["JoinTypeRelationalVisitor"]
16: 
17: 
18: class JoinTypeRelationalVisitor(RelationalVisitor):
19:     """
20:     A visitor pattern implementation that traverses the relational tree
21:     and collects only join types.
22:     """
23: 
24:     def __init__(self) -> None:
25:         # Track join types
26:         self._join_types: set[JoinType] = set()
27: 
28:     def reset(self) -> None:
29:         self._join_types = set()
30: 
31:     def visit_inputs(self, node) -> None:
32:         for child in node.inputs:
33:             child.accept(self)
34: 
35:     def visit_scan(self, scan: Scan) -> None:
36:         pass
37: 
38:     def visit_join(self, join: Join) -> None:
39:         """
40:         Visit a Join node, collecting join types.
41: 
42:         Args:
43:             join: The join node to visit.
44:         """
45:         # Store the join types
46:         for join_type in join.join_types:
47:             self._join_types.add(join_type)
48: 
49:         self.visit_inputs(join)
50: 
51:     def visit_project(self, project: Project) -> None:
52:         self.visit_inputs(project)
53: 
54:     def visit_filter(self, filter: Filter) -> None:
55:         self.visit_inputs(filter)
56: 
57:     def visit_aggregate(self, aggregate: Aggregate) -> None:
58:         self.visit_inputs(aggregate)
59: 
60:     def visit_limit(self, limit: Limit) -> None:
61:         self.visit_inputs(limit)
62: 
63:     def visit_empty_singleton(self, singleton: EmptySingleton) -> None:
64:         pass
65: 
66:     def visit_root(self, root: RelationalRoot) -> None:
67:         self.visit_inputs(root)
68: 
69:     def get_join_types(self, root: RelationalRoot) -> set[JoinType]:
70:         """
71:         Collect join types by traversing the relational tree starting from the root.
72: 
73:         Args:
74:             root: The root of the relational tree.
75: 
76:         Returns:
77:             List[JoinType]: A list of join types found in the tree.
78:         """
79:         self.reset()
80:         root.accept(self)
81:         return self._join_types
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/join.py
````python
  1: """
  2: Representation of the a join node in a relational tree.
  3: This node is responsible for holding all types of joins.
  4: """
  5: 
  6: from enum import Enum
  7: 
  8: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import RelationalExpression
  9: from pydough.types.boolean_type import BooleanType
 10: 
 11: from .abstract_node import RelationalNode
 12: 
 13: 
 14: class JoinType(Enum):
 15:     INNER = "inner"
 16:     LEFT = "left"
 17:     RIGHT = "right"
 18:     FULL_OUTER = "full outer"
 19:     ANTI = "anti"
 20:     SEMI = "semi"
 21: 
 22: 
 23: class Join(RelationalNode):
 24:     """
 25:     Relational representation of all join operations. This single
 26:     node can represent multiple joins at once, similar to a multi-join
 27:     in other systems to enable better lowering and easier translation
 28:     from earlier stages in the pipeline.
 29: 
 30:     However, unlike a traditional Multi-Join in most relational algebra
 31:     implementations, this join does not ensure that joins can be reordered
 32:     and provides a specific join ordering that is the only guaranteed
 33:     valid ordering.
 34: 
 35:     In particular if we have 3 inputs A, B, and C, with join types INNER
 36:     and SEMI, then the join ordering is treated as:
 37: 
 38:     (A INNER B) SEMI C
 39: 
 40:     It should be noted that this isn't necessarily the only valid join ordering,
 41:     but this node makes no guarantees that the inputs can be reordered.
 42:     """
 43: 
 44:     def __init__(
 45:         self,
 46:         inputs: list[RelationalNode],
 47:         conditions: list[RelationalExpression],
 48:         join_types: list[JoinType],
 49:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
 50:         correl_name: str | None = None,
 51:     ) -> None:
 52:         super().__init__(columns)
 53:         num_inputs = len(inputs)
 54:         num_conditions = len(conditions)
 55:         num_join_types = len(join_types)
 56:         assert (
 57:             num_inputs >= 2
 58:             and num_conditions == (num_inputs - 1)
 59:             and num_conditions == num_join_types
 60:         ), "Number of inputs, conditions, and join types must be the same"
 61:         self._inputs = inputs
 62:         assert all(isinstance(cond.data_type, BooleanType) for cond in conditions), (
 63:             "Join condition must be a boolean type"
 64:         )
 65:         self._conditions: list[RelationalExpression] = conditions
 66:         self._join_types: list[JoinType] = join_types
 67:         self._correl_name: str | None = correl_name
 68: 
 69:     @property
 70:     def correl_name(self) -> str | None:
 71:         """
 72:         The name used to refer to the first join input when subsequent inputs
 73:         have correlated references.
 74:         """
 75:         return self._correl_name
 76: 
 77:     @property
 78:     def conditions(self) -> list[RelationalExpression]:
 79:         """
 80:         The conditions for the joins.
 81:         """
 82:         return self._conditions
 83: 
 84:     @property
 85:     def join_types(self) -> list[JoinType]:
 86:         """
 87:         The types of the joins.
 88:         """
 89:         return self._join_types
 90: 
 91:     @property
 92:     def inputs(self) -> list[RelationalNode]:
 93:         return self._inputs
 94: 
 95:     @property
 96:     def default_input_aliases(self) -> list[str | None]:
 97:         """
 98:         Provide the default aliases for each input
 99:         to this node. This is used when remapping the
100:         names of each input for differentiating columns.
101: 
102:         Note: The lowering steps are not required to use this alias
103:         and can choose any name they want.
104:         """
105:         return [f"t{i}" for i in range(len(self.inputs))]
106: 
107:     def node_equals(self, other: RelationalNode) -> bool:
108:         return (
109:             isinstance(other, Join)
110:             and self.conditions == other.conditions
111:             and self.join_types == other.join_types
112:             and self.correl_name == other.correl_name
113:             and all(
114:                 self.inputs[i].node_equals(other.inputs[i])
115:                 for i in range(len(self.inputs))
116:             )
117:         )
118: 
119:     def to_string(self, compact: bool = False) -> str:
120:         conditions: list[str] = [cond.to_string(compact) for cond in self.conditions]
121:         correl_suffix = (
122:             "" if self.correl_name is None else f", correl_name={self.correl_name!r}"
123:         )
124:         return f"JOIN(conditions=[{', '.join(conditions)}], types={[t.value for t in self.join_types]}, columns={self.make_column_string(self.columns, compact)}{correl_suffix})"
125: 
126:     def accept(self, visitor: "RelationalVisitor") -> None:  # type: ignore # noqa
127:         visitor.visit_join(self)
128: 
129:     def node_copy(
130:         self,
131:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
132:         inputs: list[RelationalNode],
133:     ) -> RelationalNode:
134:         return Join(inputs, self.conditions, self.join_types, columns, self.correl_name)
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/limit.py
````python
 1: """
 2: This file contains the relational implementation for a "limit" operation.
 3: This is the relational representation of top-n selection and typically depends
 4: on explicit ordering of the input relation.
 5: """
 6: 
 7: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import (
 8:     ExpressionSortInfo,
 9:     RelationalExpression,
10: )
11: from pydough.types.integer_types import IntegerType
12: 
13: from .abstract_node import RelationalNode
14: from .single_relational import SingleRelational
15: 
16: 
17: class Limit(SingleRelational):
18:     """
19:     The Limit node in the relational tree. This node represents any TOP-N
20:     operations in the relational algebra. This operation is dependent on the
21:     orderings of the input relation.
22:     """
23: 
24:     def __init__(
25:         self,
26:         input: RelationalNode,
27:         limit: RelationalExpression,
28:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
29:         orderings: list[ExpressionSortInfo] | None = None,
30:     ) -> None:
31:         super().__init__(input, columns)
32:         # Note: The limit is a relational expression because it should be a constant
33:         # now but in the future could be a more complex expression that may require
34:         # multi-step SQL to successfully evaluate.
35:         assert isinstance(limit.data_type, IntegerType), (
36:             "Limit must be an integer type."
37:         )
38:         self._limit: RelationalExpression = limit
39:         self._orderings: list[ExpressionSortInfo] = (
40:             [] if orderings is None else orderings
41:         )
42: 
43:     @property
44:     def limit(self) -> RelationalExpression:
45:         """
46:         The limit expression for the number of rows to return.
47:         """
48:         return self._limit
49: 
50:     @property
51:     def orderings(self) -> list[ExpressionSortInfo]:
52:         """
53:         The orderings that are used to determine the top-n rows.
54:         """
55:         return self._orderings
56: 
57:     def node_equals(self, other: RelationalNode) -> bool:
58:         return (
59:             isinstance(other, Limit)
60:             and self.limit == other.limit
61:             and self.orderings == other.orderings
62:             and super().node_equals(other)
63:         )
64: 
65:     def to_string(self, compact: bool = False) -> str:
66:         orderings: list[str] = [
67:             ordering.to_string(compact) for ordering in self.orderings
68:         ]
69:         return f"LIMIT(limit={self.limit}, columns={self.make_column_string(self.columns, compact)}, orderings=[{', '.join(orderings)}])"
70: 
71:     def accept(self, visitor: "RelationalVisitor") -> None:  # type: ignore # noqa
72:         return visitor.visit_limit(self)
73: 
74:     def node_copy(
75:         self,
76:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
77:         inputs: list[RelationalNode],
78:     ) -> RelationalNode:
79:         assert len(inputs) == 1, "Limit node should have exactly one input"
80:         return Limit(inputs[0], self.limit, columns, self.orderings)
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/project.py
````python
 1: """
 2: This file contains the relational implementation for a "project". This is our
 3: relational representation for a "calculate" that involves any compute steps and can include
 4: adding or removing columns (as well as technically reordering). In general, we seek to
 5: avoid introducing extra nodes just to reorder or prune columns, so ideally their use
 6: should be sparse.
 7: """
 8: 
 9: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import (
10:     ColumnReference,
11:     RelationalExpression,
12: )
13: 
14: from .abstract_node import RelationalNode
15: from .single_relational import SingleRelational
16: 
17: 
18: class Project(SingleRelational):
19:     """
20:     The Project node in the relational tree. This node represents a "calculate"
21:     in relational algebra, which should involve some "compute" functions and
22:     may involve adding, removing, or reordering columns.
23:     """
24: 
25:     def __init__(
26:         self,
27:         input: RelationalNode,
28:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
29:     ) -> None:
30:         super().__init__(input, columns)
31: 
32:     def node_equals(self, other: RelationalNode) -> bool:
33:         return isinstance(other, Project) and super().node_equals(other)
34: 
35:     def to_string(self, compact: bool = False) -> str:
36:         return f"PROJECT(columns={self.make_column_string(self.columns, compact)})"
37: 
38:     def accept(self, visitor: "RelationalVisitor") -> None:  # type: ignore # noqa
39:         return visitor.visit_project(self)
40: 
41:     def is_identity(self) -> bool:
42:         """
43:         Checks if a project is an identity project. This means that
44:         every column is just a mapping to a column of the same name.
45:         """
46:         return all(
47:             isinstance(val, ColumnReference)
48:             and key == val.name
49:             and val.input_name is None
50:             for key, val in self.columns.items()
51:         )
52: 
53:     def node_copy(
54:         self,
55:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
56:         inputs: list[RelationalNode],
57:     ) -> RelationalNode:
58:         assert len(inputs) == 1, "Project node should have exactly one input"
59:         return Project(inputs[0], columns)
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/README.md
````markdown
  1: # Relational Nodes
  2: 
  3: This subdirectory of the PyDough directory deals with the representation of relational nodes used in the relational tree to build the final SQL query.
  4: 
  5: The relational_nodes module provides functionality to define and manage various relational nodes that can be used within PyDough.
  6: 
  7: ## Available APIs
  8: 
  9: ### [abstract_node.py](abstract_node.py)
 10: 
 11: - `Relational`: The abstract base class for all relational nodes. Each implementation class must define the following:
 12:     - `columns`: The columns of the relational node.
 13:     - `inputs`: The inputs to the relational node.
 14:     - `node_equals`: Determines if two relational nodes are exactly identical.
 15:     - `to_string`: Converts the relational node to a string.
 16:     - `accept`: Visits the relational node with the provided visitor.
 17:     - `node_copy`: Creates a copy of the relational node with the specified columns and inputs.
 18: 
 19: ### [relational_root.py](relational_root.py)
 20: 
 21: - `RelationalRoot`: The root node in any relational tree. This node is responsible for enforcing the final orderings and columns as well as any other traits that impact the shape/display of the final output.
 22: 
 23: ### [single_relational.py](single_relational.py)
 24: 
 25: - `SingleRelational`: The base abstract class for relational nodes that have a single input, such as `Filter`, `Project`, `Limit`.
 26: 
 27: ### [scan.py](scan.py)
 28: 
 29: - `Scan`: The relational node representing a base table in the relational tree.
 30: 
 31: ### [filter.py](filter.py)
 32: 
 33: - `Filter`: The relational node representing a filter operation in the relational tree.
 34: 
 35: ### [project.py](project.py)
 36: 
 37: - `Project`: The relational node representing a project operation in the relational tree.
 38: 
 39: ### [limit.py](limit.py)
 40: 
 41: - `Limit`: The relational node representing a limit operation in the relational tree.
 42: 
 43: ### [join.py](join.py)
 44: 
 45: - `Join`: The relational node representing a join operation in the relational tree.
 46:     - `JoinType`: Enum class used to describe the various types of joins.
 47: 
 48: ### [aggregate.py](aggregate.py)
 49: 
 50: - `Aggregate`: The relational node representing an aggregation operation in the relational tree.
 51: 
 52: ### [empty_singleton.py](empty_singleton.py)
 53: 
 54: - `EmptySingleton`: The relational node representing a constant table with 1 row and 0 columns, used as a base case when converting into relational nodes.
 55: 
 56: ### [column_pruner.py](column_pruner.py)
 57: 
 58: - `ColumnPruner`: Module responsible for pruning columns from relational expressions.
 59: 
 60: ### [relational_visitor.py](relational_visitor.py)
 61: 
 62: - `RelationalVisitor`: The basic Visitor pattern to perform operations across an entire relational tree.
 63: 
 64: ### [relational_expression_dispatcher.py](relational_expression_dispatcher.py)
 65: 
 66: - `RelationalExpressionDispatcher`: Implementation of a visitor that works by visiting every expression for each node.
 67: 
 68: ### [tree_string_visitor.py](tree_string_visitor.py)
 69: 
 70: - `TreeStringVisitor`: Implementation of a visitor that converts relational nodes into a tree string.
 71: 
 72: ### [join_type_relational_visitor.py](join_type_relational_visitor.py)
 73: 
 74: - `JoinTypeRelationalVisitor`: Implementation of a visitor that collects join types from a relational tree.
 75: 
 76: ## Usage
 77: 
 78: To use the relational_nodes module, you can import the necessary classes and call them with the appropriate arguments. For example:
 79: 
 80: ```python
 81: from pydough.relational.relational_nodes import (
 82:     Scan,
 83:     Filter,
 84:     Project,
 85:     Limit,
 86:     Join,
 87:     RelationalRoot,
 88:     JoinType,
 89: )
 90: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import (
 91:     ColumnReference,
 92:     LiteralExpression,
 93: )
 94: from pydough.types import Int64Type, BooleanType
 95: 
 96: # Create a scan node
 97: scan_node = Scan("table_name", {"column_name": ColumnReference("column_name", Int64Type())})
 98: 
 99: # Create a filter node
100: filter_condition = LiteralExpression(True, BooleanType())
101: filter_node = Filter(scan_node, filter_condition, scan_node.columns)
102: 
103: # Create a project node
104: project_node = Project(filter_node, {"column_name": ColumnReference("column_name", Int64Type())})
105: 
106: # Create a limit node
107: limit_expression = LiteralExpression(10, Int64Type())
108: limit_node = Limit(project_node, limit_expression, project_node.columns)
109: 
110: # Create a join node
111: join_condition = LiteralExpression(True, BooleanType())
112: join_node = Join([scan_node, filter_node], [join_condition], [JoinType.INNER], scan_node.columns)
113: 
114: # Create a relational root node
115: root_node = RelationalRoot(limit_node, [("column_name", ColumnReference("column_name", Int64Type()))])
116: 
117: # Convert the root node to a string
118: root_node_str = root_node.to_string()
119: ```
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/relational_expression_dispatcher.py
````python
 1: """
 2: Implementation of a visitor that works by visiting every expression
 3: for each node.
 4: """
 5: 
 6: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import (
 7:     RelationalExpressionVisitor,
 8: )
 9: 
10: from .abstract_node import RelationalNode
11: from .aggregate import Aggregate
12: from .empty_singleton import EmptySingleton
13: from .filter import Filter
14: from .join import Join
15: from .limit import Limit
16: from .project import Project
17: from .relational_root import RelationalRoot
18: from .relational_visitor import RelationalVisitor
19: from .scan import Scan
20: 
21: __all__ = ["RelationalExpressionDispatcher"]
22: 
23: 
24: class RelationalExpressionDispatcher(RelationalVisitor):
25:     """
26:     Applies some expression visitor to each expression in the relational tree.
27:     """
28: 
29:     def __init__(
30:         self, expr_visitor: RelationalExpressionVisitor, recurse: bool
31:     ) -> None:
32:         self._expr_visitor: RelationalExpressionVisitor = expr_visitor
33:         self._recurse: bool = recurse
34: 
35:     def reset(self) -> None:
36:         self._expr_visitor.reset()
37: 
38:     def get_expr_visitor(self) -> RelationalExpressionVisitor:
39:         return self._expr_visitor
40: 
41:     def visit_common(self, node: RelationalNode) -> None:
42:         """
43:         Applies a visit common to each node.
44:         """
45:         if self._recurse:
46:             self.visit_inputs(node)
47:         for expr in node.columns.values():
48:             expr.accept(self._expr_visitor)
49: 
50:     def visit_scan(self, scan: Scan) -> None:
51:         self.visit_common(scan)
52: 
53:     def visit_join(self, join: Join) -> None:
54:         self.visit_common(join)
55:         for cond in join.conditions:
56:             cond.accept(self._expr_visitor)
57: 
58:     def visit_project(self, project: Project) -> None:
59:         self.visit_common(project)
60: 
61:     def visit_filter(self, filter: Filter) -> None:
62:         self.visit_common(filter)
63:         filter.condition.accept(self._expr_visitor)
64: 
65:     def visit_aggregate(self, aggregate: Aggregate) -> None:
66:         self.visit_common(aggregate)
67: 
68:     def visit_limit(self, limit: Limit) -> None:
69:         self.visit_common(limit)
70:         limit.limit.accept(self._expr_visitor)
71:         for order in limit.orderings:
72:             order.expr.accept(self._expr_visitor)
73: 
74:     def visit_empty_singleton(self, singleton: EmptySingleton) -> None:
75:         pass
76: 
77:     def visit_root(self, root: RelationalRoot) -> None:
78:         self.visit_common(root)
79:         for order in root.orderings:
80:             order.expr.accept(self._expr_visitor)
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/relational_root.py
````python
 1: """
 2: Representation of the root node for the final output of a relational tree.
 3: This node is responsible for enforcing the final orderings and columns as well
 4: as any other traits that impact the shape/display of the final output.
 5: """
 6: 
 7: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import (
 8:     ExpressionSortInfo,
 9:     RelationalExpression,
10: )
11: 
12: from .abstract_node import RelationalNode
13: from .single_relational import SingleRelational
14: 
15: 
16: class RelationalRoot(SingleRelational):
17:     """
18:     The Root node in any relational tree. At the SQL conversion step it
19:     needs to ensure that columns are in the correct order and any
20:     orderings/traits are enforced.
21:     """
22: 
23:     def __init__(
24:         self,
25:         input: RelationalNode,
26:         ordered_columns: list[tuple[str, RelationalExpression]],
27:         orderings: list[ExpressionSortInfo] | None = None,
28:     ) -> None:
29:         columns = dict(ordered_columns)
30:         assert len(columns) == len(ordered_columns), (
31:             "Duplicate column names found in root."
32:         )
33:         super().__init__(input, columns)
34:         self._ordered_columns: list[tuple[str, RelationalExpression]] = ordered_columns
35:         self._orderings: list[ExpressionSortInfo] = (
36:             [] if orderings is None else orderings
37:         )
38: 
39:     @property
40:     def ordered_columns(self) -> list[tuple[str, RelationalExpression]]:
41:         """
42:         The columns in the final order that the output should be in.
43:         """
44:         return self._ordered_columns
45: 
46:     @property
47:     def orderings(self) -> list[ExpressionSortInfo]:
48:         """
49:         The orderings that are used to determine the final output order if
50:         any.
51:         """
52:         return self._orderings
53: 
54:     def node_equals(self, other: RelationalNode) -> bool:
55:         return (
56:             isinstance(other, RelationalRoot)
57:             and self.ordered_columns == other.ordered_columns
58:             and self.orderings == other.orderings
59:             and super().node_equals(other)
60:         )
61: 
62:     def to_string(self, compact: bool = False) -> str:
63:         columns: list[str] = [
64:             f"({name!r}, {col.to_string(compact)})"
65:             for name, col in self.ordered_columns
66:         ]
67:         orderings: list[str] = [
68:             ordering.to_string(compact) for ordering in self.orderings
69:         ]
70:         return (
71:             f"ROOT(columns=[{', '.join(columns)}], orderings=[{', '.join(orderings)}])"
72:         )
73: 
74:     def accept(self, visitor: "RelationalVisitor") -> None:  # type: ignore # noqa
75:         visitor.visit_root(self)
76: 
77:     def node_copy(
78:         self,
79:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
80:         inputs: list[RelationalNode],
81:     ) -> RelationalNode:
82:         assert len(inputs) == 1, "Root node should have exactly one input"
83:         assert columns == self.columns, "Root columns should not be modified"
84:         return RelationalRoot(inputs[0], self.ordered_columns, self.orderings)
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/relational_visitor.py
````python
  1: """
  2: The basic Visitor pattern to perform operations across an entire
  3: Relational tree. The primary motivation of this module is to allow
  4: associating lowering the Relational nodes into a specific backend
  5: in a single class, but this can also be used for any other tree based
  6: operations (e.g. string generation).
  7: """
  8: 
  9: from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
 10: 
 11: from .aggregate import Aggregate
 12: from .empty_singleton import EmptySingleton
 13: from .filter import Filter
 14: from .join import Join
 15: from .limit import Limit
 16: from .project import Project
 17: from .relational_root import RelationalRoot
 18: from .scan import Scan
 19: 
 20: __all__ = ["RelationalVisitor"]
 21: 
 22: 
 23: class RelationalVisitor(ABC):
 24:     """
 25:     High level implementation of a visitor pattern with 1 visit
 26:     operation per core node type.
 27: 
 28:     Each subclass should provide an initial method that is responsible
 29:     for returning the desired result and optionally initializing the tree
 30:     traversal. All visit operations should only update internal state.
 31:     """
 32: 
 33:     @abstractmethod
 34:     def reset(self) -> None:
 35:         """
 36:         Clear any internal state to allow reusing this visitor.
 37:         """
 38: 
 39:     def visit_inputs(self, node) -> None:
 40:         """
 41:         Visit all inputs of the provided node. This is a helper method
 42:         to avoid repeating the same code in each visit method.
 43: 
 44:         Args:
 45:             node (Relational): The node whose inputs should be visited.
 46:         """
 47:         for child in node.inputs:
 48:             child.accept(self)
 49: 
 50:     @abstractmethod
 51:     def visit_scan(self, scan: Scan) -> None:
 52:         """
 53:         Visit a Scan node.
 54: 
 55:         Args:
 56:             scan (Scan): The scan node to visit.
 57:         """
 58: 
 59:     @abstractmethod
 60:     def visit_join(self, join: Join) -> None:
 61:         """
 62:         Visit a Join node.
 63: 
 64:         Args:
 65:             join (Join): The join node to visit.
 66:         """
 67: 
 68:     @abstractmethod
 69:     def visit_project(self, project: Project) -> None:
 70:         """
 71:         Visit a Project node.
 72: 
 73:         Args:
 74:             project (Project): The project node to visit.
 75:         """
 76: 
 77:     @abstractmethod
 78:     def visit_filter(self, filter: Filter) -> None:
 79:         """
 80:         Visit a filter node.
 81: 
 82:         Args:
 83:             filter (Filter): The filter node to visit.
 84:         """
 85: 
 86:     @abstractmethod
 87:     def visit_aggregate(self, aggregate: Aggregate) -> None:
 88:         """
 89:         Visit an Aggregate node.
 90: 
 91:         Args:
 92:             aggregate (Aggregate): The aggregate node to visit.
 93:         """
 94: 
 95:     @abstractmethod
 96:     def visit_limit(self, limit: Limit) -> None:
 97:         """
 98:         Visit a Limit node.
 99: 
100:         Args:
101:             limit (Limit): The limit node to visit.
102:         """
103: 
104:     @abstractmethod
105:     def visit_empty_singleton(self, singleton: EmptySingleton) -> None:
106:         """
107:         Visit an EmptySingleton node.
108: 
109:         Args:
110:             singleton (EmptySingleton): The empty singleton node to visit.
111:         """
112: 
113:     @abstractmethod
114:     def visit_root(self, root: RelationalRoot) -> None:
115:         """
116:         Visit a root node.
117: 
118:         Args:
119:             root (Root): The root node to visit.
120:         """
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/scan.py
````python
 1: """
 2: This file contains the relational implementation for a "scan" node, which generally
 3: represents any "base table" in relational algebra. As we expand to more types of
 4: "tables" (e.g. constant table, in memory table) this Scan node may serve as a parent
 5: class for more specific implementations.
 6: """
 7: 
 8: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import (
 9:     RelationalExpression,
10: )
11: 
12: from .abstract_node import RelationalNode
13: 
14: 
15: class Scan(RelationalNode):
16:     """
17:     The Scan node in the relational tree. Right now these refer to tables
18:     stored within a provided database connection with is assumed to be singular
19:     and always available.
20:     """
21: 
22:     def __init__(
23:         self,
24:         table_name: str,
25:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
26:         unique_sets: set[frozenset[str]] | None = None,
27:     ) -> None:
28:         super().__init__(columns)
29:         self.table_name: str = table_name
30:         self._unique_sets: set[frozenset[str]] = (
31:             set() if unique_sets is None else unique_sets
32:         )
33: 
34:     @property
35:     def inputs(self) -> list[RelationalNode]:
36:         # A scan is required to be the leaf node of the relational tree.
37:         return []
38: 
39:     @property
40:     def unique_sets(self) -> set[frozenset[str]]:
41:         """
42:         Returns a set of all sets of data columns of the scan that define
43:         a unique row, in terms of the original table columns.
44:         """
45:         return self._unique_sets
46: 
47:     def node_equals(self, other: RelationalNode) -> bool:
48:         return isinstance(other, Scan) and self.table_name == other.table_name
49: 
50:     def accept(self, visitor: "RelationalVisitor") -> None:  # type: ignore # noqa
51:         visitor.visit_scan(self)
52: 
53:     def to_string(self, compact=False) -> str:
54:         return f"SCAN(table={self.table_name}, columns={self.make_column_string(self.columns, compact)})"
55: 
56:     def node_copy(
57:         self,
58:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
59:         inputs: list[RelationalNode],
60:     ) -> RelationalNode:
61:         assert not inputs, "Scan node should have 0 inputs"
62:         return Scan(self.table_name, columns, self._unique_sets)
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/single_relational.py
````python
 1: """
 2: Base abstract class for relational nodes that have a single input.
 3: This is done to reduce code duplication.
 4: """
 5: 
 6: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import RelationalExpression
 7: 
 8: from .abstract_node import RelationalNode
 9: 
10: 
11: class SingleRelational(RelationalNode):
12:     """
13:     Base abstract class for relational nodes that have a single input.
14:     """
15: 
16:     def __init__(
17:         self,
18:         input: RelationalNode,
19:         columns: dict[str, RelationalExpression],
20:     ) -> None:
21:         super().__init__(columns)
22:         self._input: RelationalNode = input
23: 
24:     @property
25:     def inputs(self) -> list[RelationalNode]:
26:         return [self._input]
27: 
28:     @property
29:     def input(self) -> RelationalNode:
30:         return self._input
31: 
32:     def node_equals(self, other: RelationalNode) -> bool:
33:         """
34:         Determine if two relational nodes are exactly identical,
35:         excluding column ordering. This should be extended to avoid
36:         duplicating equality logic shared across relational nodes.
37: 
38:         Args:
39:             other (Relational): The other relational node to compare against.
40: 
41:         Returns:
42:             bool: Are the two relational nodes equal.
43:         """
44:         # TODO: (gh #171) Do we need a fast path for caching the inputs?
45:         return isinstance(other, SingleRelational) and self.input.equals(other.input)
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/relational_nodes/tree_string_visitor.py
````python
 1: """
 2: Definition of a relational tree visitor used to convert relational trees into
 3: a multiline string of their full tree-like representation.
 4: """
 5: 
 6: __all__ = ["RelationalVisitor"]
 7: 
 8: 
 9: from .relational_visitor import RelationalVisitor
10: 
11: 
12: class TreeStringVisitor(RelationalVisitor):
13:     """
14:     RelationalVisitor implementation that converts relational nodes into a tree
15:     string.
16:     """
17: 
18:     def __init__(self):
19:         self.lines: list[str] = []
20:         self.depth = 0
21: 
22:     def visit_node(self, node) -> None:
23:         """
24:         Generic visitor implementation used by visit_xxx methods.
25:         """
26:         self.lines.append(f"{' ' * self.depth}{node.to_string(compact=True)}")
27:         self.depth += 1
28:         self.visit_inputs(node)
29:         self.depth -= 1
30: 
31:     def make_tree_string(self) -> str:
32:         """
33:         Method called after the visitor is run on the entire relational tree to
34:         convert the entire tree to a single tree-like string.
35:         """
36:         return "\n".join(self.lines)
37: 
38:     def reset(self) -> None:
39:         self.lines.clear()
40:         self.depth = 0
41: 
42:     def visit_scan(self, scan) -> None:
43:         self.visit_node(scan)
44: 
45:     def visit_join(self, join) -> None:
46:         self.visit_node(join)
47: 
48:     def visit_project(self, project) -> None:
49:         self.visit_node(project)
50: 
51:     def visit_filter(self, filter) -> None:
52:         self.visit_node(filter)
53: 
54:     def visit_aggregate(self, aggregate) -> None:
55:         self.visit_node(aggregate)
56: 
57:     def visit_limit(self, limit) -> None:
58:         self.visit_node(limit)
59: 
60:     def visit_empty_singleton(self, empty_singleton) -> None:
61:         self.visit_node(empty_singleton)
62: 
63:     def visit_root(self, root) -> None:
64:         self.visit_node(root)
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/README.md
````markdown
  1: # Relational
  2: 
  3: This subdirectory of the PyDough directory deals with the representation and manipulation of relational algebra used to build the final SQL query.
  4: 
  5: The relational module is divided into two main submodules: relational expressions and relational nodes.
  6: 
  7: ## [Relational Expressions](relational_expressions/README.md)
  8: 
  9: The relational_expressions submodule provides functionality to define and manage various relational expressions that can be used within PyDough.
 10: 
 11: ### Available APIs
 12: 
 13: - `RelationalExpression`: The abstract base class for all relational expressions.
 14: - `ColumnReference`: The expression implementation for accessing a column in a relational node.
 15: - `CallExpression`: The expression implementation for calling a function on a relational node.
 16: - `WindowCallExpression`: The expression implementation for calling a window function on relational nodes.
 17: - `LiteralExpression`: The expression implementation for a literal value in a relational node.
 18: - `ExpressionSortInfo`: The representation of ordering for an expression within a relational node.
 19: - `RelationalExpressionVisitor`: The basic Visitor pattern to perform operations across the expression components of a relational tree.
 20: - `ColumnReferenceFinder`: Finds all unique column references in a relational expression.
 21: - `CorrelatedReference`: The expression implementation for accessing a correlated column reference in a relational node.
 22: - `CorrelatedReferenceFinder`: Finds all unique correlated references in a relational expression.
 23: - `RelationalExpressionShuttle`: Specialized form of the visitor pattern that returns a relational expression.
 24: - `ColumnReferenceInputNameModifier`: Shuttle implementation designed to update all uses of a column reference's input name to a new input name based on a dictionary.
 25: 
 26: ### Usage
 27: 
 28: To use the relational_expressions module, you can import the necessary classes and call them with the appropriate arguments. For example:
 29: 
 30: ```python
 31: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import (
 32:     CallExpression,
 33:     ColumnReference,
 34:     LiteralExpression,
 35:     ExpressionSortInfo,
 36:     ColumnReferenceFinder,
 37:     ColumnReferenceInputNameModifier,
 38:     CorrelatedReferenceFinder,
 39:     WindowCallExpression,
 40: )
 41: from pydough.pydough_operators import ADD, RANKING
 42: from pydough.types import Int64Type
 43: 
 44: # Create a column reference
 45: column_ref = ColumnReference("column_name", Int64Type())
 46: 
 47: # Create a literal expression
 48: literal_expr = LiteralExpression(10, Int64Type())
 49: 
 50: # Create a call expression for addition
 51: call_expr = CallExpression(ADD, Int64Type(), [column_ref, literal_expr])
 52: 
 53: # Create an expression sort info
 54: sort_info = ExpressionSortInfo(call_expr, ascending=True, nulls_first=False)
 55: 
 56: # Create a call to a window function
 57: window_call = WindowCallExpression(RANKING, Int64Type(), [], [], [sort_info], {})
 58: 
 59: # Convert the call expression to a string
 60: call_expr_str = call_expr.to_string()
 61: 
 62: # Find all unique column references in the call expression
 63: finder = ColumnReferenceFinder()
 64: call_expr.accept(finder)
 65: unique_column_refs = finder.get_column_references()
 66: 
 67: # Modify the input name of column references in the call expression
 68: modifier = ColumnReferenceInputNameModifier({"old_input_name": "new_input_name"})
 69: modified_call_expr = call_expr.accept_shuttle(modifier)
 70: 
 71: # Find all unique correlated references in the call expression
 72: correlated_finder = CorrelatedReferenceFinder()
 73: call_expr.accept(correlated_finder)
 74: unique_correlated_refs = correlated_finder.get_correlated_references()
 75: ```
 76: 
 77: ## [Relational Nodes](relational_nodes/README.md)
 78: 
 79: The relational_nodes submodule provides functionality to define and manage various relational nodes that can be used within PyDough.
 80: 
 81: ### Available APIs
 82: 
 83: - `Relational`: The abstract base class for all relational nodes.
 84: - `RelationalRoot`: The root node in any relational tree.
 85: - `SingleRelational`: The base abstract class for relational nodes that have a single input.
 86: - `Scan`: The relational node representing a base table in the relational tree.
 87: - `Filter`: The relational node representing a filter operation in the relational tree.
 88: - `Project`: The relational node representing a project operation in the relational tree.
 89: - `Limit`: The relational node representing a limit operation in the relational tree.
 90: - `Join`: The relational node representing a join operation in the relational tree.
 91:     - `JoinType`: Enum class used to describe the various types of joins.
 92: - `Aggregate`: The relational node representing an aggregation operation in the relational tree.
 93: - `EmptySingleton`: The relational node representing a constant table with 1 row and 0 columns.
 94: - `ColumnPruner`: Module responsible for pruning columns from relational expressions.
 95: - `RelationalVisitor`: The basic Visitor pattern to perform operations across an entire relational tree.
 96: - `RelationalExpressionDispatcher`: Implementation of a visitor that works by visiting every expression for each node.
 97: - `TreeStringVisitor`: Implementation of a visitor that converts relational nodes into a tree string.
 98: 
 99: ### Usage
100: 
101: To use the relational_nodes module, you can import the necessary classes and call them with the appropriate arguments. For example:
102: 
103: ```python
104: from pydough.relational.relational_nodes import (
105:     Scan,
106:     Filter,
107:     Project,
108:     Limit,
109:     Join,
110:     RelationalRoot,
111:     JoinType,
112: )
113: from pydough.relational.relational_expressions import (
114:     ColumnReference,
115:     LiteralExpression,
116: )
117: from pydough.types import Int64Type, BooleanType
118: 
119: # Create a scan node
120: scan_node = Scan("table_name", {"column_name": ColumnReference("column_name", Int64Type())})
121: 
122: # Create a filter node
123: filter_condition = LiteralExpression(True, BooleanType())
124: filter_node = Filter(scan_node, filter_condition, scan_node.columns)
125: 
126: # Create a project node
127: project_node = Project(filter_node, {"column_name": ColumnReference("column_name", Int64Type())})
128: 
129: # Create a limit node
130: limit_expression = LiteralExpression(10, Int64Type())
131: limit_node = Limit(project_node, limit_expression, project_node.columns)
132: 
133: # Create a join node
134: join_condition = LiteralExpression(True, BooleanType())
135: join_node = Join([scan_node, filter_node], [join_condition], [JoinType.INNER], scan_node.columns)
136: 
137: # Create a relational root node
138: root_node = RelationalRoot(limit_node, [("column_name", ColumnReference("column_name", Int64Type()))])
139: 
140: # Convert the root node to a string
141: root_node_str = root_node.to_string()
142: ```
143: 
144: ## [Relational Utilities](rel_util.py)
145: 
146: The rel_util file contains a myriad of useful utilities for dealing with relational nodes and relational expressions.
````

## File: PyDough-5ff410e3bbe246a24b52fd56934c7b6c23da3fb0/pydough/relational/rel_util.py
````python
  1: """
  2: A mixture of utility functions for relational nodes and expressions.
  3: """
  4: 
  5: __all__ = [
  6:     "add_expr_uses",
  7:     "bubble_uniqueness",
  8:     "build_filter",
  9:     "contains_window",
 10:     "extract_equijoin_keys",
 11:     "false_when_null_columns",
 12:     "fetch_or_insert",
 13:     "get_conjunctions",
 14:     "only_references_columns",
 15:     "partition_expressions",
 16:     "passthrough_column_mapping",
 17:     "transpose_expression",
 18: ]
 19: 
 20: from collections import defaultdict
 21: from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Mapping
 22: 
 23: import pydough.pydough_operators as pydop
 24: from pydough.types import BooleanType
 25: 
 26: from .relational_expressions import (
 27:     CallExpression,
 28:     ColumnReference,
 29:     CorrelatedReference,
 30:     ExpressionSortInfo,
 31:     LiteralExpression,
 32:     RelationalExpression,
 33:     WindowCallExpression,
 34: )
 35: from .relational_nodes import (
 36:     Filter,
 37:     Join,
 38:     RelationalNode,
 39: )
 40: 
 41: null_propagating_operators = {
 42:     pydop.EQU,
 43:     pydop.LET,
 44:     pydop.LEQ,
 45:     pydop.GRT,
 46:     pydop.GEQ,
 47:     pydop.LET,
 48:     pydop.NEQ,
 49:     pydop.STARTSWITH,
 50:     pydop.ENDSWITH,
 51:     pydop.CONTAINS,
 52:     pydop.LIKE,
 53:     pydop.LOWER,
 54:     pydop.UPPER,
 55:     pydop.LENGTH,
 56:     pydop.YEAR,
 57:     pydop.QUARTER,
 58:     pydop.MONTH,
 59:     pydop.DAY,
 60:     pydop.HOUR,
 61:     pydop.MINUTE,
 62:     pydop.SECOND,
 63:     pydop.DATETIME,
 64:     pydop.DATEDIFF,
 65:     pydop.JOIN_STRINGS,
 66:     pydop.ADD,
 67:     pydop.SUB,
 68:     pydop.MUL,
 69:     pydop.DIV,
 70: }
 71: """
 72: A set of operators with the property that the output is null if any of the
 73: inputs are null.
 74: """
 75: 
 76: 
 77: def get_conjunctions(expr: RelationalExpression) -> set[RelationalExpression]:
 78:     """
 79:     Extract conjunctions from the given expression.
 80: 
 81:     Args:
 82:         `expr`: The expression to extract conjunctions from.
 83: 
 84:     Returns:
 85:         The set of filter conditions whose conjunction forms `expr`.
 86:     """
 87:     if isinstance(expr, LiteralExpression) and expr.value:
 88:         # If the expression is a true literal, there are no predicates as the
 89:         # conjunction is always True.
 90:         return set()
 91:     elif isinstance(expr, CallExpression) and expr.op == pydop.BAN:
 92:         # If the expression is an AND call, flatten to obtain the conjunction
 93:         # by gathering the conjunction of all of the inputs.
 94:         result = set()
 95:         for arg in expr.inputs:
 96:             result.update(get_conjunctions(arg))
 97:         return result
 98:     else:
 99:         # Otherwise, the expression itself is the conjunction.
100:         return {expr}
101: 
102: 
103: def partition_expressions(
104:     expressions: Iterable[RelationalExpression],
105:     predicate: Callable[[RelationalExpression], bool],
106: ) -> tuple[set[RelationalExpression], set[RelationalExpression]]:
107:     """
108:     Partition the given relational expressions into two sets based on the given
109:     predicate.
110: 
111:     Args:
112:         `expressions`: The expressions to partition.
113:         `predicate`: The predicate to use for partitioning.
114: 
115:     Returns:
116:         A tuple of two sets of expressions, the first of expressions that cause
117:         the predicate to return True and the second of the remainder.
118:     """
119:     true_expressions: set[RelationalExpression] = set()
120:     false_expressions: set[RelationalExpression] = set()
121:     for expr in expressions:
122:         if predicate(expr):
123:             true_expressions.add(expr)
124:         else:
125:             false_expressions.add(expr)
126:     return true_expressions, false_expressions
127: 
128: 
129: def only_references_columns(
130:     expr: RelationalExpression, allowed_columns: set[str]
131: ) -> bool:
132:     """
133:     Checks if a relational expression contains only column references from the set of allowed columns.
134: 
135:     Args:
136:         `expr`: The expression to check.
137:         `allowed_columns`: The set of allowed columns.
138: 
139:     Returns:
140:         Whether `expr` meets the criteria.
141:     """
142:     match expr:
143:         case LiteralExpression() | CorrelatedReference():
144:             return True
145:         case ColumnReference():
146:             return expr.name in allowed_columns
147:         case CallExpression():
148:             return all(
149:                 only_references_columns(arg, allowed_columns) for arg in expr.inputs
150:             )
151:         case WindowCallExpression():
152:             return (
153:                 all(
154:                     only_references_columns(arg, allowed_columns) for arg in expr.inputs
155:                 )
156:                 and all(
157:                     only_references_columns(arg, allowed_columns)
158:                     for arg in expr.partition_inputs
159:                 )
160:                 and all(
161:                     only_references_columns(order_arg.expr, allowed_columns)
162:                     for order_arg in expr.order_inputs
163:                 )
164:             )
165:         case _:
166:             raise NotImplementedError(
167:                 f"only_references_columns not implemented for {expr.__class__.__name__}"
168:             )
169: 
170: 
171: def false_when_null_columns(expr: RelationalExpression, null_columns: set[str]) -> bool:
172:     """
173:     Returns whether an expression is guaranteed to be False, as far as a filter
174:     is concerned, if certain columns are null.
175: 
176:     Args:
177:         `expr`: The expression to check.
178:         `null_columns`: The set of columns that are null.
179: 
180:     Returns:
181:         Whether `expr` meets the criteria.
182:     """
183:     match expr:
184:         case LiteralExpression() | CorrelatedReference():
185:             return False
186:         case ColumnReference():
187:             return expr.name in null_columns
188:         case CallExpression():
189:             if expr.op in null_propagating_operators:
190:                 return any(
191:                     false_when_null_columns(arg, null_columns) for arg in expr.inputs
192:                 )
193:             return False
194:         case WindowCallExpression():
195:             return False
196:         case _:
197:             raise NotImplementedError(
198:                 f"false_when_null_columns not implemented for {expr.__class__.__name__}"
199:             )

202: def contains_window(expr: RelationalExpression) -> bool:
203:     """
204:     Returns whether a relational expression contains a window function.
205: 
206:     Args:
207:         `expr`: The expression to check.
208: 
209:     Returns:
210:         Whether `expr` contains a window function.
211:     """
212:     match expr:
213:         case LiteralExpression() | CorrelatedReference() | ColumnReference():
214:             return False
215:         case CallExpression():
216:             return any(contains_window(arg) for arg in expr.inputs)
217:         case WindowCallExpression():
218:             return True
219:         case _:
220:             raise NotImplementedError(
221:                 f"contains_window not implemented for {expr.__class__.__name__}"
222:             )
